incident_description:
On August 3, 2025, a fire nearly started when we attempted to power on our 65 Samsung QN65Q6FNAFXZA. The unit sprayed sparks from the back for about 5-6 seconds and emitted a white/gray smoke. My wife and I were using the product at the time, with our dog on her bed right next to the TV. While there were no injuries, it did result in damage to the dresser it was sitting on.

After this occurred, we immediately contacted Samsung, who then escalated our case to a Specialty Claims department. They then scheduled an appointment for a technician to inspect the unit, but declined to acknowledge that this is a serious safety issue and only offered/recommended a repair and to keep using the TV.

Samsung then closed our ticket saying the TV was working when it isn't, and has also not been responsive even after numerous calls to their customer service line and directly to the rep assigned to our case. We believe it's important for us (and others) to be aware of what could have even caused an issue like this, and we would have hoped that they document and take this issue seriously so that others are not affected or even harmed by a potentially hazardous product.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident posed a significant risk due to the emission of sparks and smoke, potentially causing a fire.

incident_description:
Incident Report: Apple USB-C Charger Burn Injury

What happened that made you want to report?
While using an Apple USB-C charging cord with an approved charging base to charge a [REDACTED] doorbell, the cord overheated to an extreme and unsafe temperature. Upon unplugging it, I sustained a severe burn to my left index finger. The cords connector was dangerously hot, measuring 185F two minutes after unplugging, indicating it was even hotter at the moment of injury. This poses a serious fire and burn hazard.

What type of product(s) were being used?

Apple USB-C charging cord
Approved charging base (compatible with USB-C)
[REDACTED] doorbell device
Who was using the product(s)?
I, the consumer, was using the product.

How were the product(s) being used?
The Apple USB-C cord was plugged into an approved charging base and connected to a [REDACTED] doorbell for charging. This was normal, intended use of the product.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?
Yes. I sustained a burn injury to my left index finger. Additionally, the sudden shock and pain from the burn triggered significant emotional distress, which in turn caused a flare-up of my Crohns disease.

How did any injuries occur?
After noticing the [REDACTED] doorbell was not charging, I unplugged the Apple USB-C cord from the charging base. The metal connector of the cord was extremely hot and caused a severe burn to my left index finger, leaving a visible burn imprint. I immediately dropped the cord due to the pain. Two minutes later, I measured the connector temperature at 185F, confirming the extreme overheating.

The sudden burn caused intense stress and anxiety, which directly exacerbated my Crohns disease. Stress is a known trigger for my condition, and the emotional distress from this incident initiated a flare-up, worsening my overall health beyond the physical burn injury.

Key Safety Concerns

The cord reached a dangerously high temperature during normal use.
The overheating posed a burn hazard and potential fire hazard.
The incident caused both physical injury (burn) and secondary medical complications (Crohns flare due to stress and emotional distress).
This occurred during standard, intended use with approved equipment.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe burn injury, and the likelihood of such an event occurring during normal use is high given the extreme overheating.

About 3 weeks ago I heard noises after she went to bed and I thought she was throwing up in her sleep. I turned her over and she was red sweaty and her lips were blue and she had a blank stare and I got her awake and she was terrified and started to try to get up but was falling all over the place. I took her to the emergency room and was told she had a seizure. She never had one before until recently. I noticed she had been watching something called [REDACTED] recently and also playing with her friends on a virtual reality game meta quest 2. I also noticed that there was a warning that both toy and videos can cause seizures in children who have something called photo sensitivity to light. Point is why can they make toys and entertainment for children that can cause seizures and actually have a toy with such a warning label? I wouldnt take medication that might cause me seizures. incident_description:
I am writing to formally lodge a complaint regarding a burn injury sustained by my son due to a bedwetting alarm device purchased from Amazon, following the recommendation of his pediatrician.
On the advice of our pediatrician, we purchased a wireless bedwetting alarm designed to assist with nighttime enuresis. The device consists of a small moisture sensor placed in the childs underwear and a wireless receiver that vibrates and sounds an alarm when moisture is detected. (2025 New Wireless Bedwetting Alarm for Boys & Girls. Sold by OVEVVE-US. Shipped by AMAZON)
Prior to use, we tested the alarm by placing the sensor under running water. The receiver responded appropriately by vibrating and sounding the alarm, confirming it was functioning as intended.
We used the device for the first time on the evening of August 30th 2025. As instructed in the product manual, we placed the sensor in my sons underwear. My son placed receiver in the waistband of his pajama pants, so he could feel the vibration when the alarm sounded. The manual states: "Place the receiver where the child can hear the alarm. Monitoring begins."  It does not warn against placing the receiver in direct contact with the skin.
My son went to bed at approximately 8:00 PM and slept through the night. Upon waking at 7:30 AM on August 31st 2025, he complained of pain on his left hip. Upon examination, I discovered a deep burn on his skin, approximately 1.5 cm wide, with a blue corrosive stain and an indentation matching the shape of the prongs on the receiver. My son had wet the bed during the night but did not wake up due to being a heavy sleeper, and he remained lying on the receiver until morning.
Upon inspecting the device, I noticed two small metal prongs on the back of the receiver, the side that had been pressed against his skin. These prongs were coated with a blue corrosive substance, which appears to have transferred to and embedded into his skin.
My father, a retired medical doctor with over 30 years of experience, examined the injury and confirmed it to be a third-degree burn, penetrating multiple layers of skin. As of September 5th, the wound still requires daily cleaning and bandage changes, and it is expected to leave a permanent scar.
This incident has caused significant distress and pain to my child, and I am deeply concerned that this product poses a serious safety risk to other children. There was no warning in the product documentation about the potential for burns or the dangers of placing the receiver against the skin.
I am requesting the following:
1.	A formal investigation into the safety of this product.
2.	Immediate review and revision of the products instructions and safety warnings.
3.	Assurance that steps will be taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.
Please advise on the next steps for submitting supporting documentation, including photographs of the injury, and product details.
Thank you for your attention to this serious matter. I look forward to your prompt response
justification: The incident resulted in a third-degree burn, causing significant pain and a permanent scar, making it a severe injury (3). The likelihood is high (4) as the device was used as intended and the injury occurred due to a lack of safety warnings.

incident_description: My daughter and son-in-law gave me a white Anker 733 power bank (model A1651) as a Christmas gift in December 2024. They ordered two it on Amazon - one (white) for me and another (black) for my husband, but he did not need it and gave it away to our married granddaughter (I just warned her about possible danger of this product). Yesterday I plugged the device in a perfectly fine electric outlet in my son's house in Georgia (where we are visiting now but will return to our home in Wisconsin by 3 September) and connected it to my [REDACTED] for charging. In about 10 minutes the power bank began burning emitting lots of horribly smelling (most likely toxic) smoke. Thankfully, I was in the same room with the device, so I immediately unplugged it and took it outside. It was hot and burning so I poured water on it. It is still warm to the touch today and smells badly. If we were upstairs, in the bathroom, in the backyard, or away for a walk at the time of the incident, there could have been a devastating fire.
justification: The power bank's spontaneous combustion posed a significant fire risk, but no injuries occurred due to immediate action.

incident_description:
In December 2023, I recieved a phone battery pack() as a Christmas gift. I used it without issue until January 2025, when in burst into flames while charging at my workplace ([REDACTED]). It caught my clothing on fire, and I was able to pay myself out , unplug it from the power strip the charger it was plugged into, and blow out the fire so that it was only smoldering and not actively on fire. I evacuated with the rest of my lab, was checked out by emts on the scene, and did not immediately show any injuries, though my hands and face had soot from the fire on them, and gave a report to the fire Marshall, who collected my clothes as evidence, as well as the remains of the battery pack. I tried to show them
The item from my Amazon wishlist, but it was no longer sold, and we could tell from the vendor name that it was some Chinese company that did not advertise its contact number to report the incident. Upon returning home, my hands, especially my right hand tingled the rest of the evening, I suspect from either  a mild electric shock from unpluging the item, or from whatever was in the spot from the exploded lithium ion battery pack. My left eye was also sore and watering, so I repeatedly flushed it with water that day, and needed to reapply eye drops for 2 days afterward, and I suspect I had a bit of the soot in my eye. I have since been understandably traumatized and leary of anything containing a lithium battery, particularly while charging. Today, my father (who purchased the item as a gift for me) was emailed by Amazon that there was a recall for the product in question, and informed me I should report it here.
justification: Injuries sustained (tingling hands, sore eye) due to battery pack explosion while charging, despite no immediate visible injuries.

I was charging my Apple iPhone 15 Pro overnight on my bedside table using the official Apple charging cable and adapter. When I woke up in the morning, I reached for the phone and the top-left corner was extremely hot to the touch. The device was so hot it burned my arm when I brushed against it, leaving a red mark.

The overheated corner also left a scorch/burn mark on my bedside table. When I turned the phone on, the screen showed permanent damage in the top-left corner (a black orb with a green ring), consistent with overheating of the display above the logic board/battery.

Since then, the device has repeatedly heated up when charging, drains battery rapidly, and shuts down unexpectedly. I have stopped charging it because of the fire risk, but the phone remains unsafe to use.

This incident caused personal injury (burn to my arm), property damage (burn mark on wooden bedside table), and shows clear signs of product failure. I am reporting this as a serious lithium-ion battery and safety hazard.

incident_description:
I am writing to file a complaint regarding the safety and performance of the Schneider Electric Square D Whole Home Surge Protective Device (SPD), model HEPD80, Serial Number RY2138.

This product, designed to protect an entire home from electrical surges, failed to perform its intended function during a recent lightning event at my residence in [REDACTED]. The failure of this device resulted in significant damage to my downstream electronic equipment.

According to the manufacturer's response to my warranty claim (Claim #[REDACTED]), the device showed "no damage and tested within an acceptable tolerance range." Their position is that a surge must leave a "distinct damage signature" for the warranty to be valid. This suggests a potential product defect: a device that fails to protect but also fails to indicate its failure in a way the manufacturer deems acceptable.

The manufacturer's subsequent statement that they have the right to destroy the returned device, which is the physical evidence of the product's failure, is also concerning. This action prevents an independent evaluation of the product's performance and could hinder future investigations into similar product failures.

My installer, Poss Electric, has experienced similar issues with this company, reporting that the product "never seems to work" and that they have had to fight for partial payments for other clients. This pattern indicates that the failure of this product may not be an isolated incident, but rather a widespread issue affecting consumers nationwide.

The fundamental safety issue is that this product provides a false sense of security. Consumers install this device with the expectation of protection from power surges. When it fails, it leaves valuable electronics and appliances vulnerable, potentially leading to financial loss and creating a false sense of security regarding electrical safety in the home.

I believe an investigation by the CPSC is warranted to determine if the Schneider Electric Square D HEPD80 presents a safety risk to the public and if the manufacturer's claims process is designed to obscure product defects.

Sincerely,

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in significant property damage but no physical injuries, and the likelihood of similar occurrences is high given the installer's experience and the manufacturer's response.

incident_description:
I recently purchased the Samsung Galaxy Buds Pro 3 and have experienced a recurring, harmful issue. When inserting the earbuds, they intermittently produce a loud, sharp popping sound. This sound is sudden and painful, and it causes temporary ringing in my ears each time it happens. The ringing sometimes lasts for several minutes afterward.

This problem has occurred multiple times (roughly every other time I put the earbuds in) and is not the result of misuse. I have the latest firmware installed and have tried disabling Active Noise Cancellation (ANC), Ambient Sound, and other features in the Galaxy Wearable app, but the issue still occurs.

Based on my experience, this appears to be a design flaw in Samsungs noise cancellation and microphone correction system. It seems that the earbuds attempt to automatically adjust or over-correct when detecting interference, which results in an intense and harmful popping sound.

This is a potential hearing safety hazard. Even though I stopped using the product, the effect (ringing in my ears) is strong enough that it caused lingering discomfort. I believe Samsung failed to design this product safely or warn consumers about this risk.
justification: The incident involves temporary injury (ringing in ears) with each occurrence, making it severe despite being non-permanent.

incident_description:
On August 7, 2025, I was wearing an Apple Watch Series 9 with Gold Milanese Loop band while making coffee using a small French press. As I pressed the plunger, the press leaked and sprayed hot coffee onto multiple areas of my body  my face, chest, hip, and left wrist.
All areas except my wrist sustained only minor, likely first-degree burns. However, the burn under the Milanese Loop band was immediate, deep, and severe. The stainless steel mesh rapidly conducted heat and trapped the scalding liquid against my skin. Despite my husband removing the band within seconds, the damage was already done.
Within minutes, a large blister formed on my inner wrist. Over the next few days, the burn worsened, eventually becoming infected. On August 13, 2025 (day 6), I went to [REDACTED] Medical Center in [REDACTED], where I was prescribed antibiotics and referred to a burn unit specialist. Due to cost, I have not been able to attend the specialist appointment.
I believe the material properties and design of the Milanese Loop band greatly increased the severity of my injury compared to Apples other band materials. Stainless steel has a high thermal conductivity (~1416 W/mK) and effusivity (~8000 J/mKs), which causes instant heat transfer to skin. The mesh design retains hot liquid in contact with skin longer, delaying cooling and worsening burns. Apples other band materials (silicone, woven nylon, braided loop, leather) take significantly longer to reach skin burn thresholds and do not trap liquid in the same way.
This hazard is especially concerning because watch bands are worn on the wrist/forearm  areas frequently used when cooking, pouring hot drinks, or working near steam. In my case, the same liquid exposure caused only minor burns to unbanded skin but a deep partial-thickness (second-degree) burn under the Milanese Loop band.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe, second-degree burn and subsequent infection, warranting a severity level of 3.

Dell replaced the GPU and retrieved the failed one. However, the replacement GPU is now showing the same symptoms (freezing, black screens, requires emergency shutdown) and occurs 2-3 times per hour in August 2025.

I believe this is a repeat safety hazard tied to Dell's OEM RTX 3080 design. This defect poses a risk of fire or electrical damage inside the home. I am requesting Dell to escalate this as a systemic issue and not just replace it again with the same model.

When the incident first happened white smoke FILLED my house. I had to evacuate my fianc and our dog and crawl back in to cut the power. Our home smelled like burnt plastic for MONTHS. When Dell responded so promptly telling me they would send a new graphics card and send a out a specialist to install it I figured it was a one off thing and I was happy they resolved it. Now that it is happening again and I am seeing some people online report a similar experience I have reason to believe that they have sold thousands of graphics cards with the wrong capacitor which, under load, bursts and turns into an arc welder starting an electrical fire. 

If you [REDACTED] "White cloud of smoke coming out of aurora alienware" you will see someone else's experience. They had him ship the entire computer in to replace his card.

I recently purchased a new Samsung Smart TV (2025 Model Number QN43Q8FAAFXZA).  I was using the the remote control in my hand when I felt and heard a little pop noise.   I flipped it over because it felt like it came from the back of the remote and discovered that inside of the unit the Solar charging panel has shattered in multiple places.   The shatter patterns looks almost as if it was improperly placed.   Because this device charges via both solar and USBC, the two charging methods are connected internally.   This could pose a major safety threat to users in regards to overheating or possibly worse, resulting in fire damage.  This is not unlike how solar chargers that use a solar panel on top of the battery pack are dangerous because they can cause overheating due to the placement of the battery and the absorption of light energy which radiates heat as well when making contact with the solar panels.   
Under the plastic cover beneath which sits the solar panel, there is now discoloration of the panel with a rainbowing effect to it. 

Remote is still functioning despite this which could result in users being completely unaware of this problem placing them at further risk, especially children and the elderly or disabled.   Device also has grip sensors which could malfunction and cause this as well and could further destabilize the product potentially or be a cause of this occurring if someone grips it too hard etc.    There is no removable battery to prevent further overheating of the device which means the device remains faulty and continuing to pose a risk to all around it should the lithium ion battery combust internally from the heat caused by charging or normal everyday operation.   

The remote has not been dropped, it hasn't been placed in direct sunlight or by windows, and has been only in an air conditioned room.  It does feel slightly warm to the touch.
justification: Potential for severe injury due to fire risk from overheating lithium-ion battery, given the remote's continued functionality despite the damaged solar panel.

incident_description:
I need to report a serious product safety incident involving a replacement
laptop battery I purchased through Amazon:

       *Product Name*: SUNNEAR L18C4PF3 Laptop Battery

       *Date of Purchase*: April 30, 2025

       *Product Link*: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08L7VYFWG?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title

This battery was delivered on May 2, 2025, and was installed in my [REDACTED]
shortly after. About two months later, on July 7, 2025,
it caused a fire in my home while charging. The following is a detailed
incident report outlining the fire, resulting emergency room visit,
property damage, and emotional distress caused by this failure.

On July 7, 2025, at approximately 8:45 PM MT, I was at my desk in my
bedroom with my laptop charging beside me on my bed. Suddenly, the laptop
began to hiss and pop. As I turned my head, smoke started pouring from the
device. Within seconds, the computer violently burst into flames. Flames
approximately 2.5 to 3 feet high erupted from between the laptops lid and
keyboard.

I was so panicked that I do not fully remember how I got the laptop
outside. I acted on instinct, trying to prevent the flames from spreading
through my apartment. I tossed the laptop on the ground just a few feet
away from my apartment. I was shocked didnt suffer physical burns. When I
re-entered, my apartment was filled with thick smoke and the stench of
burning plastic. I immediately opened windows, turned on a couple of air
purifiers, and ran fans to clear the smoke.

My quilt was burned, and my backpack, which had been sitting on my bed, had
a burn hole in the back. I used a wet washcloth to cover the still-smoking
laptop to prevent re-ignition. Shortly after, I began experiencing a tickle
in my chest and a persistent cough that didnt exist before this incident.
I went to the emergency room to be checked for smoke inhalation. The doctor
confirmed irritation in my upper respiratory tract from the smoke exposure.
I can still smell and taste the smoke as I write this.

[REDACTED]  As
a full-time college student, I recently had my work hours reduced, and my
rent increased. I have no idea how I will pay this bill. That laptop was an
important tool for my education, and now I need to find a way to replace it.

After returning from the ER, I found a melted glob of melted plastic on the
rug next to my bed; likely dripped from the laptop as I carried it outside.
This rug has now also been damaged.

Its important to emphasize the seriousness of this incident. I live in a
building shared with six other residents. If I hadnt been present to
respond immediately, the flames could have spread to my bedding and nearby
furniture. My upstairs neighbors later told me they could smell the smoke
in their unit. This was not a minor malfunction. This was a violent,
extremely high-risk failure of a product that should never have been sold.

Since the incident, Ive felt extremely uneasy about using any laptop at
all. As someone who relies heavily on technology for school and work, this
fear is impacting my ability to function normally. The emotional distress
from the fire (and the thought of it happening again) has been weighing on
me.

I want to make it clear that I have never experienced anything like this
with my laptop before (it was originally purchased in early 2020). The
device had always functioned properly until I installed the new SUNNEAR
battery in May 2025. I followed all the instructions that came with the
battery and used it solely for academic and personal purposes. The fire
occurred while it was charging normally. There was no misuse or tampering
involved. This was the first and only time Ive ever seen my device (or any
device for that matter) behave like this, and the only major change leading
up to the incident was the installation of this battery. Ive worked in IT
support and device troubleshooting for the past two years, and Im fully
capable and knowledgeable on the proper installation of hardware components
such as laptop batteries. I handled this installation correctly and
followed all the manufacturer's instructions closely. I am confident the
incident was caused by a failure in the product, and not user error.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (smoke inhalation) and significant property damage, warranting a severity level of 3.

Manufacturer: Zepp Health (Huami)
Where Purchased: Best Buy, Concord Mills, NC
Date of Purchase: June 7, 2025
Date of Injury Onset: Around June 19, 2025

I developed two separate areas of skin irritation after wearing the Amazfit Bip 5 smartwatch for about 12 days. The first issue was on the underside of my wrist where the optical heart-rate sensor sits. It left a round red mark that looked like a mild burn and started to peel. The second reaction happened where the band touched my skin, and that spot became dry and flaky with some lingering irritation.

There wasnt a burning feeling, but both reactions showed up in the exact areas where the device was resting on my skin. The skin is still healing now.

I wore the watch during daily use, and I kept the band clean and dry. I didnt apply any chemicals or soaps, and the fit wasnt too tight. Ive since returned the product to Best Buy and stopped wearing it.

After looking into it, I found several online reviews and forum posts from other users who had similar issues. These included reports of rashes, red marks, and irritation under the sensors or from the watch bands, especially in the Amazfit Bip series.

Im submitting this report to document what happened in case it helps bring attention to a possible product safety concern.
justification: Skin irritation and burns (severity 3) are likely (likelihood 4) due to allergic reaction to the watch materials, as evidenced by similar reports from other users.

incident_description:
My M16R1 Alienware laptop caught fire underneath while using it in normal gaming conditions.  I was sitting on my couch, connected to UK power using an official Alienware slim 330w charger.  The laptop gave off a strange smell of burn soil or other plastics smell.  I shut it down immidiately, removed the power cable, and set it aside.

The smell took 5-10min to stop emanating from the laptop, and a few hours to clear the room.

The next day i opened the rear case of the laptop as normal when doing any sort of SSD or ram upgrades, or fan cleaning using compressed air cans, only to discover melting on the motherboard at the DC ribbon cable that connects the external power jack to the motherboard.  Specifically the end of the ribbon where the motherboard port is.

The melting was extensive enough that an arc flash or fire flash occured leaving a scour mark on the motherboard, but thankfully did not burn me or the laptop tray.

 (I'm a US citizen, the laptop was purchased in the states, is used for game development, gaming, and business while travelling, and transitioning to living abroad)

This flaw in the motherboard design extends to at least 19+ other cases spanning multiple models of this generation of laptop.  Specifically the M16R1 and M18R1 laptops.

In my expanded findings after it happened to me, I noted posts from users indicating the laptop was OFF and PLUGGED IN and still caught fire while folks were out of the house.

My incident it was ON and UNDER USE on my lap, potentially allowing fire to jet towards my genitals through a laptop tray that allowed adequate venting.

The laptop design is flawed in that it is drawing too much current over very small connections too close to eachother on the motherboard connection point feeding from the DC IN ribbon.  The pins may be too small and narrow to handle the expected needs of a combination of a higher end CPU with the max power demand of the 4090 GPU.

In other posts the DC IN barrel jack design is flawed as the inner pin can arc, warp, and then subsequently cause arcing and smoke/fire when a user tries to reinsert it unaware of the initial issues.

There is no safety mechanism or control circuitry at the DC in jack port, or the DC jack cable to prevent an arcing condition, and the design leads to an arcing/melting/fire condition under the laptop due to the flipped motherboard design.

In addition a few users have indicated their batteries exceed hot to touch temperatures during this situation, suggesting that when the power connection melts and breaks the power in, the laptop suddenly draws all available charge from the battery, which is not able to handle a max CPU/GPU load at that time.  This can potentially cause a run away battery fire or motherboard fire event when and if it occurs in conjunction with the charger/DC IN cable failure.

I was lucky i shut mine off fast enough.

There is a unique situation where someone sleeping while running high CPU/GPU load (maybe they fell asleep running VR with the goggles on) or they are out of the house where this product can fail and cause the desk surface to ignite from a failing power connection.

Again the DC IN ribbon connection, the ribbon itself, and the DC jack were not designed to handle the load of this model correctly.  This may be a design that was reused in future models, as I've seen similar posts (only a few so far) indicating repeat conditions.

19 cases. 2 leading to fire risk or damage directly (one burnt couch, one burnt surface)
justification: The incident involved a fire under the laptop while in use, posing a risk of property damage and potential injury, but no injuries were reported.

I would like someone to tell me something other than to go get my vitals checked considering my blood pressure has returned to normal but I still have symptoms.

incident_description:
Incident Description:
I am reporting a serious safety incident involving my Apple MacBook Pro, which caught fire after weeks of abnormal overheating. In addition to the fire itself, I am deeply concerned about Apples refusal to provide any investigation details, technical explanation, or written documentation  effectively leaving the consumer completely unprotected.

Details of the Incident:
On March 13, 2025, my MacBook Pro began overheating to dangerous levels during normal use and charging. It became too hot to touch, and when unplugged, the battery would drain within minutes. The battery health status still reported as Normal, despite these clear signs of malfunction.

On March 28, my husband opened the back panel to check for any visible issue. Upon slightly lifting the battery  with no force or damage involved  it ignited immediately, producing sparks and flames. He ran outside and placed it on our deck, where the fire burned part of the deck surface and filled our home with smoke and fumes.

This was not due to misuse or tampering. We were simply trying to understand the source of the heat after weeks of abnormal behavior. The device caught fire from minimal contact.

Apples Response:
I contacted Apple immediately. I was transferred to their Safety Department, but I received no clear process or safety guidance. I was asked inappropriate questions (e.g., What color was the flame?). When I asked how to handle the remaining battery components before traveling, I was told, I dont know. Call the emergency line. I shipped the laptop to Apple for review and followed up several times. After weeks of no response, I received a final phone call stating:

Apple determined this was not a product failure. No written documentation or investigation results would be provided. I explicitly requested written communication due to the seriousness of the matter. Apple refused. I was told the case would only be handled over the phone. No repair, refund, or replacement would be issued. Apple refuses to disclose their testing process or criteria. I asked for a simple written summary of their findings and was told I will not receive one. The case is closed, and I was shut down.

Why I'm Reporting to the CPSC:
A laptop that catches fire under minimal contact is a serious safety hazard. Apples refusal to document their findings or provide any transparency means there is no way to verify that an investigation occurred at all. There is no consumer protection mechanism in place for incidents like mine  especially when Apple refuses to share any information in writing. If such a small movement can trigger ignition, then any normal handling, bump, or drop could pose similar fire risk to other consumers.

As a result of this failure, Ive also been unable to perform my work duties since this laptop was my primary device.

I am urging the CPSC to investigate Apples handling of this case, evaluate the safety of the battery system involved, and ensure that proper consumer protections and accountability are in place  especially in cases involving fire-related product failures.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (burns to the deck surface) and posed a significant risk to the consumer's home and family.

She called out for the fire extinguisher, but before we could reach it, the battery continued to smoke and started sparking. My daughter grabbed a pair of sweatpants and rushed the battery and charger out of the house. As she threw it to the ground, it began to explode. My son used the fire extinguisher on it, but it continued to explode. We called the fire department, and they fully extinguished it.

Had it not been for my daughter's quick actions, the house might have burned down. Most importantly, we were unaware that lithium batteries could explode and continue to do so until fully extinguished. Thankfully, my daughter was not injured while removing the battery, and only some furniture, clothing, and plants were damaged. Additionally, my asthma was triggered, and I had to stay out of the house for at least 40 minutes to air it out and use my inhaler for the next two weeks. incident_description:
I purchased 2x 200 W USB-PD chargers from eBay seller "[REDACTED]" on December 6, 2024.  I received them on December 20.  They worked for almost two months.

On February 18, 2025, my wife and I woke up at about 2 AM to the smell of burning plastic.  We identified this charger as the cause.  It had apparently burned out by the time we found it.

I had my laptop plugged into the 100W USB-C port at the time.  The charger was in our bedroom.  The laptop battery was fully charged, and the laptop was in S3 suspend; it draws 6 W in this state.  The laptop had discharged to 94% by the time we found this problem.

Based on the charring of the PCB, I believe the charger was actually on fire, not just overheated.  Fortunately, it did not catch anything else on fire.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire hazard, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' (Level 2) with a 'Possible' (Level 3) likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
Amazon.com is selling dangerous and illegal (against NEC) male-to-male power cables, colloquially called
"suicide cables". These are dangerous because when plugged into an electrical outlet the exposed conductors on
the other end of the cable are energized and can shock anybody touching them. Adding to the danger, these
cables are often used to "backfeed" electrical power from a generator into a home electrical outlet instead of
using a safe and legal interlock or transfer switch. The backfed voltage can make its way to the transformer and
be multiplied thousands of times and injure or kill linemen during an outage. Here are examples of these
products on Amazon.com. Many are listed and this is not
exhaustive:www.amazon.com/dp/B0DX6BH6SZ
justification: The sale of 'suicide cables' poses a high likelihood of injury to users and linemen due to their dangerous design and common misuse.

I have singed airways and nasal passageways, making breathing painful as well as a persistent heavy cough. I'm dealing with anxiety and trauma from having what I thought was a safely made product from a reputable company literally blow up in my face. Due to the defective product causing these injuries, I am missing work, I'm in pain and I'm missing events with family and friends. I have talked to several firms, but I keep being told that their retainer fees would take all compensation received. I have also been told by all of them that my claim valid since I have all of the evidence, including a video of the incident, as I have a camera in my home. None of the physicians have been able to give me a length of recovery time, just that the breathing issues could last months, if not longer. They have not given a base timeline on when my eyes will recover or if this may turn into a life-long condition.

incident_description:
I am a cochlear implant user and need to replace four batteries every day. The new child-resistant packaging for these batteries is difficult to open, and the process poses several risks. Due to the packagings tight seal, it requires to use sharp scissors to cut it open. The required circular cutting motion caused sharp plastic shards to fly away, and I cut my finger on the packaging. Additionally, the force required to open the package caused some of the batteries to fly out uncontrollably, posing a sure danger of ingestion to a baby or child, something that was initially only a potential danger.

The old packaging was much more user-friendly, as it allowed us to not only store new batteries safely but also to put used batteries back in the same packaging, helping track their usage and prevent them from being lost. This made the process more efficient and safer overall. The new packaging, however, does not offer this functionality and makes it more difficult and dangerous to handle.

Once the packaging is cut, it becomes sharp and unsafe to carry around in pockets or store near children, as it can easily cause injury. The new design creates an unnecessary safety hazard that the previous packaging did not have.

This packaging is not only child-proof, but also adult-proof, making it dangerous and impractical for people like me who rely on these batteries daily. The excessive difficulty and risk involved in opening the package make it an unsafe design for medical device users.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (cut finger) and posed a high likelihood of ingestion danger to children.

incident_description: I purchased 48-volt lithium batteries from BatteryEVO.com for my [REDACTED] in the spring of 2024.  In October, 2024, the charging unit that I purchased along with the new batteries began to release plumes of smoke from out of the cooling fan port.  I subsequently discovered that internal electronics, including a capacitor were burned out.  BatteryEVO customer service reluctantly agreed to send me a replacement charging unit.  Just 4 months later, while charging my batteries, I walked into my garage and smelled the strong odor of something burning.  I then noticed smoke emanating from the cooling fan of the replacement charge unit.  I made a video recording of the smoke, and then the Arc-fault dedicated circuit breaker in my breaker panel tripped because there was a small arcing fire within the battery charger.  It became obvious to me that there is an engineering defect in these charging units.  I contacted BatteryEVO and explained the situation, and also suggested they contact their supplier/manufacturer of the charger units about this dangerous engineering defect.  Several days later after not hearing back regarding my issue, I called BatteryEVO and was told that they would not issue a working replacement, and apparently, have no intention of taking corrective action regarding this defective device.  It is only a matter of time before one of these charge units burns down a house or business, and potentially kills someone.
justification: The incident involved smoke and fire, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description:
Subject: Safety Report for Magnetic Snap Wireless Charger (Tracking Number [REDACTED])  Fire, Shock, and Mislabeled Power Hazard

Product Details:
		Product Name: Magnetic Snap Wireless Charger
		Tracking Number: [REDACTED]
		Distributed by: Jem Accessories Inc.
		Purchased From: Five Below
		Input/Output Specs (as listed on packaging): 9V/2A, 5V/3A, 12V/1.5A (Output: 5W/7.5W/10W)

Description of the Hazard:

I purchased the Magnetic Snap Wireless Charger from Five Below, and after limited use, the device emitted a burning smell, suggesting a potential electrical short circuit or overheating issue. Upon further inspection, the charger fell apart, revealing twisted, uninsulated wires inside the device. These wires were completely exposed and poorly secured, creating a serious risk of fire and electric shock.

Additionally, I noticed several major safety and compliance issues with the product:
	1.	Invalid FCC ID:
THE FCC ID printed on the product is invalid. Since this is a wireless charger that emits RF energy, it is required by law to have FCC certification.
	2.	Mismatched Power Ratings (10W vs. 15W):
The product packaging states the charger provides 10W output, but the circuit board is labeled for 15W. This indicates a potential overpowering risk if connected to a higher-power USB-C charger, which could lead to overheating, thermal runaway, or fire hazards.

Photos and Evidence:

I have attached photos of the internal wiring showing the twisted, exposed wires, circuit board markings, and the packaging. The mismatched power ratings are clearly visible on the circuit board (labeled 15W) and the product packaging (stating 10W output).

Why This Is a Serious Risk:
		Fire Hazard: The burning smell and exposed wires indicate a serious fire risk. The charger could overheat and ignite, especially during overnight charging or unattended use.
		Electric Shock Hazard: The twisted, uninsulated wires pose a direct risk of electric shock if they come into contact with the metal charging surface or external components.
		Device Damage and Battery Explosion: The mismatched power ratings could result in overpowering connected devices, potentially causing battery swelling, leaks, or explosions.
		Missing FCC Certification: The lack of an FCC ID suggests the product may not meet U.S. regulatory requirements for wireless charging devices.

I respectfully request that the CPSC investigate this product for safety violations and consider issuing a recall to protect consumers. The product poses serious risks of fire, electric shock, and device damage, and the manufacturer and retailer should be notified immediately.
justification: The exposed wires and mismatched power ratings pose a high likelihood of fire or electric shock incidents.

incident_description:
On September 18th 8:06PM a fire occurred in my garage caused by a defective SafPow 42V 2A Battery Charger. The charger was connected to electric scooter and malfunctioned, resulting in a thermal runaway event that led to a fire. The incident caused significant property damage, personal injury, and financial losses.

Sequence of Events:

1. Fire Origin:

The SafPow 42V 2A Battery Charger was actively charging the [REDACTED] electric scooter at the time of the incident.

The charger overheated and caused the scooter's battery to ignite, resulting in a rapidly spreading fire.



2. Spread of Fire:

The fire destroyed a [REDACTED] electric scooter and caused severe damage to three additional scooters stored nearby:

[REDACTED]

Despite attempts to mitigate the damage, all four scooters were declared total losses.



3. Personal Injuries:

While attempting to move the burning [REDACTED] scooter out of the garage to protect my family, I sustained multiple injuries:

Broken Nose: The burning scooter struck me in the face, resulting in a nasal fracture requiring splinting and pain management.

Burns to Both Hands: First-degree burns were sustained while handling the burning scooter.

Facial and Lip Injuries: A deep gash above my upper lip (now a permanent scar) and a bitten-through lower lip requiring antiseptic treatments and healing ointments.

Inhalation of Toxic Fumes: Prolonged exposure to smoke and hazardous fumes emitted during the fire.





Impact and Losses:

Property Damage:

The fire destroyed all four electric scooters, leaving no salvageable parts. The estimated replacement cost for the scooters is $8,898.


Medical Costs:

Out-of-pocket expenses for personal injury care include burn care supplies, wound treatment, nasal fracture care, and protective gear, totaling $165.


Emotional and Physical Strain:

The injuries and incident have had a lasting impact on my physical health, emotional well-being, and ability to conduct daily activities, including managing my business.



Attempts to Resolve:
I have made extensive efforts to contact Amazon regarding this incident. These efforts include speaking to numerous supervisors and managers, being referred to their partners such as [REDACTED], and repeatedly following up with their claims adjusters. Despite my persistence:

The claims adjusters have ceased responding to my inquiries.

Supervisors and managers have been unwilling to engage in direct communication or provide clarity on the resolution process.

Responsibility has been shifted to the third-party seller, despite Amazon's role in facilitating the sale and the product's inclusion in a global recall due to severe fire and burn hazards.


Additional Note:
The SafPow 42V 2A Battery Charger involved in this incident was recalled one week after the fire, underscoring the danger posed by this defective product. The lack of accountability and resolution has exacerbated the financial and emotional toll of this incident.
justification: Injuries sustained while attempting to control the fire caused by a defective product.

incident_description: While investigating a carbon monoxide alarm incident in a residence, I confirmed the presence of high levels of carbon monoxide in the home (garage) using a [REDACTED] gas monitor. When searching for a source for carbon monoxide in the garage, the only possible source appeared to be an 80V Greenworks Pro lithium ion battery that had been left on its charger for several months. There was no notable damage to the battery or charger and there did not appear to be any other problems other than the presence of carbon monoxide in the area. After unplugging the battery charger from AC power and ventilating the garage and rest of the home, there was no return of carbon monoxide to the home. incident_description:
Hello
On November 24th I bought a battery for a heated vest on Amazon ./ ... https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0DDPZX598?ref=ppx_pop_mob_ap_share
I wore it a couple of times as it powered a heated vest. 
On December 4th 2024, I wore the heated vest and battery for work. Got home after work and set it on the table next to my bed to recharge. I went to my bedroom at approximately 9:30pm. I unplugged the battery from the charging cable and left it on the table next to my bed.
At approximately 11pm. This battery spontaneously combusted.
The sound of the battery exploding and fire woke me up. I jumped up and ran from the upstairs bedroom to the garage to get a fire extinguisher. I ran back upstairs to the flames and put out the fire. 
I started a fan blowing the smoke and fire extinguisher contents out the windows.
I went to check on the carpet to make sure the fire was out. I discovered a pile of plastic burnt into the carpet. But it felt hot to the touch, At which point I ran back to the garage and got a hammer to remove the glob melted into the carpet. I discovered burning embers under the glob. I poured water onto this. Then cut out the carpet and carpet pad to confirm it was no longer burning.   

If this battery had exploded at 11AM instead of 11PM my wife and I would have been at work and likely would have lost our house. It's shocking to think a $60 item can destroy your home. 

I have been very disappointed with Amazon for not pulling this product off the site. And disappointed that the Seller has not made contact with me about the request to pull the product. And the requested refund and payment for damages.
Thanks [REDACTED]

incident_description:
TL;DR: A new USB Thumb Drive was, in NORMAL use, running at appx. 120 degrees F. There are numerous complaints about this model's running hot.

Our Church records the audio portion of our services, sermons, and music; for uploading or for shut-ins. Our 16-year old Compact Flash Card (CF) digital-audio recorder stopped working two weeks before Christmas; the company that made it no longer exists. We went to our go-to vendor, B&H Photo. We bought a new digital-audio recorder that can record to SD Cards, to USB Thumb Drives, or to both. We took B&H's CSR's recommendations as to buying media for the new recorder. The SD card worked fine, but we had problems with the USB Thumb Drive, the SanDisk 32GB Ultra Dual Drive Luxe USB 3.1 Flash Drive (USB Type-C / Type-A) (All-Metal Housing), B&H SKU SADDC432GA46. The music staff had problems getting the Thumb Drive recognized by the new recorder. When the Thumb Drive was inserted, the recorder froze up. Wanting to have the option of recording to two mediums, one as a Back-Up, I myself was able to get the new recorder to Format the SanDisk 32GB , and I made two brief recordings. One of ambient noise, the other of my awful piano playing.

(I am an Audio & Music Industry Professional of more than 40 years experience. A recording I produced for my own label was In-Flight Music on Unites States Presidential Aircraft "Air Force One," during the Clinton Presidency. I placed music in a #1 Hollywood Box-Office major-studio film release, and I placed music on the US #1 Daytime Drama. [REDACTED] not only sells, but also offers FREE downloading of my Christmas string-quartet albums. And I am very technically oriented! But I studied Violin, and not Piano.)

To figure out What Was What, I took the the SanDisk 32GB Ultra USB Thumb Drive home. I listened to the two recordings on it, and then I erased it and re-formatted it and transferred two "Known Good Recordings" to it on my desktop, and then I decided to move the SanDisk 32GB to my laptop, to make sure that the "Known Good Recordings" played back on a different computer.

I went to the [REDACTED] and Ejected the SanDisk 32GB from the Desktop. I then grabbed the USB Thumb Drive to take it out of the "USB to Thunderbolt" Adapter, and I yelled. I looked at my index finger to see if it was burned. Not visibly. But this is the worst bad outcome I have ever had with a Consumer Electronics product.

I AM VERY VERY CONCERNED THAT AS THE USB THUMB DRIVE AGES, IT MIGHT GET CLOSER AND CLOSER TO CATCHING FIRE WITH TERRIBLE CONSEQUENCES.

But the temperature of the USB Thumb Drive was perhaps hotter than the kitchen hot water, which is 120 deg F. I used a meat thermometer on it (but I did not spear the USB Drive, because its case is metal) and the meat thermometer, which touched the drive only on one edge, read 102 degrees F. Which, based on experience, is what you would expect from 120 deg F reality.

I was THUNDERSTRUCK that a B&H Photo CSR would recommend a product that had more than 30 totally negative reviews... for running hot. Please go here, and then click on reviews and then pick on the "2 Star"and "1 Star" reviews. "Was so hot I could not touch it. Had to get a towel to pull it out..HOT!" 

B&H's negatively-responding customers tell a sad tale about SanDIsk's "Denial" and "Obfuscation" and "Refusal."

I phoned B&H and very politely (not using some favorite Yiddish words such as [REDACTED]--and I am IRISH!) let them know that I was flabbergasted that B&H's CSRs would recommend to good customers of nearly 20 years standing, a product that bid fair to destroy a laptop, or worse.

B&H issued a return with free shipping.

But, c'mon now. The CSR pretended not to hear me, and changed the subject when I said that I wanted B&H to send a memo to all CSRs, NOT to recommend this product.

So, her reward is... I AM WRITING TO YOU.

BTW, I was very much in the CE (Consumer Electronics) marketplace when a formerly revered US high-end audio electronics manufacturer quietly outsourced an amplifier's manufacturing to China--to boost profits. I was rooting that the result (50 house fires) would totally put them out of business, but it only crippled them. Rats. 
[REDACTED]

Not to make myself totally obnoxious, but... not seeing a future as a violinist or a choral singer, I went to law school ([REDACTED]). I helped [REDACTED] get a new trial for convicted wife-attempted-murderer [REDACTED] (they made a movie out of that case) and I was [REDACTED]. I was co-counsel on the largest Involuntary Bankruptcy in [REDACTED].

Not to brag. But I have an adult frame of reference for these matters.

Between SanDisk's blowing off a legitimate customer complaint and B&H's fecklessly recommending a product they would have known in crap, just from reading their own web site--I think some people need some lessons.

I contacted JBL the manufacture, and Harman International, the parent company of JBL to request help in correcting the faulty (in correcting designed) bracket. No one was willing to correct the faulty bracket, even claiming that it wasnt designed to do what we wanted it to do even though it was clearly stated in the Installation guide that it was indeed supposed to do exactly what we intended it to do.    
In addition the speaker bracket as designed is a safety hazard because if you try to tilt the speaker as intended it will put undo stress on the bracket to the point it could break thereby allowing the 60lbs speaker to fall to the ground possibly injuring or even killing an innocent bystander that happened to be standing or sitting under or near the speaker.

incident_description:
In mid-April 2024, I purchased an HP Dragonfly G4 notebook computer.   It is used only by me, a retiree, for checking email and paying bills.  From the day that I started using the computer, it was behaving very strangely.  It would turn itself off randomly as if the power had dropped.  Sometimes I had to wait 5-10 minutes to restart it.  At night, I would shut it down, and would see the shutting down message on the screen.  In the morning, I would find it on?  I am the only person in the house and I knew I shut it down properly.  Finally, in early October, the computer turned itself off and I could not restart it.  I had used it for only five months on an occasional basis.
The computer was still under warranty.  I went back and forth with HP for about a month.  I was unwilling to send the computer in for repair because there was my personal information on the hard drive.  Since I could not turn it on, I couldnt remove / secure my information.  
I told HP I would send the computer in for repair if I could remove/keep the hard drive with my info on it.  They agreed and send me a video.  I previously worked on computers in my career.  When I opened the cover, I could readily see that there was a thermal event, as evidenced by charring on the connection from the battery to the board.  This could well as caused a fire or explosion in my home.  
I know from my professional experience that once this happens it is virtually impossible to repair the computer because other components of the computer are damaged and weakened.  Often a technician cannot see or diagnose all the damage and the computer will have continuous problems even after repair.  
I told HP what I had found and asked for a refund.  They refused.   So, I paid $1100 plus tax for a useless computer.
In addition, in my many interactions with HP, I noticed they were opening service cases and immediately closing them, even though the issue was unresolved.  I am sure this improves their internal statistics.  
The company is totally unconcerned with the quality and safety of their products.  Prior to this computer, I had an HP laptop and it lasted only two years.  There was a problem with the touchpad sticking.  Many of the internal components in HP computers are cheaply made in China.  I will never buy another HP product again.
justification: Potential for severe injury or property damage due to thermal event, given the computer's tendency to randomly turn off and the likelihood of undetected damage.

incident_description:
This report pertains to a product sold by Amazon in United States. It is called: "NEWDERY for Apple Watch Charger, 10000mAh Portable Charger Power Bank". It's Amazon product page is here: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0BZTXZZ77/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1

Here is what happened. The product was bought in August, in USA where I reside. It was used sporadically in the last 2 months. 
We (my partner, our toddler son, and  I) traveled to Uruguay on September 27, 2024, and are staying until October 10.

At about 4am on October 1, while sleeping in a guest room of a family member's house,
we were woken up by a crackling hissing noise emanating from this Newdery charger (power bank). 
It was spinning around and it was on fire -- thin tongues of flame
were emanating from it. The fire resembled several firecrackers lit at once. It was emanating from the underside
of the unit and was extremely hot. It took us about 10 seconds to (sort of) put the fire out,
while the unit (on its own) was spinning around the floor, like a whirling dervish.  Finally, I used a large
pillow to extinguish the flame and then I carried (holding it between two shoes) the still glowing/hissing/crackling
carcass of the unit to the kitchen sink and immersed it in water. It continued to hiss for another 4-5 seconds.

It is an absolute miracle that the fire started with us being in the room. Otherwise, it would've burned down the entire
house where we were staying. It is also fortunate that the floor was tiled! If it was a linoleum, carpet, or wood floor,
much more damage would have been done. Another miracle is that none of us was burned, though it came close.
The damages amounted to burned sheets, a pillow, a mattress, and quite a few clothes. PLEASE NOTE that we
have photo evidence for all of this.

The entire floor where the unit burned was covered in black soot and the air stunk terribly. All 3 of us
inhaled some of that soot while putting out the fire. 

Also, when we originally went to sleep that night (4 hours before the fire, around 11pm) the unit was left *unplugged*,
meaning that it was not charging anything and it was also not being charged. It was on the floor in the middle
of the room near some of our suitcases  and clothes, but nothing was either touching it or covering it.

I tried to report this dangerous product to Amazon via its normal "product review" feature.
After I submitted a review, Amazon replied with an idiotic
form email saying that the review couldn't be accepted  because "it violated community standards"!!?

I believe it is imperative to (1) notify customers, both past and potential, about this dangerous product
and, (2) stop Amazon from peddling it to people.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the fire caused significant property damage and could have been catastrophic if not contained.

incident_description:
A rechargeable lithium battery exploded in my battery charger. No one was injured. There was no subsequent fire. I will provide details about both the battery and the charging unit.
The battery was an ER14505 size "AA" 3.7V Rechargeable Lithium-Ion cell manufactured by "PKCELL". I do not know if the cell had a Mfg. date or serial/batch info printed on it because the case was severly damaged in the explosion. The cell had no observable defects before being put into the charger. I did not personally purchase the PKCELL batteries, I acquired them from a releative who no longer needed them.
The charger was a [REDACTED]. The charger was purchased by me on February 28, 2024 and had been used about 3 times prior to this incident. This was the first time that I had charged 3.7V ER14505 cells in the unit. Following the incident the charger was intact, with some explosion residue on it. I immediately removed power from the unit, and after reviewing some MSDS information about the potential residue from the explosion the unit has been bagged and retained.
There were four of the "PKCELL" AA batteries in the charger at the time of the incident. The batteries were being charged at a level of 300mA. That charging value was [REDACTED]. 
I was not injured in the explosion, but seconds before it occured my hand and face were inches away from the unit. I was simply VERY lucky! There was no apparent property damage. I had just checked the progress of the charging unit without touching it, took two steps away and it exploded. Thankfully I was on the opposite side of a large vice on my workbench which shielded me from the blast. It was very loud, generated about a 2 foot diameter fireball and quickly filled my garage with acrid smoke setting off the smoke detector across the room. I set up fans to clear the smoke and left the room as quickly as possible. The three other batteries that were in the charger at the time of the explosion were ejected by the force. One of them landed about 8 feet away behind me. The cells that were in the charger next to the one that exploded were not visibly damaged but have also been bagged and will never be used again. The 8 foot ceiling of my garage and my entire work area was splattered with explosion residue (wet black fragments and dust) which I have been carefully removing.
justification: Although no one was injured, the incident resulted in a loud explosion, fireball, and smoke, making it an incident with potential for injury.

incident_description:
Bose QC35 Wireless Headphones radomly turn-on and connect to Cell Phone.  This sounds like a simple technical inconvenience, but it has the effect of silently disabling the audio to/from your cell phone.  When this occurs, you can still initiate a call (e.g. to 911), but then you are unable to hear the dispatcher, and they are unable to hear you.  (Basically, your phone audio is now connected to your QC35 headphones, which may be in a distant room, and you have no idea this is happening.) This is a dangerous defect.
, in that it randomly, but silently, prevents you from completing phone calls, including requests for emergency services (911).  Online forums show that Bose is aware of this issue, and until recently they would replace units with this defect, at the consumers request. There are no longer offering replacements.  But, the random and dangerous nature of this problem warrants a recall.

Report Updated 8/23/24:

This defect allows the QC35 product to silently and randomly disable the audio of a previously-paired cell phone.  If you are a caregiver who relies on a cell phone to reach emergency services (as I am), then you may be unable to communicate with emergency services, yet you will have no idea why.  This can dangerously delay the response time of emergency services, or prevent an emergency response altogether..

Once you are aware of this defect/behavior (which takes some troubleshooting that is beyond the grasp of most users), then you can dispose of the defective device.  But, Bose has made no attempt to notify users of this defect and associated risk.  It seems that it is just a matter of time before a user experiences this outage at a moment when they are engaged in , or attempting to initiate,  a life-or-death call.
justification: The defect can cause injury by preventing users from hearing or being heard during emergency calls, potentially delaying response times or preventing help altogether.

incident_description:
Six years ago I contracted with a local solar panel installer for a rooftop solar system.  I also had them add to that system a 10 kilowatt lithium battery to provide household power backup in the event of a power grid failure.  The battery was from LG Energy Solution and came with a 10 year warranty(Model RESU 10H).
     Three years later LG advised that my battery was part of a lot that was subject to a recall it was coordinating with the CPSC, due to a risk of the battery overheating and causing fire and harmful smoke.  It promised a replacement within a few months, but it actually took two years.  I see that LG was involved with CPSC three separate times for this recall, in 2020, 2021, and 2022.
     About a year later - Thursday, August 1, 2024 - I was summoned to the basement by a smoke alarm, to discover the replacement battery overheating and smoking.  Luckily I was able to contact the solar installer by phone and he guided me through shutting down the system, which cooled down the battery.  He came the next day to remove the battery, and one of the same ones he had installed as part of a solar system for my son.
     I am furious that a major company like LG would subject me or anyone else to this kind of risk, long after it became aware of the problem and said it had been fixed.  It is apparent that despite the documented risk of fire with this model, LG is issuing replacements of it instead of its newer models.  These older models constitute a clear and present danger of fire, without warning, to any household in which they are installed.  I would like LG to be forced to recall all of these batteries for anyone affected, and also refund the $7000 purchase price for me and my son.  Neither of us desire to have another backup battery from LG at this point.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries, but the potential for fire and harmful smoke was high, as demonstrated by the battery overheating and smoking.

Amazon.com is selling dangerous and illegal (against NEC) male-to-male power cables, colloquially called "suicide cables". These are dangerous because when plugged into an electrical outlet the exposed conductors on the other end of the cable are energized and can shock anybody touching them. Adding to the danger, these cables are often used to "backfeed" electrical power from a generator into a home electrical outlet instead of using a safe and legal interlock or transfer switch. The backfed voltage can make its way to the transformer and be multiplied thousands of times and injure or kill linemen during an outage.

Here are examples of these products on Amazon.com. Many are listed and this is not exhaustive:

[REDACTED] 

https://www.amazon.com/Extension-Household-Adapter-Generator-Transfer/dp/B0D6GMF8N6
 3 Prong Dual Male Extension Cord, 12AWG 125V 15A Male to Male Extension Cord, Household Adapter Cable, 21.6" 5-15p Generator Adapter Cords for Transfer Switch (Yellow+Blue)

incident_description:
The Apple iPhone 15 pro max titanium is dangerously defective.  It emits a constant low voltage electrical current constantly even when not connected to a charger, but also when in use.  It is measurable with a multimeter and an oscilloscope.  I have personally had more than one of these devices that have done this, and there are (after some light research) similar complaints online and in my social circle.  When in use it give a constant oscillating voltage that is passed into points of contact, such as your hands.  It starts as a tingle or pulsing, which turns uncomfortable the longer you use it. It causes discomfort and tingling, either stinging or numbness during short term use like a phone call, and when used longer it leads to muscle contractions, a burning/ frostbite like feeling in the hands, arms, etc, loss of tactile function, as well as localized swelling in my situation (i have photos) that takes days to subside, even if/ when you stop using the phone.  There is also a steady drainage of the battery as this occurs which causes the phone to not function as it should in terms of charge time (but that is a non-concern in comparison) . It also gets extremely hot.
Apple refuses to acknowledge the issue and claims it is static electricity when you first complain.  If you pursue the issue they continue to deny it is happening even though employees at the Apple Store (and many other individuals) can feel it happening with the defective devices.  My first phone to do this was eventually replaced when it became such a problem that it started creating errors in the phones function.  It was replaced with the same model, and the new one does exactly the same.  When reported to Apple i was told it cant happen, especially twice, despite my first device being replaced for exactly this issue.  Apple customer support refuses to acknowledge the issue, except for those who will say it is an accepted issue within their threshold of risk.  The associated risk of having electricity transfer from my phone to my body in a way that causes discomfort and tactile problems should be zero.  Their solution is to purchase a heavier case or a different model or brand of  phone.  I shouldnt have to purchase an accessory or anything else to not be hurt by my phone. Especially when I am already using a silicone case from Apple, a glass screen protector, and their mag safe charging system with a surge protector for extra caution.  This has been happening since receiving my first of this model in January 2024  and is currently still happening. My first phone was replaced on May 27th 2024.  It should also be noted that this problem does not fall under their limited warranty, as per customer service.
justification: The incident causes discomfort, tingling, muscle contractions, and localized swelling, leading to loss of tactile function, thus qualifying as an injury.

incident_description: We recently encountered a dangerous situation with an HP Pavilion Notebook/Laptop (model 15-aw053nr) that nearly resulted in an explosion, fire, and personal injury. During normal use, the HP Notebook began to automatically charge its internal battery which had been latently degrading unbeknownst to the consumer. This resulted in a loud pop, a cracked notebook case and a ruptured lithium ion cell. The consumer had just seconds to unplug the notebook and place it on a non-flammable surface; otherwise a burn, fire, or explosion likely would have resulted. Since 2016, internal lithium-ion batteries made for Hewlett Packard devices have been affected by several inherent design and manufacturing issues that substantially affect the safety of consumers. The issues have prompted ongoing and repeated expansions of current battery recalls for HP notebooks. We regularly check the device's notification center and also run the complimentary HP Battery Recall Utility software on a regular basis. The previous industry design standards made it possible for consumers to easily view and proactively remove batteries if showing visible signs of degradation. CPSC needs to investigate the surrounding issues including; (1) The average consumer no longer has access to inspect the device battery,  (2) The notebook continues to automatically charge a degrading internal lithium-ion cell, potentially creating a life threatening situation, (3) the device fails to notify the consumer when the battery is failing, and (4) The notebook fails to detect and automatically cut power to a dangerous battery. We feel as consumers that the agency needs to critically review and update safety and design practices. This needs to ensure the prevention of a devestating catastophe related to these internal lithium-ion batteries, especially considering that these products are designed to be placed on or near the consumer's body. As an individual with disabilities, the consumer received help with this report.
justification: The incident involved a near-explosion and potential fire, resulting in a cracked case and ruptured battery, which could have caused injury.

incident_description:
Two technicians at my work cautioned me to be careful of the battery banks used on carts to charge/power laptops on the move, as they had both been shocked by power on the male wall plug while it wasn't connected to the wall. They described grabbing the plug so they could insert it into the wall receptacles in order to charge them, and getting shocked where their arms would go painfully stiff and numb. No lasting injuries were reported.
This alarmed me and as I have an electrical engineering background, I decided to quickly investigate. What I discovered is that all these units appear to have a design flaw that backfeeds 40-50VAC onto the input male power plugs across the live and ground, and and the neutral and ground prongs of the input cable when the 120VAC output is enabled from the battery pack. There should NEVER be live power of any kind on the charging cord EXCEPT when plugging into the wall to charge the units. I was able to replicate this problem across half a dozen different units so it's extremely unlikely it's a one-off flaw and not an inherent, dangerous design flaw. 40-50VAC is unlikely to permanently injure a healthy person, but this could certainly kill someone with a heart condition or a pacemaker. The products are being used as intended as mobile power supplies.
The units in question are the ALLPOWERS R600 available on Amazon with 4.8 stars. I also discovered checking a number of online databases, that the UL, CE and FCC certification markings on the product are most likely false as I've been unable to find and verify them for this product in any fashion.
justification: The design flaw causing 40-50VAC on the input plug when enabled, poses a high likelihood of injury, especially to those with heart conditions or pacemakers.

On a Thursday afternoon, we suddenly noticed smoke in our kitchen. We were able to identify quickly that the smoke was coming from one of our cabinets. I opened the cabinet and found smoke forcefully flowing out of one of our Ryobi 40V batteries for our lawn mower and string trimmer. I was able to remove the battery to the yard, where the battery began to actually flame and burn. We called the fire department, who advised us to just let it burn out in a fire pit until it exhausted all of the lithium in the battery. 

We suffered some minor smoke damage in our cabinet, as well as some melting of the casing of the other two Ryobi 40V batteries that were in the cabinet. The batteries were all purchased new with new equipment in May of 2023, and used within manufacturer guidelines.  The batteries were kept on the charger only when charging, and removed once they were fully charged. We always stored them off the charger in a kitchen cabinet that is dry and maintained at 68-74 degrees year round. The batteries had stored for the winter and had not been disturbed since Oct/Nov of 2023, so there was no apparent event that would cause the battery to suddenly combust. We were lucky (a) to have been home to notice the smoke and remove the burning battery before it caused a house fire, and (b) to have enough time to research how to extinguish the battery and NOT use a standard fire extinguisher or water on it, which actually makes battery fires worse. If either of these things had gone differently, we could have had a lot more damage or injuries.
justification: Minor property damage occurred, but no injuries were reported due to quick response and correct fire extinguishing method.

incident_description:
The product in question is a power strip that's included with nightstands and other furniture. Upon testing, I determined that the outlets in the power strip are incorrectly wired so that the hot and neutral lines are reversed in the outlets  in the power strip, causing an electrical shock hazard in case of a device that's wired with a metal case connected to the wide blade. I used an electrical outlet tester and confirmed with a multimeter that the small blade on the outlets is connected to the wide blade on the plug, and the wide blade on the outlets is connected to the small blade on the plug.

Of the two I originally ordered, only one was wired incorrectly. I took that one out of service immediately and requested a replacement from the seller. The replacement was also wired incorrectly. I again contacted the seller, and received a second replacement, which is also wired incorrectly.

No one has been injured, because I tested these before putting them in service.

I believe that many furniture products for sale are using power strips from the same vendor, but I haven't acquired others to test.
justification: Although no injuries have occurred, the reversed wiring poses a significant shock hazard, making it likely that someone could be injured if they use a metal-cased device.
