incident_description:
I bought a new 65ÃÂ Samsung QLED tv (model QN65Q90TAFXZA) three weeks ago. Upon turning it on for the first time the setup audio came on, but the screen stayed black. After about 60 seconds there were loud popping noises and smoke started coming out of the top of the housing. I ran over and unplugged it and got my wife to grab one end of it and we rushed it outside as it continued to smoke. We got back inside and my wife was very shaken up. She is currently 13 weeks pregnant and began freaking out about whether breathing in that smoke could have hurt the baby. My entire house also smelled like chemical smoke, so I opened up all the windows (it was below freezing outside) and turned on a box fan. I then called Samsung, and they told me that this is something they take very seriously and I would be contacted within 24 hours by the group that handles this type of thing. 

Two days go by with no call. I call back and they tell me that I was supposed to get a call and they will make sure I do, and that I will definitely get a call in 24-48 hours. Two more days goes by with no call, so I call again asking if they can just transfer me to whoever is supposed to call me. They transfer me and I speak with someone who asks me to explain exactly what happened, then repeats everything I told her back to me to make sure she has all the details. She then asks what resolution IÃÂm looking for. I told her I would like a replacement since the tv caught on fire as soon as I turned it on, and I donÃÂt feel safe with it in my house given what happened. She tells me she will see what they can do, and I will be contacted within 48 hours for next steps.

A few hours later I get a call from a local repair shop saying they have been asked to come look at the tv and see what happened. I schedule an appointment and a few days later a tech comes out to take a look. He opens it up and sure enough one of the connectors on a driver board had caught on fire and melted the connector and board. He plugs the tv back in and the connector starts popping and flaming and says ÃÂYep, thatÃÂs definitely the issueÃÂ. He takes pictures of everything and puts the TV back together and tells me that they will order a new board and once itÃÂs in they will replace the board and it should be good as new. I expressed to him that I donÃÂt want the TV in my house at all. It still stinks like burnt chemicals, and I donÃÂt trust it. At this point I have seen the TV catch fire twice, and I want nothing to do with it. He tells me that he has no say in the matter and IÃÂll have to talk to Samsung about it.

I call Samsung back and tell them I wonÃÂt accept a replacement part and that I donÃÂt feel safe with the TV in my house given that IÃÂve seen it catch on fire twice now. They said that they would put in an inquiry to see if it would be possible to get a replacement, and that I should get a response to the inquiry in 48 hours. This was on Friday. This morning I get a call from Samsung and they say that despite my experience they are only offering to replace the board that caught on fire with a new one, and that their policy does not allow them to provide any other resolution. Despite expressing to them multiple times that we donÃÂt feel safe with the tv in the house, and that weÃÂre already concerned about the smoke exposure to my pregnant wife, they told me that their policy does not offer any other resolution.
justification: The incident resulted in smoke inhalation by the pregnant wife, which could potentially harm the fetus, warranting a severity level of 3.

Frustrated I decided to remove the battery myself and I discovered that the battery was severely swollen, double the original thickness on one cell.  The heat generated by these devices exasperates the problem and sooner or later the other cell was going to swell as well.  This could have caused anything from leaking electrolyte and internal damage to the device to external smoke and heat damage, up to and including a fire hazard.  I have removed the defective battery and the unit is now safe, but the company refused to do anything about it and they are potentially putting people at risk.  The official recommendation I got from their support team was this:  "As you mentioned the possibility of a swollen battery, it's important to note that in such cases, visible signs of swelling would typically be seen on the Cloud Key itself. Since your Cloud Key is still functional, we encourage you to continue using it."  The case is made of 2mm thick aluminum and is incapable of swelling with the battery so there is no possible way aside of disassembly to determine if the problem exists.  Also the fact that they suggest to continue using the device with a known safety defect is alarming.  Instead they should be repairing these under an extended warranty period given they recognized the problem as a design flaw and no longer include batteries in new versions of the product.
justification: Potential fire hazard due to swollen battery, though no immediate incident occurred.

incident_description: Product is ANKER POWERHOUSE 767, ordered from seller "ankerdirect" on EBAY (identifies as FANTASIA TRADING, LLC), apparently a wholly owned subsidiary of ANKER INNOVATIONS LIMITED.  The product is an all in one portable power station (lithium iron phosphate battery pack, inverter, and associated electronics) which controls battery charging and subsequent output of stored energy through an inverter to provide power to household electrical devices which run on alternating current.  It is marketed to people desiring a source of electrical power during a utility power outage (among others).  I first tested the unit by plugging  three devices into it: cable modem, wireless router, and ethernet switch.  The router and switch powered up, the modem ([REDACTED]) did not.  When plugged into a household 120-volt receptacle, the modem powered up normally.  Having extensive electrical experience in my 76 years, I began investigating by plugging in my $5 three-light 120-volt receptacle tester, and found (to my amazement) hot and neutral reversed on this $2000 piece of gear.  An online search of "120 volt receptacle hot neutral reversed" will amply describe why this is incorrect and dangerous, so I won't go into that here.  I then searched online forums to see if anybody was talking about such a problem, and found multiple examples of people with the same experience who had made the company aware of the problem, and received replacement units without the problem.  Others who bought units long after the problem was made known to the company, and supposedly fixed, reported receiving units with the problem.  Apparently, the company produced many units, with the problem built into a random subset of the units, due to inadequate instructions and subsequent testing.  Then the units were sent to multiple stock points.  Upon learning of the problem, the appropriate action by the company would have been a recall and "stop sale" order, since detecting the problem is easy and cheap.  The complicating factors are that the unit weighs 67 pounds, and the packaging is heavy duty and strapped for [REDACTED] shipment, and the multiple stock points.  Opening the shipment units to do the simple test is taxing, so thus far, the company has just continued to ship out units like there is no problem, and replace the problem units as they are identified and returned.  The problem with this approach is that many devices will operate in what appears to be normal fashion, but with the risk of electrical shock that comes with the reversed leads.  The typical customer may have no devices (as I did) that check for the reversal and refuse to power up.  The typical customer will have no experience that leads them to look for such a problem, and no tools to identify it, and will suffer the risk without any warning.
justification: Potential for severe injury due to reversed hot and neutral wires, with a high likelihood of occurrence given the widespread distribution of affected units.

incident_description: As a Fire Chief and Fire Investigator, firefighters responded to a fire in a private, single-family residence for a reported structure fire. Upon the extinguishment, the undersigned conducted an origin and cause investigation for this fire loss. The power bank was not being charged nor charging any other device at the time of the fire any was found on the floor in the bedroom. It was obvious that the device experienced "thermal runaway" and internally exploded (photographs of the device are available by the undersigned). The device was left at the scene so private insurance company could see the cause of the fire. The homeowner reported hearing a "sizzling" noise and shortly thereafter a "boom". The structure filled with smoke and the device ignited Class A combustible materials to burn. No injuries to any civilian or firefighter. The homeowner purchased the device on December 7, 2002.

I disassembled to disconnect the battery management system because it was overheating and I didn't want it to burn my house down (no safe place to store it outside away from structures).
Evidence of overheated components on the battery management circuits.
The battery cells tested ok.  The pack tested ok at 36.2 volts.
No injuries because I took prompt action.
Bosch refuses to cover the warranty.
justification: Potential fire hazard due to overheating battery management system, but no injuries occurred due to prompt action.

incident_description:
Brief summary: I bought some stickers meant to be placed on a cellular phone on Amazon. They are radioactive, emitting beta radiation detectable with a Geiger counter.

- What happened that made you want to report?
I tested the product with a Geiger counter, and found that it emits harmful beta radiation. I used an antique [REDACTED]  Geiger counter, which is capable of detecting Beta and Gamma radiation. A metal shield can be slid into or out of position to block or allow Beta particles, so that only Gamma rays will be measured.
I checked the instrument against its included calibration test source and found it to agree within the specification written on the sticker. I then sampled the background radiation of my living room with the Beta shield open, and found a background activity basically too low to measure with my meter, well below .1 mR/h.
I then placed the instrument's probe with the Beta shield open against the pack of stickers, still in their packaging. My meter measured in the neighborhood of .1mR/h. I then closed the Beta shield on the probe and repeated the test, which was not measurably higher than background radiation again. I can conclude that the stickers emit Beta radiation, but not Gamma radiation.
- What type of product(s) were being used?
The product is a pack of four stickers that CLAIM to "Reduce mobile phone radiation injury on the human brain." They appear to be one of many examples of products marketed towards people who incorrectly believe that the 5G cell phone network is harmful to human health, and that these stickers will somehow prevent this harm.
The name of the Amazon listing of the product I purchased was:
"EMF&5G Blocker 4 pcs for Mobile Phones 2021 Latest Model ÃÂ EMF Protection Cell Phone Stickers - 24K Gold EMF Pro Neutralizer - 5G Mobile Phone Protector - Anti-Radiation 7 Shilds for All Devices"
The URL is here: [REDACTED]
- Who was using the product(s)?
I personally examined the product.
- How were the product(s) being used?
I did not remove the product from its packaging, as I was suspicious that it might be radioactive. I saw a video on YouTube where an electronics hobbyist brought a Geiger counter near a pack of similar "anti-5G" stickers purchased from Amazon, and his instrument recorded a non-trivial amount of ionizing radiation being emitted by the stickers. That video can be viewed here: [REDACTED]

The stickers' packaging RECOMMENDS placing them on appliances and personal electronic devices, including cell phones. Given how cell phones are often kept in close proximity to the human body for extended periods (carried in a clothing pocket, charged on or near a bed overnight, held to the ear for calls), if these stickers were placed on a cell phone, the user would likely receive a concentrated dose of beta radiation near where the device is kept.

Additionally, given that stickers often appeal to children, who may place stickers directly on their own bodies or even ingest stickers, these items present a particularly great risk to children. If a child ate one of these stickers, the radioactive materials present in these stickers may settle in their bodies. The EPA warns that the greatest risk from beta radiation emitters is incurred when particles are inhaled or swallowed.

- Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?
I did not experience any injury. However, sources of ionizing radiation, especially when kept close to the human body, ingested, or inhaled, present health risks due to the ability for ionizing radiation to damage human DNA. As mentioned, I think children would be especially at risk, as you children may sometimes eat small objects, which would cause radioactive material to come to rest in their bodies and present a long-term risk.
- How did any injuries occur?
N/A but see above.
justification: The stickers emit beta radiation, posing a significant health risk, especially to children who may ingest them.

Yesterday (03/24), I was recording a video and the stabilizer function wasn't working well. I mindlessly tried to take my phone out and forgot that I have to be super careful so my fingers aren't pinched. As I tried to expand the arms wide enough, I was holding the stick with my left hand and my phone in my right hand. Since the arms are so bulky, it makes it very hard to maneuver the phone out.

As I pulled my phone out, my pointer finger got trapped on the back between the sliding spring loaded parts near the base. It was pinched so hard that I couldn't easily pull my finger out. Trying to open the clamp with one hand is near impossible, so I would have to yank my finger out as it's being pinched. It took about 15 seconds of sheer panic trying to figure out how to release my finger before I had no choice but to pull it out without lifting the clamp. This caused a raised bruise on my finger and was quite painful.

I should not have to use so much force for an object -- because it is poorly constructed -- that results in pinched fingers every single time. I emailed the company asking for a refund and explained how their product injured me. I did not receive a personalized response addressing the injury, just a generic response on how to return the item.
justification: The incident resulted in a physical injury (raised bruise) and significant pain, warranting a severity level of 3.

The [REDACTED] (product) is a headphone [REDACTED] that allows you to stream [REDACTED] audio over the internet using a computer, phone, or tablet.

Everything below describes what happened in more detail and is a copy of what I sent to the manufacturerÃÂs support team:

I wanted to bring a safety concern to your attention that I have with the [REDACTED]. I also wanted to warn you that IÃÂm going to raise this concern with the US Consumer Product Safety Commission, who can force recalls, so please warn the appropriate business teams on your end as well.

My concern is with the digital volume control and your [REDACTED] feature. On my first day of use with the [REDACTED], three times I experienced the volume suddenly rising to its maximum level, 100%, or close to it. This happened with three different connected devices: a desktop computer, a laptop, and a phone. This has caused an increase in my tinnitus which had otherwise been stable for the last couple decades.

My first question is: can this feature be disabled so that the sole control over the volume is the knob on the [REDACTED]? My second question is: do you have a volume limit feature similar to iOS or other platforms?

As for the instances with the desktop and laptop computers, IÃÂm still not sure of the actions, keystrokes, accidental mouse swipes, or what exactly caused the volume to rise to maximum immediately.

However, I do know how it happened on the iPhone. With the iPhone, there seems to be a delay of a number of seconds between when you click the volume up button on the phone and when the [REDACTED] reacts. Combine that with the fact that one click on the [REDACTED] knob raises the volume by 1db, but one click on the volume button on the phone raises the volume on the [REDACTED] MANY decibelsÃÂ that was the disaster. 1db is insignificant. So I believe, pressed volume up once and heard no changeÃÂ and then pressed it a few more times thinking the volume change was minute per pressÃÂbut it turned out that the volume increase was huge, but just delayed. And then I got full volume. Again.

The safety concern is threefold: (1) damage to human hearing, (2) electronic damage to equipment, and (3) physical damage to equipment. And we know how expensive headphones can get.

Even if it turns out that [REDACTED] can be turned off or the volume can be limited, or both, I still must report this to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission, because this risk is the same for all users when the product comes out of the box at present. But I strongly suggest these two features in future firmware updates if they do not presently exist, and I suggest that something be done so that by default, my experience becomes impossible.

I will most likely return the [REDACTED] to where I bought it if the firmware doesnÃÂt support disabling [REDACTED] and making a volume limit. ItÃÂs a real shame too, because this is the best portable [REDACTED] IÃÂve heard.

Thanks,
[REDACTED]

With an Ohmmeter I checked and found that my AC200MAX had was wired with Reverse Polarity.  

I contacted Bluetti' via phone at their office in Las Vegas and through email correspondence with no satisfaction whatsoever.  I asked them for a replacement product and I was told that they could not guarantee that the replacement unit would not have the same Reverse Polarity issue.  

To sum up:  Bluetti's opening online discount opening offer for the AC200MAX was for a total sale of 500 units "first come first served."  Since Bluetti products are manufactured in China my assumption is that at a minimum, there may very well be 500 of these units out there with that are wired incorrectly with Reverse Polarity which presents the very real danger of serious injury or electrocution resulting in death.  

My AC200MAX still sits unused and with the Reverse Polarity wiring since it was ordered on Aug 20, 2021 and Bluetti.  I have complained to the Nevada Consumer Affairs Commission (since Bluetti's office is in Nevada and I have complained to the Arizona Attorney General's office and thus far I have not received results from either.  

I have exchanged over 40 emails with Bluetti and my AC200MAX still remains dangerous and unusable and I am absolutely sure that there are many hundreds, if not many thousands of the AC200MAX power station out there in consumer's hands that have a lethal potential.  One of my primary goals in all of this is to get Bluetti to issue a recall of said units but after many correspondences with them they are REFUSING to do so.  This to me, shows a blatant disregard for the health and safety of every consumer that owns one of these units in question.

PLEASE NOTE:  that I have in my possession ever correspondence with Bluetti and the preponderance of evidence that I have clearly shows that they know about this serious issue, yet, have refused to correct it by issuing a recall which is the only way to insure the health and safety of their own customers.  I am more than willing to share any or all of this information with your agency upon request.  I might also note that I also have emails from Bluetti stating the "management was negligent."  This statement came from a Bluetti employee in customer service and is entered in part of the record with both agencies that I have complained to. incident_description:
Samsung TV was in use when backlight suddenly stopped working on left side of screen. While on phone with Samsung support with TV on, bottom right of screen became visibily warped with white bubbles. I tried touching the warped area to see if it was something peeling off, but it was extremely hot so I could not keep my finger on the screen at all. The whole right side had become hot, but the bottom right was too hot to touch. No permanent injury, but could have been seriously burned if I kept my finger on there for more than a couple of seconds. Per instructions from Samsung support representative (and instinct), I unplugged the TV within 15 seconds of getting burned. _

I was ending the support call with the Samsung representative when I noticed the warping, and at no point did the representative suggest the backlight failure might be due to a larger issue that would result in a burning or fire hazard. I don't remember if the representative told me to touch the area or if I did so on my own volition, but in any case I was never warned about the possibility of burning or fire while troubleshooting the issue. _

This TV was purchased a little over 3 years ago, so failure like this was unexpected. It was in a good temperature and humidity environment (in living room, away from open windows or direct sunlight, with plenty of space for heat dissipation, frequently dusted off TV stand), and never moved off the TV stand since purchase in November 2018. _

I have a bad photo of the backlight failure, but no photo of the burning screen since I was on the phone with Samsung support when that occurred and immediately unplugged the TV. I can take more photos or videos upon request, but that requires me plugging in the TV again which I have avoided since the fire hazard became clear. _

Other reports to the CPSC and posts on both the US and EU Samsung Members Community forums indicate similar problems on Samsung TVs: extreme overheating, melting screen and plastic in lower-right area, in some cases with actual flames/fire. Some of those other reports mention similar backlight or other failures, followed by overheating or fire.
justification: Potential for serious burn injury was high due to extreme heat, though no permanent injury occurred.

incident_description:
On more than one occasion, but most recently, the 2nd of February, the silicone tips on the Tzumi ProBuds V2 wireless earbuds have become stuck in my ear canal after removal of the earbud from my ear.

The earbuds (purchased from Walmart, though I believe they're sold at [REDACTED] stores as well) come with three sizes of silicone tips, fitted in the package with the standard medium size. After having the medium silicone tips twice get lodged a couple centimeters inside my ear (requiring the use of tweezers to retrieve them, after about a half an hour of trying), I switched to the largest size. This prevents them from getting so far inside my ear, but it is still possible for them to move and become stuck.

The lip around the speaker of the earbud is insufficient to hold onto the silicone piece and the slightest force knocks it loose. For people using these earbuds, especially the medium and small sized silicones, it is not at all difficult for these tips to become loose in the ear canal and get stuck, potentially prompting a hospital visit for removal - it's almost come to that for me, more than once.

These are cheap earbuds, so I don't expect perfection, but I believe this is a valid hazard that people should be made aware of. I own a set of equally priced wired earbuds with a strong retention mechanism - a sort of rubber sleeve the fits snugly around the stem where the speaker is. I think this kind of design is necessary for a safe product that is placed inside your ear.
justification: Potential injury due to silicone tips getting stuck in the ear canal, requiring medical intervention.

incident_description: I am a longtime Samsung product user. I have used their Galaxy  line for years. I own their phones, smart watches, and earbuds, and I upgrade regularly when new devices become available. I have been using the [REDACTED] for almost two years and am very happy with them. For Christmas this year, I asked my husband for the superior Samsung Pro buds. I wore them for about three weeks with giddy happiness until my right ear became infected with an achy sore inside my outer ear underneath the concha, right above my tragus. I've never had this happen before with any earbud ever, and I've used many many different brands in my life so I immediately looked it up after I noticed putting in these Samsung earbuds aggravated the spot. I came across so many instances of the Pro earbuds causing terrible infections in ears that mine seemed lucky not to have caused worse. The trouble seems to be caused by the use of nickel and people being allergic to nickel which I definitely am. I can't use anything in my pierced ears except titanium or sterling silver. Samsung needs to recall these Pro earbuds and re-assess them. No other buds of theirs have caused this problem while the Pro are the most expensive and supposedly "best" earbud they have. I stopped using them for one week until my right ear healed and tried them again. The same injury again occurred. I have now stopped using them altogether and what a shame.
justification: The user experienced an injury (ear infection) due to an allergic reaction to nickel in the earbuds, which has been widely reported for the Samsung Pro buds.

incident_description:
I am manager of a popular computer repair shop.  Over the last few months, we have seen four Lenovo IdeaPad S340-15IWL laptops enter the shop with the same set of problems: all screws inside the laptop are not properly torqued down, and one or more screws from the 2.5" hard disk caddy inside the unit will eventually work their way loose, bounce around inside the chassis, and eventually short something out.  In two cases, it simply shut the computer off and it came back to life after the screw was removed.  In two other cases, it shorted something significant enough that the computer never worked again.  Our concern is that the screw(s) could easily short the battery lines, potentially causing a fire or explosion.  It appears consistent that this line of laptop suffers from manufacturing deficiencies with screws (internal and external) not being properly tightened, so this problem is likely to continue occuring for other people.

We are reporting this problem as "Consumer" as there does not appear to be an option for professionals in a product field.  The address given (for "where it happened" is that of our shop.
justification: Potential for property damage and safety risk due to loose screws causing shorts, with a high likelihood of recurrence based on consistent manufacturing issues.

incident_description:
I purchased a Nest Hello video doorbell approximately 3 years ago.  

This summer, it started rebooting when the button was pressed and not ringing the doorbell.

After searching on-line, I found out there is a lithium ion battery in it that is not documented.  It's sealed in to the product with heavy tape, and not able to be inspected.

Google, Nest is one of their product lines, will not repair a Nest doorbell when it is out of warranty.  

Since the product was not repairable by Google, I ordered a new battery from a reputable supplier, and opened the doorbell.   

The battery in it was not only defective, but was swollen, like the ones about to catch fire.   I saved the battery in a safe place (bucket of sand, outside.)  

Not having a way to inspect a potentially hazardous battery either physically, or via software and not notifying customers of this dangerous situation is the core of my complaint.

In the event of a fire, the doorbell is physically attached to the outside of a house, with low voltage wires penetrating the wall to the inside of the building.  This could  lead to an extremely hazardous situation for the customer since smoke detectors would not detect the initial onset of fire.

Customers might also not be able to address this situation because of:

 1: Not being aware there is a dangerous battery in the product.
 2: Not being able to see the problem since the battery is sealed inside the product.
 3: Not being notified via software that there is a problem with the battery.
 4: Google will not repair the Nest Hello doorbell when it is out of warranty.  This refusal to repair it extends to replacing the battery.

I avoided a fire by being proactive and fixing a product that the manufacturer will not support after warranty.  Others might not be so lucky.
justification: The undocumented, non-replaceable lithium ion battery in the Nest Hello doorbell could potentially cause a fire, posing a significant risk of injury.

incident_description:
I have seen several SONNET branded alarm clock charging stations at IHG Holiday Inn hotels. These clocks pose electrocution danger, fire risk, and show no evidence that they have been tested by UL or verification of FCC part 15 compliance.  I am an electronics engineer, these alarm clocks have 3 prong convenience outlets on the top to connect grounded appliances. However, the supply line cord for the device is two prong and therefore eliminates the ground for any device plugged into the convenience outlets. Furthermore, the line cord on the device is 18AWG which cannot safely carry more than 7 amperes of current. There appears to be no current limiting device on the unit that would prevent someone from plugging in a high powered appliance and seriously overloading the line cord, possibly starting a fire. This scenario is especially feasible in the hotel environment I have seen these devices where housekeeping may be tempted to plug commercial grade vacuum cleaners into the convenience outlets. The user of the vacuum would thereby also be exposed to electrocution should there be a fault in the vacuum. 

I believe these devices are extremely dangerous and should be recalled and removed from sale. 

Device is Sonnet Model R-1414 AM/FM Alarm Clock Radio
justification: The alarm clock's inadequate wiring and lack of safety certifications pose a high risk of electrocution and fire, especially in a hotel environment where high-powered appliances may be used.

This is a problem inherent in the internal design of the device, and as such all examples of two related product models (a 9-outlet and a 12-outlet model) share the defect.

The reseller from which the purchase was made (woot.com) has been clearly notified of the defect by multiple customers, and yet refuses to take the complaints seriously or take down the product listing:

https://electronics.woot.com/offers/aduro-surge-wall-tower-outlet-dual-usb-7?ref=w_gw_zl_bs_1
[REDACTED]
justification: The design defect poses a risk of electrical shock or damage to connected appliances, making it likely that an incident will occur if the product is used.

incident_description:
I had a Surface Book that, through normal use, developed screen yellowing due to excess heat. Turns out the heat was coming from the li-ion battery, which eventually heated and swelled up to the point that it a) melted the glue that kept the screen inside the bezel and b) pushed the screen out of the bezel on that side, bulging it out and leaving a considerable gap.

The battery had been swelling for a very long time before it got to this point, making it impossible to close the laptop flush anymore.

A swollen and overheating li-ion battery is a huge risk that may have led to an explosion, and it likely had been leaking hazardous gasses!

Microsoft was no help at all when I reported the issue, and offered nothing but a discount on another same-model  Surface Book, with no guarantee that it wouldn't be bringing the same hazard into my home again.
justification: The incident involved a swollen and overheating li-ion battery, posing a significant risk of explosion and exposure to hazardous gases.

incident_description:
I bought a CloudKey Gen2 Plus from Ubiquiti Networks on 1 Jun 20. One of the reasons I bought it was the internal battery would allow the device to gracefully shutdown when power was lost. The device worked for a period of time. Last month (Sep 21) I unplugged the device to make some changes to my network and the device immediately shutdown, it did not gracefully shutdown. Upon investigation, a large number of users of the device were complaining on line of similar issues. A number of users had disassembled their devices and discovered Lithium Ion Battery pack had swollen. These are passively cooled devices which are tightly packed. The battery sits under the CPU which does get quite hot (upwards of 60C. I pulled my device apart and discovered that the batter had swollen as well.

This condition presents a significant safety hazard and these devices are meant to be left unattended. if the battery swells and ruptures it could cause a fire. After repeated inquiries Ubiquiti has yet to acknowledge this as an issue.
justification: Battery swelling and potential rupture poses a significant fire risk, as devices are meant to be left unattended.

incident_description: I purchased a GreatLite Cree 700 LM E54 Tactical Rechargeable Flashlight, EXPE54-E01 that contains 2 GreatLite IRC 18650 2200mAh 3.7v Li-ion rechargeable batteries. The batteries must be removed from the flashlight and charged in a separate device. The polarity labels (positive and negative) on one of the batteries are incorrect. If you place the batteries in a charger with the polarity reversed, these batteries will explode due to their volatility and send hot molten metal and debris everywhere, and will cause a fire. I cannot stress enough how volatile the chemistry in these batteries becomes when shorted by placing them incorrectly back into the flashlight with the polarity reversed. One of these batteries shorted while charging and it caused a small fire on my counter but I was able to toss the battery and charger into the sink to put it out. I initially thought I placed them into the charger incorrectly until I noticed the labeling of the anodes was incorrect from the manufacturer. I purchased several of these flashlights and now I have to contact the people I gave them to and inform them of the mislabeled anodes on the batteries.
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident resulted in a small fire, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' (severity level 2). The likelihood is high (4) as the incorrect polarity labels can easily lead to such incidents.

My daughter is crawling, and partially sitting up. But not pulling to stand yet. She was able to get the strip pulled off and in the process of pulling on it removed the cord from the strip she pulled and then into her crib. which very easily could have resulted in the death of my daughter. Not only is the product against AAP recommendations, they donÃÂt make this clear at all this is the case. incident_description:
The charger was plugged in the outlet at 3:00am and her adult son was awakened between 5:30am - 5:45am to a fire.  Flames, smoke and a burning odor, were emitting from the charger.  The flames were just below the bottom of his desk and the charger was setting on a small stand near the desk.  The flames were between 1' - 2' high.

The son woke up and pulled the charger from the surge protector and placed it into the sink.  The parents came into the bathroom, while the son went back to his room to put out the melting plastic and other items that caught fire.

There was a surge protector that was plugged into the wall outlet.  The surge protector has USB ports on it.  The charger was connected to the surge protector by a cord that was plugged into its usb port section.  The surge protector did not sustain any damage.  

While the charger was in the bathroom, it exploded, sending hot pieces of flaming/melted plastic across the bathroom.  There are burn marks on the wall, flooring and minor burn marks on the ceiling, sink and bathtub.  The son used a towel to extinguish the flames from the charger, in the bathroom, at 5:57am.

The following number (BC 1848A) is listed on the charger, but there is no indication as to what that number is.

The 23 year old son sustained 2 burns on his left arm, inside of his elbow, where a piece of plastic burned the inner portion of his elbow.  He sustained a small blister to his right hand and right fingers.  He also sustained bruising to his chest and abdomen.  The son has not seen a doctor for his injuries.  However, the bruising to the chest and abdomen has continued to worsen and changed color to a deep purple.

6/18/2021:  The consumer reported this incident to the retailer and advised them that she would be contacting CPSC.  She asked the rep. ([REDACTED]) if the product could be pulled from the shelves.  The rep. could not answer that.
justification: The incident resulted in injuries to the son, with burns on his arm and hand, and bruising to his chest and abdomen, despite no fatalities.

incident_description: HidrateSpark is a Bluetooth-connected smart water bottle that reminds one to drink water through a smartphone-connected app.  The bottle reads the water level and calculates your water intake.  The charging cable provided does not have overcurrent or short circuit protection and is connected to the device using a magnetic connector with EXPOSED terminals.  Because it is magnetic, the connector is attracted to metal objects.  In the event that the terminals come in contact with exposed metal, an electrical connection is made and the connector then shorts the 5v power supply.  I had a bottle charging on my desk and disconnected it.  The cable came in contact with some exposed metal near my worksurface causing the power supply (phone charger to get extremely hot.  It happed again when plugged into a USB hub causing it to shut down the hub and all of the USB components on my computer including my mouse and keyboard.  Cables can be contructed with simple short circuit protection with the simple addition of a Polyfuse Resttable fuse that will disconnect the circuit due to overcurrent and reset once the fault is removed.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident caused significant disruption to work, with the power supply overheating and shutting down connected USB devices.

Pieps and Black Diamond DSP, DSP Pro, and DSP Sport avalanche beacons have a design flaw that has been linked to at least one fatality, one miraculous near miss, and anecdotal reports of beacons mysteriously turning off.

Avalanche beacons are essential safety equipment used to facilitate the discovery of people buried under snow following an avalanche. The design flaw in these beacons can lead to the beacon silently disabling its key radio transmission function without notifying the user.

The beacon is known to be increasingly susceptible to this behavior when cracking appears in the locking tab that prevents the main switch from sliding out of "Send" mode.  I noticed the cracking in my own model of the beacon today.

Anecdotally, Black Diamond is aware of many beacons being returned with the same flaw. Due to public pressure, they have instituted a "we will warranty it for you if you are concerned" policy and are offering free or low-cost upgrades to those with affected beacons. Retailers such as REI are taking it seriously-enough that they are notifying consumers who have purchased affected beacons proactively, as they would normally do in a recall.

If this situation hasn't crossed the line into recall territory, it is very close.  Reasonable summaries of the situation can be found here: [REDACTED]
justification: The design flaw has been linked to at least one fatality and near miss, indicating a high likelihood of severe incidents.

incident_description:
The battery on my 2018 HP Spectre x360 (HP Battery 928372-855) laptop, which I have since replaced, would quickly overheat after only an hour and a half of use, and became so bloated that it eventually split the case.  
     When I initially noticed the case was splitting around August 2020, I thought it was because the screws became lose.  I took it to an IT person for repair and was told the battery inside had bulged and expanded so much it split the hard case. I was told to immediately stop using it, and to contact HP. He speculated that the battery had likely started expanding months prior.
    The IT person also said it is highly unusual on such a reasonably new brand-name laptop (2 yrs) of moderate use and believe it to be a manufacturer's defect and was a safety risk. I contacted HP and although they initiated a battery recall with some other models, they told me they did not with this particular model and claimed a bloated battery is not a safety issue. IT professionals with whom I've consulted strongly disagree and contend the heat and gas emissions can pose safety and health issues to users. 
     It's also evident from HP's own user forum that this is a common issue and those users who continue to use their laptops despite the bulging and overheating may be exposed to harm. I believe this is especially dangerous because most users who purchase HP laptops would not think they would have to replace their batteries within the first year and half to two years of purchasing it and may not recognize the damaged battery since it wouldn't be apparent until their case splits. Further most would not immediately stop using their laptops even if the defective battery is noticed, as the laptop would still function.  
     I have since replaced the battery and a comparison between the new and old original battery, showed the original to three times its size. When I had the original battery, I did not leave my laptop plugged in all the time and generally not when I'm using it, I used the appropriate charger, I shut it down daily, used vented laptop tray, and was not negligent at all in the care of my laptop. A less careful user can easily be put in harm's way with this laptop's defective battery. Although I have replaced my battery, I felt compelled to alert you of the potential hazards of keeping these batteries on the market and HP's refusal to recall them.
justification: The battery's overheating and expansion poses a safety risk, as it could potentially cause burns or start a fire, despite HP's claim that it's not a safety issue.

incident_description:
I purchased a Renogy inverter/charger (R-INVT-PCL1-20111S) on 11/30/2020 as part of a solar power and lithium battery upgrade for my RV.  The first unit that I purchased directly from Renogy was not working correctly, so I purchased a second one from Renogy and also a third from Amazon.  All three inverter/chargers had the same Issue.  There is a circuit within the unit called the Automatic Neutral to Ground bonding circuit that is a safety feature required by UL458 to prevent ground loops and ungrounded AC circuits in mobile homes that is not working correctly.  In fact, it is programmed to work backward, bonding when it should be unbonded and unbonding when it should be bonded.  This caused over $200 worth of damages to my RV, caused the GFCI circuit within my RV to trip constantly and posed the potential for electrocution hazard because it caused 60VAC to be present between ground an neutral of the AC receptacles.  I have since replaced the Renogy inverter/charger with a unit from [REDACTED], a competing manufacturer, which works correctly.  Renogy has denied the hazards I witnessed and has done nothing to correct the problem other than to provide a (yet to materialize) refund for returning the items.  I have lots of email correspondence with them stating UL458 compliance but at the same time discounting the need for this automatic circuit despite it being outlined in their user manual.  I have created videos of the issue:
[REDACTED]
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident caused significant damage ($200) and posed a potential electrocution hazard, making it likely to recur.

-I went to plug in the usb communication cable into my computer from the UPS so it can tell the computer if this is a power outage and how much battery percent and run time is left, when I was shocked by the usb cable because there is 60volts on the outer metal shield.
-Electric Shock
-By touching the outside metal shield of the usb cable

incident_description: New ROKU TV fell over when barely touched on its side.  The legs are very flimsy and do not safely support the 32" tv.  The fall cracked the screen of the tv.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (cracked screen) but no injuries, and the likelihood of it happening again is possible due to the TV's unstable legs.

incident_description: I have a Microsoft Surface 4. While I was using it, my screen began to just pop off in the left hand corner. It rapidly popped off further, heated up a lot, and the started making a lot of noise. I later learned that this was due to the battery beginning to bulge. I called the microsoft help line, and they said that the product has done this with many other customers, it is not safe to use, but that the only way to save my files is to use it. I immediately shut off the product.
justification: While no injury occurred, the incident involved a potentially hazardous product malfunction, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' scenario.

incident_description: My toddler dropped my phone from our couch (maybe a 2 foot drop) while it had a Casely Power 2.0 case on it. It seemed fine when I picked it up, so I put it back in my pocket. About 30 seconds later I could smell something burning. After a minute of checking for the source of the burning smell I realized that it was coming from me. I pulled out my phone and there was a flame coming from the indicator lights on the case and smoke coming from it. My husband and I were able to safely remove my phone and put out the fire. We had to air out our home because of the chemical/electrical smell, and placed the case on the concrete in our backyard just in case it reignited. Luckily the flame was not against my skin, but it had started to burn through my sweater.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire, making it an incident with no injury.

incident_description: The item is a wireless electronics charger. It was plugged in on my wood end table in my living room, and the bottom of the device had melted and must have sparked a few times under the pad without us knowing. We could smell burning and found it during the search.
justification: The device caused a fire, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: My Dell XPS 13 9350 laptop battery began swelling. A Dell representative told me via web chat 2/6/2021 that this was a "fire hazard." This battery is a replacement I bought from Dell in 2019 to replace the original factory-installed battery, which also swelled.
justification: While no injury occurred, the swelling battery poses a fire hazard, making it an incident.

incident_description:
Samsung Galaxy A51 5G got so hot I was unable to hold the phone from the bottom. Smoke came out from the upper left of the display.
I still have the phone.
justification: The phone overheating and emitting smoke indicates a potential fire hazard, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: The problem was the battery in an HP Pavilion Notebook (15-au063nr). I recently noticed that the keyboard was acting funny. It would sometimes just fail to register  a response from the keys. I then noticed that the left side of the keyboard had raised up and even unattached itself. I was aware of the HP battery recalls but was informed that my laptop was not affected. I have computer experience so I removed the battery. It was nearly twice its normal size. It had expanded so much it pushed the keyboard up. It did not explode yet, but I am afraid what might have happened if I had not found it. I replaced the battery but the computer has not operated properly since. I was not injured, but the computer is nearly useless.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a significant hardware malfunction that rendered the laptop nearly useless.

incident_description: I have at least 10 Ryobi Lithium rechargeable batteries 4ah , Model P108 ,( manufacturer dates 2016 thru 2020, purchased through Home Depot ) that have cracks on the posts and /or body of the batteries, potential fire /explosion hazard..  I checked and this P108 battery has been recalled in the past with  same model P108 number, a different part number. (listed on your site as well with previous recall and complaint).   I contacted Ryobi and sent pics noting my P108 battery issues and concerns.  I have the items and photos. (your site showed an error code when I tried to upload).
justification: Potential fire/explosion hazard due to cracked batteries, though no incidents reported yet.

incident_description: I am using an ACR Resqlink beacon that is brand new. I put the belt clip on the back of the unit. When I went to pull the clip off the back of the unit with the provided rope my finger got slashed and it left a scar. I have been unable to get the company to call me back or email me. I have left messages.
justification: Injury occurred due to improper use of the beacon's belt clip, which is possible given the lack of clear instructions or user training.

incident_description:
While using the "Volta XL Improved" cable to charge my [REDACTED] computer, my [REDACTED] displayed a warning that it was using a low-voltage charger, which was incorrect and unexpected. I was using the charger that came with the [REDACTED].

I went to re-seat the cable and found the Volta cable's magnetic tip became very hot. I dropped it to avoid being burned. After disconnecting the cable from the computer,  I observed  that both the magnetic tip and the cable  had been melted or otherwise damaged. I later  discovered the right USB-C port on the [REDACTED] no longer accepts connections (power or data).
justification: Damage to the cable and computer port, but no injuries reported.

incident_description:
I was in the process of changing LR-41 batteries in a small battery light and placed the three used LR-41 batteries on a ledge above the kitchen sink. There was no source of heat and it was a cloudy day. There was a loud explosion which came from one of the batteries exploding. I have photos of the exploded battery. Though there was no fire that followed, I wanted to bring this to your attention. I am also reporting this to the US Consumer Product Safety Division.

I realize that this has been a problem in the past and perhaps this was just a defective battery. Other than reporting this, I do not expect any follow up.
justification: Though no injury occurred, the explosion posed a potential hazard, and similar incidents have been reported in the past.

incident_description: I purchased a Sonos Move speaker (https://www.sonos.com/en-us/shop/move.html) which comes with a charging base. While charging, the wire that runs from the wall adaptor to the charging base become hot, it separated as I picked it up, and sparked.   It had not been previously damaged in any way by me during use.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the sparking and separation of the charging wire indicates a potential fire hazard, making it an incident with possible reoccurrence.

incident_description:
I received a Power Pod keychain phone charger for Christmas. Tonight I removed it from its packaging to  use. I plugged it into my phone; the blue light was on, but it was not charging my phone. I assumed the power pod was not charged, so I plugged it into a USB puck in a kitchen wall outlet using the manufacturer's provided cord. I noticed when I plugged it in, its red light turned on.
About one hour later, I heard a loud pop and turned around to see it on fire on our kitchen counter. I was in the adjacent dining area with my two young children and was able to quickly unplug the device from the wall outlet and put out the fire with a rag. The fire had already spread to several items on the counter and burned the counter itself. No injuries occurred.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident resulted in property damage and could have escalated to a more severe level.

incident_description:
Hello,

I had a scary experience and start of an electrical fire yesterday morning. I contacted Amazon about their branded cable product  but received a response about the product warranty and $10 credit. 

My amazonbasics cable almost lit my house on fire yesterday, 1/10/21. The cable was bought September 2019 and has been used infrequently. My other [REDACTED] cable died so I used the AmazonBasics cable this morning. When I plugged the cable in it wasn't charging my phone. I went to grab the cable I use in my car and but had not unplugged the AnazonBasics cable before I left. When I came back a few moments later there were sparks and the cable end plastic around the charging end that connects to the device was bulging like a balloon. When the plastic cooled it shrunk back down but you can still see heat damage. I could smell smoke but it had not lit on fire yet, just a few sparks from the end. I unplugged and have the cable set aside.

This is dangerous. I've never had another brand of cable spark, smoke, or heat up.

Thanks.
justification: Although no fire was ignited, the incident involved sparks and heat damage, posing a potential risk.

incident_description:
My daughters ([REDACTED]) laptop cord caught fire. She yelled for me after smelling smoke. I discovered it and quickly unlplugged laptop and moved her bed away from outlet and laptop. Her sheet had burnt, the outlet as shown and the cord. What was even more alarming was how hot the actual laptop itself was. Im sure it too was about to be flames had i not found it. Hot enough it burned to touch it. 
It was plugged in behind her bed and was sitting on her nightstand. 
Cord showed no signs of damage prior to this use. Burnt her sheet, wall outlet. & cord. Laptop was hot enough it hurt to grab it. 
We live in an apartment and this not only endangered myself and my children but the entire complex.

incident_description:
The consumer indicates that he picked up his cell phone and noticed that the it was bulging from the back, which also made the screen break down the middle. The consumer notes that he can see inside the phone due to the expansion, and there also appear to be chemical burns where the screen broke.

The consumer states that he had the unit in storage for at about four years when he removed it and placed it in his counter approximately one month ago.

The consumer plans on keeping his cell phone for at least the next thirty days in case an investigation ensues however he will have to have it outside as the back was still expanding when he was submitting the report.
justification: No injuries reported, but the incident could have caused harm due to the phone's expansion and chemical burns.

incident_description:
I have a Microsoft Surface Pro 4 convertible laptop/tablet device. Recent (December 2020) I noticed the screen delaminating from the enclosure, seemingly due to bulging components. Internet searches and then correspondence with Microsoft Support confirmed that this is a known critical fire hazard due to battery swelling. The enclosure additionally appears to be made of magnesium, which would make a resulting fire likely catastrophic and nearly impossible to extinguish. Microsoft is aware of the issue and instructed that the device is not to be used. 

Microsoft said that they would send a fire-proof enclosure to return the device for investigation, but ONLY if I FIRST paid a $450 replacement fee. I replied that I would be happy to pay a replacement fee when sent a replacement, but that their retrieval and disposal (with any investigation on their part) should not be predicated by first paying a replacement fee. Microsoft replied that I should look for good holiday deals on a new device from their store or 3rd party sellers, with no mention or offer to remove the hazardous device from my household, or even how to safely dispose of this. Microsoft is clearly aware of a critical safety hazard with their product and the company is more interested in selling a new device than responsibly dealing with this safety hazard. 

Photo of the device with bulging battery and correspondence with Microsoft attached.
justification: The incident involves a known fire hazard due to battery swelling, with potential for catastrophic damage and difficulty extinguishing, making it likely to occur.

incident_description: My daughter was using an [REDACTED] Night Light kit, which includes 2 battery-operated plastic lights (2 AAA batteries each). The lights each have an on/off switch and a remote that controls the color of the light. One of the lights worked briefly, but did not respond correctly to the remote. It then stopped working, and was hot to the touch. One battery was too hot to touch, so I removed it with a plastic tool. The casing of the battery had started to melt off. The other battery did not overheat. The batteries were new Duracell brand with an expiration of March 2030.
justification: Battery overheating and casing melting pose a high risk of injury.

incident_description: I was changing an unresponsive battery in a remote control for a ceiling fan in my home. I removed the existing battery and placed it on my kitchen counter. As I was opening the package which held a replacement battery, I heard a very loud pop, similar to a low powered gunshot, and saw in my peripheral vision an object shoot across my kitchen and repel off of my cabinets (approx 20' away) before I heard it land on the floor. To my shock, the sound was the battery that I had rested just a moment before on the countertop and the object was the negative end of the battery flying across the room.
justification: The incident resulted in no injury, but the unexpected and forceful expulsion of the battery across the room indicates a potential hazard.

incident_description: My Timex clock radio T231V caught fire. There was also damage to my heavy duty extension cord.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and while it's possible for such incidents to occur, they are not common.

justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident involved electrical sparking and melting, posing a potential hazard.

Belkin 6-Outlet Power Strip Surge Protector, Flat Rotating Plug (Model BE106001-08R). The end of the plug bursted into flame in my bedroom! Luckily my daughter was awake when this occurred so no one was injured.  Tv, lamp and cable box was plugged into this outlet when incident occurred.

incident_description:

I showed the representative my device and it was confirmed that the cable I was purchasing was compatible with my device, and the two charging ports I intended to use. After using the cable for the last two months, on the evening of Sunday December 13, 2020, my phone was plugged into this cable, charging, while I held my phone in my lap. I started to hear a crackling sound and felt extreme heat in my hand, and immediatly dropped the phone on the chair and unplugged the charger from the wall, and then from my phone. There was smoke and a burning plastic smell coming from the end of the cable, and the charging port in my phone was damaged. I know with absolute certainty, that it was the cable that caused this. I tested other cables using different charging stations and different outlets in my home after this transpired; none of the other cables or products replicated this reaction. I tested the Verizon cable again, in a different outlet in my home, and once again, it started to spark, smoke, and produced a melted subtance from its metal end, which I believe is from the coating it melted off of the charging port in my phone. It also permanently damaged the charging port of my phone, in the first instance, which is visibly noticible. The following day, I returned to the store where I purchased the cable, with my phone and cable, and reported what happened to an employee named [REDACTED]. He refused the need to inspect my phone, nor the cable and was very unphased and unconcerned. I held up both the cable and my phone, in front of the representatives face, and he would barely look. He told me to call Customer Service, and that there was nothing that could be done in store. I didn't want to argue and remain in the store, because they were not honoring social distancing guidelines and had between 10 and 11 people in the small store, so I left. I returned home and called customer service as directed. 
I spoke with someone named [REDACTED] and explained what happened. [REDACTED] told me that I had to go into a store to resolve this, even though I told her I had already done this the previous day.
I asked to speak with a Supervisor and I was denied the opportunity to talk with a Supervisor, and was told that a Supervisor would call me back---one never did, even over 24 hours later. 
I called again after ending the call with [REDACTED], due to the time sensitive nature, and spoke with a representative name [REDACTED], explained what happened, and asked to speak with a Supervisor. I recieved a call back from supervisor named [REDACTED] within a couple minutes. [REDACTED] was the 4th Verizon rep who was made aware of what happened, and I explained everything again in detail. I asked [REDACTED] multiple times if I could give him the information from my receipt as well as the product information, and expressed to him that it was a grave safety concern that they look into this. [REDACTED] refused to listen when I tried to read him the information, and would not take the information identifying the product or my purchase. He simply agreed to remove the cost of the charger from next month's bill. Meanwhile, after I said I would be taking legal action, [REDACTED] gave me a big spiel about how he was going to open an investigation into the product and said that Verizon takes this very seriously, and that they would be looking into this; and yet, he had no idea what the exact product was or what the serial number was, because he said that he couldn't find the receipt, and again, would not take down the information. This is all on a recorded line.
All of the Verizon reps seemed unphased by the safety implications of this situation, even refusing to ackowledge it. 
At no point, did anyone ask me for the serial number or identifying number of the product, and everyone I spoke to, including in the store, claimed that they couldn't find my receipt, even though I currently have a copy that they emailed to me, directly from Verizon, as well as my bank statement, and I'm sure I was also filmed on a security camera in store as well.
Aside from the fact that [REDACTED] wouldn't take the information from me to identify the product, I have a strong reason to believe that [REDACTED] did not actually file any such safety investigation. One example of [REDACTED] dishonesty, is that he also stated and promised other things on our call that he was being dishonest about (i.e. he told me multiple times, on a recorded line, that he was notating my account to indicate that Verizon would refund the insurance deductable for the phone that I had to replace as a result of their faulty cable, but when I called back today, 12/16/2020, at [REDACTED], the representative I spoke to, [REDACTED], stated that [REDACTED] noted my account to say that he could not refund the deductable---demonstrating that he is a dishonest liar). I then asked to be transferred to a supervisor to confirm, and was transferred to a supervisor named [REDACTED]. 
In speaking [REDACTED], I explained the entire ordeal again, and I told her I would be filing a formal safety complaint with a federal agency, and contacting an attorney regarding the monetary losses I incurred as a result (i.e. my phone), since Verizon lied and told me in bad faith, that they would refund the insurance deductible on my next bill, if I filed the insurance claim with their insurance carrier [REDACTED], which is what I did. [REDACTED] responded and said that she would call me back within 20 minutes, before leaving for the day at 7:00 pm pst, in order to "find out how she could help me". It is now 8:10 pm pst, and [REDACTED] never called me; when I had tried to call Verizon at 7:04, the automated system says they are now closed.
I tried to post a negative review of the cable on the verizon website, warning others about the fire hazard, and Verizon would not allow my review to post to 
their website which I documented as well. 
Verizon is putting people's lives at risk. And three phone calls and a visit to the store has yielded zero concern or action to investigate. I'm lucky that I was awake when this happened or this would be a very different conversation, if I could have one at all. All it takes is for one spark to start a fire that could permanently maim or kill somebody, and I feel incredibly gratefu that I was awake, to prevent that from happening.

I would like to add an additional update to my report, to say that I made another attempt to
contact Verizon today, 12/17, since I never recieved the promised Supervisor call back from
[REDACTED].
I spoke with [REDACTED], and then [REDACTED] (Supervisor), and was again, denied the opportunity to
escalate this case to an upper manager. [REDACTED] refused to listen to the previous phone calls, and
did not take the information that identifies the faulty cable, even when I re-explained what
happened and re-iterated that they STILL have not documented the information that identifies
the cable. I reiterated that they have a duty to protect their consumers and [REDACTED] did not collect
any information about the cable. [REDACTED] also refused to provide me with the legal address of their
legal department, where I said I wanted to send a certified letter. and said that I had to
subpeona this information. I had to look it up myself on the internet.
Verizon is trying to brush this off and are endangering people's lives.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (burns) and property damage (phone charging port), and the likelihood of a similar occurrence is high given the defective product remains in circulation.

incident_description:
This TV has 2 legs on each end.  Two of the 4 leg supports extends in front of the TV and the other 2 extend behind the TV and they create a wide "V" shape on each end.  The TV was sitting on a large wooden stand and had approximately 6" of extra space, beyond the legs, on each side.  

Approximately 10 days ago, the TV fell on its own and landed on the floor.  No one was near the TV when it happened.  No one was injured.  The TV stand was not made of solid wood, so it sustained damage to the point that it is pressed inward where the TV hit it.

The consumer called the manufacturer.  She was told that a technician would be sent out.

11/29/2020:  A local technician came out and took pictures of the TV and damage.  The technician said he would pass the information on to LG.

11/30/2020:  A manufacturer's rep. called the consumer and said that there was no way that the TV could have fallen in that manner and they were not going to do anything about it.

The consumer said that her husband screwed the legs in when it was purchased and they had never experienced any problems in the past.
justification: The TV falling on its own with no one nearby indicates a possible occurrence, and while damage was caused, no injuries were reported.

incident_description: I purchased an Nvidia Shield tablet shortly thereafter it was recall for a defective battery that where catching on fire so I followed the return instructions and received my second brand new nvidia Shield tablet with the new and improved battery that was supposed to be safe I would like to let you know that the second tablet  burst into flames on 11/23/2020 there is still a serious fire hazard with this tablet.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage and could have caused injury, making it a severe event.

incident_description:

My LG television ( Model 65SJ9500, S/N 801RMXX8V314) is a fire and safety hazard. on the night of October 11th, the screen and several associated sheets of flexible plastic  fell apart and came crashing forward. Thank you 
[REDACTED]

incident_description:
What happened that made you want to report?  I had a Microsoft Surface laptop with a bulging/swelling battery that is permantely installed and sealed under the Keyboard.  I took it into microsoft and they said to stop using it immediately.  they exchanged it, and I was concerned but happy about the quick remedy.  However, about a year later the same thing happened only this time there was a loud sizzle and crackle with the keyboard bursting separating it from the chassis. How were the product(s) being used?  normal use, surfing the internet and business use
Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?  No

incident_description:
On Saturday, November 14th, 2020, our household had a GETIHU lithium ion battery explode in our kitchen. The battery made a pop noise and then there was a small flame. At the point where my husband tried to carry the battery out of the house (through a sliding glass door) with a spatula, it then fell on our hardwood floor and began spinning and spewing out ash and sparks. My husband was finally able to contain it by putting it in a bowl full of water. The damaged battery and two similar batteries now reside in a metal container on our driveway (concrete) out of fear of further combustion.

I want to report this because when I made the manufacturer aware of this through their customer service email, they have repeatedly tried to get me to send the damaged battery back to them in China via USPS (illegal). After my concern about illegally sending this damaged battery, they then suggested that I send it to a hub in California via UPS (I know that UPS allows for shipment of damaged lithium ion batteries under certain circumstances). However, they do not have the proper permits for ground shipping via UPS and they have not provided me with a safe container for transport. Moreover, they would be putting *my* name as the return address, making me liable for any damage that could happen en route.

GETIHU has pulled their listing of this product from amazon. com. I purchased one battery on August 18. 2018 and two similar batteries in June of 2019 (June 5 and June 22). The listing read as: "GETIHU Portable Charger, Ultra Slim 10000 mAh Power Bank, 4.8A High-Speed 2 USB Ports Battery Pack with LED Flashlight, Compatible with [REDACTED] 

After the battery exploded, I posted a note of warning to purchasers on Saturday, November14/ Sunday November 15 to the only listing for that battery that was still up on amazon. The listing has since been pulled from amazon. The manufacturer now sells another battery in its place, but I believe has not placed any warning to consumers of the batteries I purchased.

My concern is that there were many batteries of the kind I purchased that were sold in 2018-2019. I do not feel comfortable knowing that this incident happened to me and could happen to others in the future.

NOTE: The battery that combusted was unplugged/not-charging at the time and had been unplugged for over 10 hours. Previously it had been plugged into an outlet to charge overnight (necessary to get full charge) using a standard generic charging cable. In fact, two of these batteries had been charging in the same outlet with similar cables and were subsequently removed from charging after showing full charge. Only one of the batteries combusted.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the battery explosion and subsequent ash and spark spewing pose a significant risk of property damage and potential injury.

Battery tends to run very hot and is not charging properly. Battery meter does not measure battery information correctly. Have attempted to get help through Apple Store Genius Bar without success. Took laptop to MacMedics (Apple authorized repair center) yesterday. MacMedics confirmed battery is badly swollen / bloated. MacMedics and Apple Store will not replace battery for fire, hazardous fume, explosion-related safety concerns because it's a LiON battery that's glued to the upper case and it's difficult to remove. Indicated Apple's current recommendation for repair is to replace the entire upper case. Cost is $458 even though the issue is the same as the current recall issue because my laptop's serial number is not currently included in the covered list of serial numbers. Their laptops are not included in the current range of recall serial numbers, but they also have swollen / bloated batteries. Some have failed catastrophically. (explosion, fire, hazardous fumes) I attempted to follow up with Apple Support by phone today and was told that it's common and normal for the batteries to swell and bloat. It's expected.

incident_description:
I recently began noticing yellowish-brownish areas on the left and right side of the display on my Surface Pro 4 device, predominately on the left side.  This seemed to be heat related, since it occurred more, and the discolored area became larger, when the device was running hot, with the cooling fan constantly running at what appeared to be the maximum speed.  Eventually, it was noticed that the left side of the display bulged out and became separated from the frame.  I then began researching this further and filed a service request/case with Microsoft under the category/issue type drop down selection of "Lifted, separated, or bulging screen."  After multiple back and forth communications with Microsoft as part of the service request/case and additional research in regards to this I came to understand that the "Lifted, separated, or bulging screen" is due to the battery expanding, which separated the display from the frame.  Microsoft responded with a boiler plate response, which has contradictory language within it:ÃÂ  in one sentence they state there is ÃÂno inherent risk or safety concern associated with these expanded batteriesÃÂ and then immediately follow it with ÃÂthe lithium ion batteries used in Surface devices contain materials that can injure skin, eyes, and lungs if puncturedÃÂ and ÃÂSurface devices with expanded batteries should not be connected to AC power as it could possibly lead to rupture;ÃÂ which is not a misuse according to their labeling, i.e., you should be able to use the device while connected to AC power/a docking station (this is predominately how we use the device), however, a product design flaw created a condition where it cannot be used while connected to AC power/a docking station due to a safety concern according to them.

The device is now unusable, according to Microsoft, while plugged in due to a safety concern given the potential for the expanded battery to rupture.ÃÂ  Additionally, it canÃÂt be used when it is unplugged given the potential for a safety concern with the battery, i.e., it canÃÂt be carried around, left powered on unattended, taken on a plane, etc., given the state of the battery and the potential for it to continue to expand and rupture, or to rupture in its current expanded state.ÃÂ  This is a safety issue that is still occurring with product in the field and it needs to be addressed.  I have seen numerous complaints online in regards to this issue.ÃÂ  In some cases it was stated that the device/battery ÃÂcaught fire and exploded,ÃÂ evident from images that were provided in that case as well.  Additionally, Microsoft knows this is an unsafe condition due to the expanded battery condition regardless of whether or not it is being charged or discharged, i.e., being used, given that they stated if the device was returned for replacement a "special return box must be used for shipping the damaged Surface."

They have chosen to deal with this unsafe condition by putting out the boiler plate statements previously referenced (only after a customer has brought their particular occurrence to Microsoft's attention; customers should be made aware of this before it happens, without having to research the condition and finding out about the unsafe condition on their own), and by trying to get some defective product out of the field by replacing it if it is three years and under, where the time period was based on profit/loss and not on safety.ÃÂ  I am hoping that Microsoft will eventually get to a safety recall in regards to this, hopefully before there are additional occurrences of batteries/devices exploding and catching fire, and before anyone gets hurt.  The service request/case that I have filed with Microsoft is still open and continuously being escalated since they will not replace the failed and unsafe device without charging a substantial fee.  I just want the ability to use a safe product, a product that I paid significant money for, for longer than four years.ÃÂ  Especially now, when this product (a PC) is needed more than ever.ÃÂ  I donÃÂt think that is too much to ask for.
justification: Potential for injury due to battery expansion and rupture, as evidenced by customer reports of devices catching fire and exploding.

incident_description:
