I researched the issue, and found that there is a big recall. I'm glad I know about it now because I was unaware of it before; however, when I downloaded the HP validation utility on their recall support website, my computer failed the validation. The utility claims that my battery is not affected. Both of my laptops are clearly affected. They are, without a doubt, affected. I'm concerned about this, because my household has five HP laptops and countless other HP products. I called HP's support number for incidents related to these batteries this morning, the first time at 8:02 am CST, and the second time at 8:53 am CST. Both times, I was the "1st caller in line" for the entire phone call, nobody answered the call, and HP disconnected the phone call at 40 minutes for both phone calls. I have phone records of both calls and a recording of the second call. HP has a support webpage*, which states that if your laptop is swelling, they will replace the battery, only if the battery is under warranty, otherwise the consumer must pay for a new battery. Will this ever be resolved? Isn't HP strictly liable for their products when they are found to have manufacturing defects and are hazardous?

*https://support.hp.com/us-en/document/c05640567

The following is directly quoted from HP's website (URL above):

"A swollen battery does not present a safety issue. It is the result of the generation of gases per the normal degradation of the battery cell over time. HP has worked closely with our battery cell suppliers and third-party industry experts to help minimize the potential for HP batteries to swell over time and to identify that swollen batteries are not a safety issue."
...
"If a battery is under warranty, HP will replace the battery per the terms and conditions of the HP Worldwide Limited Warranty or applicable HP Care Packs. For batteries no longer under warranty, contact HP to purchase a genuine HP replacement battery."
justification: Both laptops are affected by the battery swelling issue, which, while not immediately dangerous according to HP, could potentially cause further damage or safety risks if left unaddressed.

Upon inspection I found that the rear panel of the tablet was swollen outwards and it was at this time I also noticed the tablet screen was swollen outwards. Upon research of this issue I came across numerous upon numerous complaints from other users of this tablet, the tablets issued before this one and the tablets issued after this one that have the same issue. The issue is that the  lithium-ion are expanding. Microsoft support reported to me that "we" users should discontinue use of the tablet computer because of risk of fire and/or explosion, however, Microsoft's own document entitled "Caring for your Surface battery" say's and I quote "Battery expansion from deterioration does not present a safety concern and is most often caused by the formation of non-flammable carbon dioxide (CO2) gas.", the next sentence say's and I quote, " If you have a device where the battery has expanded visibly beyond the mechanical enclosure, we recommend you stop using the device. You should handle the device with caution to prevent putting pressure on or risk puncturing the battery cell. If you need assistance, contact us and work with a Surface Support Advocate." Since this battery is enclosed without accessibility "we" the consumers would never know of this safety issue until it is too late.
justification: The incident involves a potential safety hazard due to battery expansion, which is common and reported by many users, but Microsoft's support advice contradicts their own documentation.

I remember the S7 Note batteries were the ones that used to blow up, back when they were introduced in the USA, so I am letting you know. I cannot replace the battery because it is sealed in the phone. I feel if I keep using it, I risk damage to person and property. The bulge is a bit more that 1/8 of an inch from the original back of the phone.
justification: Potential for property damage due to battery swelling, though no immediate threat to life.

incident_description:
My wife,[REDACTED] and I purchased two (2) Samsung Galaxy Note-9 phones in November, 2018 from Best Buy in Lakeland, FL.  We entered into a two-year contract with Sprint. We each received a charger. During the week of July 20, 2020, my wife began getting shocked while she was talking on phone, with the charger plugged in. 

After examining the charger, we discovered that the wire was frayed, with the copper wiring completely exposed. My wife reached out to Samsung Corporation who only informed her that the phone and charger were no longer under warranty. However, when my wife put me on the phone, I informed the person, at an off-shore call center, that this was an existing hazard Samsung needed to address. 
 
I requested that someone in authority call me back or else I would file a grievance through the Consumer Product Safety Commission. I did receive a return call the following day, from a woman who said I should speak with someone from their "Product Liability" office. I informed this person that I did not have the time since the return call was received before the close of business. I wanted to reach out to you first before contacting Samsung. As previously stated, my wife sustained several painful shocks. Please note she has a formerly diagnosed cardiac condition that necessitated her being placed on disability nearly a decade ago.
justification: Wife experienced painful shocks, potentially life-threatening given her pre-existing cardiac condition.

incident_description:
Consumer stated that the battery charger was charging when he heard a popping noise, they noticed that the there was a glowing ball of flame emanating from the charger.  He grabbed the fire extinguisher and contained the flames.  The unit was on the counter top, and there was soot remaining on the cabinets and other items in the kitchen.   Consumer stated that he would be cleaning the rest of items.  Fortunately they were present to prevent a house fire.

Consumer contacted the manufacturer through email but there was no response as yet.

Consumer believes that this portable charger is a fire hazard and should be reported.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant fire hazard, with flames and soot, warranting a severity level of 2.

incident_description:
Zebra GX420t Desktop Printer caught fire while not in use. The unit was plugged into an appropriate grounded outlet. Damage sustained to the printer and the connection to the power supply unit (PSU) were significant.  The unit was completely destroyed and the fire was extinguished by the fire department.  After the fire, it was discovered the PSU was subject to a voluntary recall by the manufacturer.

PSU Zebra Part #: 808101-001
PSU Date Code: 110710
justification: The incident resulted in significant damage to property but no injuries, and the likelihood of a similar event happening again is possible given the recalled PSU.

incident_description: We own an HP ENVY x2 detachable PC 13 tablet.  For several weeks before the incident my wife mentioned that her touch screen seemed to be pulling away from the body of the tablet.  We didn't pay too much attention thinking perhaps the adhesive was loosening and causing this to happen.  One day during the week of July 10, 2020 I happened to be walking past the tablet which was on my wife's desk and saw if from a side view.  I was stunned at how far the screen was pushed out from the body of the unit.  I was surprised the screen hadn't cracked yet.  I told the wife to immediately stop charging and/or using the tablet because clearly something has seriously gone wrong with the unit and I felt it was no longer safe to use.  I wasn't certain it was but i suspected the battery.  I disassembled the unit and indeed one half of the battery had swelled to the point that the vinyl covering the battery was very taunt.  Before I disturbed anything further I took several images of the battery still installed in the unit to show how distorted and expanded the battery was.   I then removed the original battery and placed it a safe area in the event the chemical/electrical process that was causing the defect would continue and possibly pose a safety issue.  At this point I purchased another OEM battery.  I replaced the battery and was able to gently push the screen and effected component back to there original position before the battery issue happened.  I didn't know how to dispose of the battery so i kept it for a period of time.  On Monday July 27, 2020 I was curious about what was causing it to swell thinking it was some sort of gas.  I wanted to release it before I deposed of it thinking it could cause an issue for some else if it wasn't released.   Not knowing what to expect I took it out to my drive.  At the urging of my wife I put on goggles and a face shield.  I took an [REDACTED] knife and punctured a small hole with the tip of the blade. I expect a small release of the gas inside.  Instead what happen was some sort of chemical reaction (i suppose) but it quickly got out of control I has shocked at the smoke, gasses and heat generated from this.  After a short time and after most of the smoke died down i thought to record what had happened using my phone. Even this video shows it still smoldering and melting.  If this has happened while still in the unit when it contacted a piece of material that punctured that vinyl covering or the battery exploded on it own the results could have been disastrous.  One or more of the following would or could have happened.  The gasses expelled are so toxic, it could in an enclosed area like a room in a house cause physical harm.  Or, since it would still be in the unit the heat could not have dissipated as it did outside of the unit and cause a fire.   With obvious results.  I checked the HP web site to see if this was a unit that was part of the recalled ones for defective batteries.  I was not.  Clearly, this situation with either this unit or these units collectively need to be investigated further.  This obviously is potentially a serious safety issue.  My hope is this bring attention to the matter.
justification: The incident involved a battery swelling and potentially causing a fire or toxic gas exposure, which could have led to property damage or injuries if it occurred while the tablet was in use.

incident_description:
Microsoft Surface pro 4 screen separated from case apparently due to too hot bulging battery.  Screen also flickering.  Unit shut down immediately. This followed after a few weeks of use, where the screen became unreadable due to fickering after about an hour of use.  I thought it might be a software issue, perhaps incompatibility with programs.

Went to Microsoft store in [REDACTED] and they said it can't be used bc it might be a fire hazard and battery might explode.  They won't it replace as its out of warranty but offered to replace with a similar refurbished unit for $600, and the process will likely take 3-5 days. The Microsoft glass screen on it would not be replaced.

I waited until now to see if there would be a Microsoft response but they never contacted me or publically said there was any other recourse.
justification: Potential fire hazard due to battery issue, but no immediate injury reported.

incident_description: Battery on iPhone X is expanding and buckling the case. I took it to Apple store and they said it could explode but was out of warranty so they did not have to do anything about it.. The phone still works.
justification: While the incident is an issue (battery expanding), it hasn't caused injury or death, and the phone remains functional.

incident_description:
On July 31st, 2020 (In Vientiane, Laos - where I am serving as a missionary), I noticed my laptop had rebooted automatically, and was not starting. Previously I had noticed that SD cards were not easily going into my SD card slot, and that occasionally my laptop would get a bit warm. When I could not get my device to boot correctly, I removed the solid state hard drive I had previously installed. Upon placing the device upside down, I notice that the plastic case was badly deformed. Initially, I though it was heat (plastic melting), though I now believe it was probably due to pressure. Upon further inspection, and breaking the Lenovo warranty sticker (a sticker placed above a screw that keeps a user from opening the laptop entirely), I found that the battery was enlarged. It was enlarged enough to bend the motherboard slightly, and deform the plastic case. The 'puffed' battery was taken and placed in a metal box outside, in a safe area, in case the battery exploded or caught on fire. Once the battery was removed, the laptop now operates as normal.

Lenovo 510-15IKB Laptop (ideapad) - Type 80SV
Serial: PF0Q1XTM

Order Number: [REDACTED]
Ordered on Thu 22 Jun 2017
17:27 EDT
Digital Receipt available. 

Photos, video of opening is linked here. Once I determined it looked like a battery, I took video of the 'maiden' opening to provide as documentation to Lenovo's engineering team. Here's the URL to access those resources. [REDACTED]
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a swollen battery that could have potentially caused a fire or explosion, hence severity level 2.

incident_description:
On the evening of July 9th 2020 while sleeping I was suddenly awoken by the sound of hissing. Looking over at my dresser to see a bright orange flame coming from my Samsung Galaxy S7 phone that I had plugged in to it's charger. Smoke started to fill the room as I got out of bed and unplugged the phone cord from then power strip when I exited the room. Informing my partner that "I think my phone is on fire" we came into the room to find it full of foul smelling smoke. We opened the bedroom window and turned on all the fans we could before leaving the room. Around 30 minutes later I returned into the bedroom to scoop up the phone into a stainless steel sauce pan and placed it outside on my balcony. We left the window open for the entire night and the following day. 

The next day my partner was feeling a tightness in their chest and went to the hospital for a check-up. The doctor said she had minor lung irritation and if it persisted over the next few days to come back. Luckily over the next day it went away on its own. Myself I did have some irritation after the incident that cleared up over time and did not seek medical attention. 

Fortunately my dresser did not burn and the phone's case seemed to have protected it. The battery did send black specks all around that stuck to bed sheets, pillows, etc but did not burn them. The black specks caused a slight tingly sensation to the skin from battery acid I'm assuming. 

The phone is a complete wreak and I feel that nothing is salvageable from it.
justification: Injury occurred due to smoke inhalation, with minor lung irritation reported.

incident_description:
I have a 3-year old old Microsoft Surface Book 1 with Performance Base laptop (1TB/16GB RAM), purchased May 2017. I recently pulled it out of my bag and found the chassis of the base was separated, exposing the internal circuitry. Upon further inspection, I realized the battery had swollen, causing this separation to occur. This is a clear fire/explosion risk, and although no injuries to myself or others have yet occurred, it may only be a matter of time due to the Lithium ion batteries swelling inside the device.

This is a health, home, and life hazard. Upon some online research, I discovered this to NOT be an isolated incident. There appears to be a problem with at least this generation of Microsoft Surface Books.
justification: While no injuries have occurred yet, the swollen battery poses a high risk of fire or explosion, making it an incident with no injury but likely to cause harm.

incident_description: At approximately 5:30 pm, Saturday July 25, 2020, I attempted to turn on my ION Tailgater Express radio on a low wall near my swimming pool, prior to a dip.  I noticed the blue light that was normally lit, was not on.  I pushed the power button and the radio button with no success.  The charger was plugged into the extension cord and the radio, so I went into the pumphouse to check the circuit breaker, which was on.  I then went back to radio, unplugged the charger connection from the radio.  To the best of my recollection, I then attempted to plug the wire back into the radio when the unit exploded.  My left arm was around the radio, my right hand was on the top of the radio and my chest was directly over the top front.  After the explosion, the next thing I remember was being on one knee near the edge of the pool, trying to get my bearings.  I could see blood dripping on the concrete surface and heard my neighbor calling me.  After the second time he called, I told him my radio had exploded.  He came over and helped me up and walked me to my house.  I went inside to clean up and change clothes before he took me to the ER at our local hospital.  Two other neighbors also came to my aid.  They said the noise rattled their windows and they could hear it with the windows closed.  I was in the ER three hours and received three stitches and skin glue in my chest area and surgical strips on my left forearm.   I returned to ER on Monday July 27 for a follow up to check the contusions on my left forearm.  I have bruising on my forearm, chest and inside of my right leg.
justification: The incident resulted in injuries requiring medical attention, but did not result in death.

incident_description: The Yongnuo YN300 Air is a small LED Video light that fits on top of the camera.   I've had it for approximately 1 year but used it very infrequently.   The light is LED so it normally remains very cool to the touch.   On my last use however, it became extremly hot and began to melt.   The back of the LED light has melted from heat.  The knob is warped and no longer round, you can see the internal wires, the back is slightly warped near the knob, and the battery pins are out of alignment, and it no longer accepts the battery.   Luckily there was no fire but it obviously became very hot without warning.
justification: Although no fire occurred, the extreme heat and melting of the LED light indicates a significant incident, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: The Lithium Ion battery pack swelled and cracked down the middle.  This battery pack came with the Yaesu FT-70DR handheld transceiver when it was purchased new in April 2019.  I immediately stopped using the device for fear the battery may leak or blowup.  Since the battery pack rests in the palm of your hand during operation, burns or physical damage to my hand was a major concern.  The retailer, Ham Radio Outlet, could not help me since the battery was out of the one year warranty.  They referred me to Yaesu, no response.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a potentially hazardous battery swelling and cracking, posing a risk of burns or physical damage.

incident_description: Power supply to the scanner was hot and smelled like it was burning, so I unplugged the scanner. I haven't plugged it back in because I'm afraid it will explode. Then I received a recall notification.
justification: Scanner's power supply overheating and emitting a burning smell indicates a potential fire hazard, though no injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
Bose Acoustimas 10 lll Home Entertainment System caught on fire while idle.  The base unit (control unit) was plugged into the stereo and electrical wall outlet but was not being used. The system had been idle for several days. No fluids were spilled on it nor any damage done to the unit, prior to the fire.

My wife was in the room, with the stereo off, when she smelled the strong scent of the plastic cabinet burning.  Luckily we were present when the fire started.  If the occurence had been 15 minutes earlier or later, the whole house might have caught on fire.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident could have resulted in significant property damage or even death if not discovered promptly.

incident_description: Purchased this USB charger a year or more ago but just started using it recently for about a week.  Charger was plugged into a surge protector.  With no phone plugged in, the USB charger heated a charger cord plugged into it to the point where the end of the cord was smoking and the rug beneath it was melted and starting to burn.  The charger itself was almost too hot to touch.  Have seen identical report on UL safety data site.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and while similar incidents have been reported, it's not yet common.

incident_description: Respondent stated that the battery was under the seat of a vehicle when it overheated and caught the seat on fire.  The door was opened and the battery exploded, it was totally destroyed leaving remaining pieces.  Respondent stated that the department was called on site and he believes that this incident should be reported for an investigation.
justification: No injuries were reported, but the incident resulted in significant property damage (destroyed battery, fire), making it a level 2 severity.

incident_description:
The subject had received the phone the day prior as a gift. He stated he had charged the phone overnight and went to make a phone call the next morning after disconnecting the phone from the wall charger. He stated he was having trouble making the call. He became irritated with the phone and began to twist the phone with his hands. As he was doing this the phone began to smoke and caught fire. He threw the phone on the floor and began stomping on the phone to extinguish the fire. He then took the phone and threw it in the toilet to ensure that the phone was extinguished. He proceeded to open a window to begin ventilating the smoke from the room.

The subject was not injured, and property damage was limited to some soot marks being left on the floor. Please let us know if there is any other information that you might need.
justification: While the incident resulted in no injuries or deaths, the phone catching fire and causing property damage (soot marks) warrants a severity level of 2.

incident_description:
Product failure resulting in fire hazard from over-current condition that was not prevented by the 40A in-line fuse.

Product is a Schumacher Charge N Ride 12V 12Ah battery for a [REDACTED] children's ride on toy that was being operated in accordance with [REDACTED]'s recommendations.

Charge N Ride battery cable/connector and [REDACTED] wiring harness/connector melted from the heat produced. Minor burn injury occurred when the connectors were separated in an attempt to prevent further burning damage to the toy and/or nearby structures.

[REDACTED] has stated that there have been many similar instances with this battery and they are currently working to get the battery removed from the market.
justification: Injury occurred due to direct contact with melted connectors, and similar incidents have been reported.

incident_description: Had ear buds plugged into the wall charging. Kept smelling something that smelled like melting plastic. Finally found that it was the ear buds melting. Charging cable is melted into ear buds, outer housing is melted and deformed.
justification: No injuries reported, but the incident could have led to property damage or fire if not noticed in time.

incident_description:
My boyfriend was using his Milwaukee grinder tool with the 12ah lithium ion battery, when all of a sudden the battery started shooting flames out of it.  He ran to get the fire extinguisher and ultimately had to hose it down to put the fire out.  Prior to retrieving the fire extinguisher he removed the battery from the grinder.  While putting out the fire, he was forced to breathe in the toxic smoke and had the hair singed from his arm and hand.   Because it would not go out immediately, it damaged my deck. 

We purchased 5 lengthy amp hour batteries at approximateky the same time.  Every one of them has died within 3 months of purchase.  The other 4 will not charge at all, and this one blew up in his hand.  The batteries we purchased are as follows.
1-8ah
3-9ah
1-12ah
We own an HVAC business, and use strictly Milwaukee tools. It is high season for us, and are losing money every day that we are forced to scrounge for tools to work with.
justification: Injury occurred due to exposure to toxic smoke and singed hair, with potential for more severe burns if not quickly extinguished.

incident_description: Son went to plug in computer,  started smoking melting slight fire went to un plugged got slight burn and shock but feels ok.  It happens so fast. Cant imagine if I did not smell the smoke Contracted store were purchased Salem NH  all the women kept saying on phone was that's terrible so, I called Nashua NH Store hoping to speak with a manager to inform them what happened . Older gentlemen answered phone  first started to tell me to bring them back to were I purchased them. then got very load all of sudden after I explained my concern for anyone else who may have purchased these ,stating you bring them back they file a report  we can not remove from store a report has to be filed first after you return them. I could not believe what I was hearing  I have photos of the product and what happened . I also tried to email corporate of 5 below with photos  email bounced back ,called a fore departure in Nashua  and explained what happened and explained every one was ok but just wanted to know who would be the proper people to contact, My concern was god forbid some one plugs in walks away or goes to bed we could have a tragedy.  Recommend fire Marshal so I sent email there with photos but that too bounced back.  5 below did reach out through Facebook asking for my email and phone number but no one has contacted me they said some one should be in touch from costumer service, Iwas going to bring product back to store Salem Nh were I purchased but was not sure if I should wait incase you need the product to view .I'm thank for [REDACTED] New gave me your info to contact after [REDACTED] reached out this all happen around some time after 6 last night
justification: Son suffered a slight burn and shock, hence severity level 3. The incident happened quickly and could have been worse, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description:
(04/01/2020)The consumer has a safety concern about the buttons on the remote control because they keep falling off. She is concerned about children and pets that may find the buttons on the floor and swallow them. 

Although the consumer purchased the product in 2019, she stated that she did not start using it until February, 2020. The buttons started falling off in April. So far, ten (10) buttons have fallen off of the remote control. The consumer taped them back in place so that she can use it.

(0622/2020)The consumer contacted the firm and was asked to send a copy of her receipt so that they can replace the remote.
justification: Buttons falling off pose a choking hazard to children and pets, though no injuries have been reported yet.

incident_description: I purchased an Owlet Baby Monitor Camera.  It came with a wall-mount and screw to attach it to the wall. As I was screwing it into the wall, the crew broke in half leaving half of the screw in my wall and the other half attached to the base which fell off in my hand.  If the screw was weakened instead of breaking completely, the camera, which is heavy and positioned above the crib, could have fallen on the baby causing injury.  Thankfully, everybody is ok.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a potential hazard (broken screw) that could have caused injury if the camera had fallen.

incident_description: Blu R1-HD Amazon Prime cellular phone, has swollen lithium ion battery after approximately 3-4 years of use. Battery is internal to the device, located under a sticker inside the phone. I have stopped using this device, but manufacturer will not address issue.
justification: The incident resulted in a malfunctioning device but no injuries, and while similar incidents are possible, they are not common.

incident_description: The base station to my Infant Optics baby monitor started smoking while charging.  The device and cord were extremely hot and smoldering when found.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident involved a potential fire hazard, making it an incident with possible reoccurrence.

incident_description: My Microsoft surfacebook 2 laptop computer was being charged at my desk overnight.  I noticed that the point where the charger connects to the computer had begun to melt and and had burnt.  I reached out to Microsoft, but they claimed it was caused by dirt without actually inspecting the product.  They refused to look at, let alone repair/replace the defective product.  I am concerned because it is clearly a fire hazard.
justification: While no injury occurred, the melted and burnt charger poses a fire hazard, making it an incident.

incident_description:
As an installer , I purchased a solid state hard drive from Office Max on June 4 2020.  The SSD (solid state drive) had been in use from June 5 to June 25 of this year. The end user notified me that he smelled something burning and asked if I would pick up the computer to have it checked out.  Upon inspection I found that the SSD had self ignited and burnt. The computer was still running when the 
problem was discovered .  No other components were damaged in the computer as the enclosure was metal and the drive was  far enough away from other components. I  contacted Sandisk /Western Digital regarding the problem and I think they have taken this problem too lightly. Had the SSD been 
installed in a laptop/notebook computer there would have been a possible fire.  I had sent them photos on the device indicating that the device was burnt almost in entirety and that the wire connections to the drive were only damaged near the drive . I feel that the SSD components of that model number be pulled from the market ASAP.  Office Max had discounted the drive to almost 25% of it's retail price . I suspect that Office Max wanted this series of drives GONE .
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the SSD self-igniting posed a potential fire risk if it had been in a laptop.

incident_description:
Surface Pro 4 (SP4) received brand new July 2017. Used SP4 as personal and work computer. On June 9, was actively using SP4 when suddenly the right side of the display popped out of the chassis. A few days before I had noted the SP4 no longer laid flat on a surface and was puzzled as to how and why that was the case when it wasn't like that before. On June 9th I used [REDACTED] to find out why the display would pop out suddenly. That's when  learned the cause was a swollen internal battery. I also learned many other people have had the same issue and have even report the issue to Microsoft on its online forum. Each person said Microsoft wasn't very responsive.

I contacted Microsoft on the following days to request resolution to the swollen battery and to learn about the exchange or replacement offering I learned about online:
June 9, 2020 - 3 times
June 10, 2020 - 2 times
June 11, 2020 - 1 time
June 15, 2020 - 4 times
June 18, 2020 - 1 time
July 1, 2020 - 2 times
July 2, 2020 - 5 times

I also reached out to Microsoft via [REDACTED] on the follow dates regarding the swollen battery:
June 9, 2020
June 10, 2020
June 12, 2020
June 15, 2020
June 16, 2020
June 18, 2020
June 26, 2020
July 1, 2020
July 2, 2020

The reason for the numerous contacts is because each time I called and attempted to speak to someone the Microsoft rep would place me on hold and then the phone system would hang up on me. Sometimes almost immediately. Other times I would be on the phone line for upwards of an hour before the phone system would disconnect me and then I would have to start all over again. Although the rep would ask me for my phone number in case we got disconnected, Microsoft had not one time attempted to call me back on any of these occasions. 

On June 18, I was finally able to speak to a Surface Support rep - [REDACTED].  He was able to add my device exchange request into the system and informed me Microsoft would send me a box so I could send the device back to them safely. The box would take 7-10 calendar days. It is now July 3rd and I still have yet to get a box!

On June 29 and July 2 I spoke with Microsoft and this is when they tell me I must pay $450 before they will send me a box. Why would Microsoft take ELEVEN (11) days before contacting me on June 29 to ask for payment (note - the Surface Support rep had asked me for the last 4-digits of my credit card also my credit card is on record with the company and has been for years). The manager I spoke with on July 2nd confirmed my credit card is on record AND admitted Microsoft was at fault for why it took ELEVEN (11) days to contact me. It then took an additional 3 days before I could speak to a manager to determine if Microsoft could overnight a box to me so that I would NOT have to wait another 7-10 days for a box. This was even more important because I'm about to embark on a multi-day road trip. I told the Microsoft rep, [REDACTED], this on June 18th and I had wanted to be sure that I could get the fire hazard swollen battery out of my house before I leave. I also said I did not want to travel with it in a car because of my concern the battery might explode while it is in the car. I was told weeks ago that even though the device is not in use nor is being charged that the battery still could explode on its own.

On July 2 I spoke to [REDACTED] a manager at Microsoft who repeatedly stated it is Microsoft's policy to collect $450 before the shipping box would be sent. She also told me she could not overnight a box to me so I could ship the device before leaving on the roadtrip. Microsoft also would not give me any information so I could use its preferred carrier and ship the device to them on my own. I was told it is against policy for a customer to ship the device to Microsoft. Microsoft was NOT willing to come up with any shipping alternatives other than to delay my trip and wait for the box to be sent to me in 7-10 days OR to dispose of the unsafe device myself (which would prevent me from receiving a replacement or exchange device (for a fee) due to the battery being a fire hazard. I honestly believe Microsoft wants to deter exchanges at the detriment of its clients.

I'm including all of this information because I am flabbergasted that even though Microsoft agrees the battery is a safety concern that Microsoft doesn't seem to care about doing what it can to provide me with the necessary shipping materials to quickly get the failed battery out of a consumer's hands and into their possession as quickly as possible.

P.S., unable to upload photos of the damaged device because the borrowed laptop I'm using now is VERY old and doesn't have something needed to get the "Add Files" feature on another page to work. I did send photos to Microsoft of the damage display due to the swollen battery on June 18th.
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a significant hardware failure (swollen battery) that could have led to property damage or injury, and it occurred repeatedly in multiple devices.

incident_description: When I was repainting my spare bedroom I was moving everything out.   The JVC model EM42FTR broke from its base at the neck and landed on my foot..  I was lucky that I was wearing my work boots when this happened..
justification: Injury occurred due to equipment failure, but the outcome could have been worse without protective footwear.

incident_description:
The consumer indicates that he was charging his cell phone overnight with the power bank when he was awaken by an explosion at 0545. He looked to his nightstand and noticed that the power bank had caught fire and there was smoke everywhere. The consumer immediately threw the power bank on the floor and then picked it up with a broom scooper to take it outside. The unit was still in flames. The consumer notes that his cell phone was not damaged.

The consumer contacted the retailer and explained the situation; the representative he spoke to informed him that he would escalate his case to the correct Department.

The consumer states that the product was used daily for one or two hours.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident of a power bank catching fire poses a significant risk to property and future occurrences are possible.

incident_description:
On Friday, June 5th around 2AM I got out of bed and went downstairs to watch TV. I plugged my phone- a new Motorola Razr that I pre-ordered back in January (delivered in February), into the same charger I use every day, placed it on the coffee table and turned on the TV. After watching TV for about an hour I decided to go back to bed. When I went to pick up the phone and go back to bed I screamed in pain and dropped the phone on the floor. It had gotten incredibly hot. It was like grabbing a hot pan out of the oven. The phone was smoking and the case was starting to melt. I suffered minor burns on my hand and there was no significant property damage- but if I had fallen asleep it would have started a fire. It could have burned the house down and my family could have been seriously hurt or killed. 

The phone was rendered inoperable and Motorola has refused to make things right. They have been jerking me around for more than a week.
justification: The incident resulted in minor burns, and if left unattended, the phone could have caused a house fire, potentially leading to serious injuries or death.

incident_description: Sound Mates [REDACTED] caught fire during charging. S/N mm19205761 bought at JC Penny's in [REDACTED] Montana on 11/29/2019
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no reported injuries, making it a level 2 severity. The likelihood is rated 3 as it's possible but not certain that similar incidents could occur.

incident_description: While wearing the Apple Air Pod pros, I experienced a high pitched sound coming from the right ear bud. The sound was extremely loud and left my right ear ringing. Now when I take the air bud out of the case, the loud sound activates. I am scared to try to fix the issue because of how loud the sound is and the possibility of damaging my hearing.
justification: The incident resulted in immediate hearing discomfort and potential long-term damage, warranting a severity level of 3.

incident_description:
Microsoft Surface book purchased 2016. Noticed today the top portion, the screen, which contains a lithium ion battery is significantly swollen. The laptop will no longer close.

Microsoft acknowledges this as a safety issue but refuses to do any corrective action other than charging a replacement fee which is as much as a new laptop.
justification: The incident involves a swollen battery, posing a potential fire hazard, but no injuries have been reported.

incident_description:

incident_description:
My Microsoft Surface Pro 4, purchased on March 12, 2017, began showing an orange-ish blotch on the lower left side of the screen in early to mid-May 2020.  The computer also became very hot to the touch.  I searched Microsoft Support and found multiple postings about this problem, all stating that the battery was swollen.  I followed the steps indicated by users and confirmed the same battery swelling; Microsoft itself stated that the battery could not be replaced or repaired and recommended that the entire unit be replaced.

I use the MSP 4 daily, as my primary computer.

My local computer repair center stated that they do not work on Microsoft products.

What alarmed me was a November 5, 2017 posting on the Microsoft Support pages, from volunteer moderator [REDACTED]:  "this sounds like the battery is expanding. and you should not use your Surface."

This 2.5 year discussion is found at  [REDACTED]

I also followed some instructions found on the same Support pages, accessed the "Surface Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) and got the following message, again one that alarmed me:
"If the orange splotch is present on the UEFI screen, it's a hardware issue and device needs replacing." 
Of course, the orange splotch was still present.

I am concerned:  (1) that Microsoft has known about this dangerous problem - a swollen battery in a computer - for over 2.5 years, and only asks consumers to pay even more money for a refurbished product that most likely will end up in the same dangerous condition; and (2) that my personal safety is at risk due to Microsoft's cavalier attitude - "you have a dangerous problem?  Send us more money."  

My problem unit:  Microsoft Surface Pro 4, intel Core 5, 4 GB memory, 128 GB solid state drive.

Bottom line:  I have a computer with a swelling battery that could explode at any time, and which leads to the computer being extremely hot to the touch.  That is NOT consumer product safety.
justification: The incident involves a swollen battery, which poses a risk of explosion and severe burns, hence a severity level of 3. The likelihood is high as Microsoft has been aware of the issue for over 2.5 years and users continue to report the problem.

incident_description:
The product is a Cord Of Steel metal phone charger for [REDACTED]. 

It was plugged in to charge a phone, where it has been for the past year without incident. There had been no damage to the cord, and nothing was done differently than any other night. My wife went to plug her phone in, and the cord sparked from the middle, and got red hot, causing my wife to drop it to the floor. After hitting the floor, the cord sparked one more time, before exploding and catching fire. The explosion happened in the middle of the cord, and sent pieces of red hot metal across the room, melting my carpet and causing spot fires outside of the main fire where the cord is. 

Due to the cord being completely metal, if the middle of the cord is on fire the rest of it will be red hot. Unfortunately I was not able to pull the cable out of the wall without grabbing the cord, and was burned on my hands pulling it from the wall. Luckily they were small burns and did not require medical attention. After the cord was unplugged from the wall, I was able to douse the cord with a heavy blanket and put out the main fire. The piece of shrapnel that followed the explosion landed about 4 feet away, and was still red hot when I used pliers and a knife to cut out my carpet and remove the piece that was smoldering in the foam carpet pad. 

The cord was plugged into an indoor certified extension cord, with 1 other item (a lamp) plugged into that as well. There were no problems with the lamp, nor the extension cord.
justification: Injury occurred due to direct contact with the burning cord, and the likelihood of such an event is high given the product's design flaw and continuous use.

incident_description:
The battery in my Dell Laptop (Dell Latitude E5570) became 'swollen' recently. This is something that happens to laptop batteries sometimes.. when the battery gets old and gets towards the end of its usable life, the casing inside the battery starts to deteriorate and the electrolyte / battery acid stuff starts to leak within the battery which releases gas, and the battery starts to bulge. This can be extremely dangerous, we've all seen videos online of smartphones and laptops exploding out of nowhere. 

This happened to my Dell battery and has happened to hundreds of other people. If you just Google 'Dell swollen battery' you'll find posts online of tons of people that this happened to. I've even read accounts of people whose laptops started smoking or even caught fire. There is risk of the battery / laptop catching on fire or even exploding. 

And even if you catch it early and take the battery out, now you have a partially broken, bulging battery that is essentially a dangerous piece of toxic waste. You can't just dispose of them normally either because it's dangerous to sanitation workers. I now have to make an appointment with my county's Household Hazardous Waste processing facility. 

This is very simply a failure of quality control on the part of Dell that is a threat to people's lives and homes. Please do something about it.
justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident poses a high likelihood of property damage or fire, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' scenario.

incident_description:
Microsoft is apparently aware of a known issue with the original Surface Book where, after a number of years, the battery in the clipboard (screen unit that houses processor and most computing parts) begins swelling.  My particular unit indicated this is happening a few days ago.  The battery has swollen to the point that it has separated the screen from its bezel (i.e., the battery is pushing the screen from its mount).  This is a huge safety issue as a swelling battery can explode or catch fire.  Microsoft has not alerted owners of these devices to this issue and only offers repair at $599.  These units should be recalled and repaired immediately.  Microsoft lists "lifted or bulging screens" in the drop-down lists for issues about this system but does not explain that the issue is caused by the battery swelling.  When I contacted Microsoft Support, the representative explained that the unit could not be shipped in this condition because of the level of hazard presented by the battery.  

This issue can cause serious bodily harm if the battery explodes.
justification: The battery swelling poses a high risk of explosion or fire, potentially causing serious injury.

incident_description:
My 20-year-old son's Blackview cellphone spontaneously caught fire last night (April 30, 2020). 

It was sitting on the wood floor of his bedroom, unplugged and not being used (he was in the room using his desk computer), when the fire alarm in his room went off. He looked around the room and saw that the phone was on fire. The burning phone made a great deal of smoke in just a few moments, partially melting onto the floor and filling his room with smoke. Luckily, he was alert and threw the phone out the window onto the back lawn, then went outside to put out the flames. Our house was filled with smoke, so I am also concerned about the health effects of our exposure to the smoke. 

If my son had been asleep at the time, with no fire alarm in his room, the phone fire could have killed him and everyone else in the house from either the smoke or the flames. The phone was in use until the day it caught fire, but this brand is clearly unsafe and potentially deadly, and should be recalled immediately.
justification: The phone's spontaneous combustion and rapid smoke production could have caused injury or death if my son was asleep and unaware.

incident_description:
My Microsoft Surface Pro 4 started showing a light brownish/yellowish tinge on the left side of the screen in mid-March 2020. Believing it had something to do with the Surface Pen which is magnetically mounted in approximately the same area, I removed the pen. I noticed the screen issue getting worse over the next couple of weeks, and then noticed the screen itself beginning to bulge from its fame as well as increased heat while the computer was on.

They offer either a refurbed model, or an upgraded model, often for a fee of several hundred dollars, although it seems a few people have not had to pay anything for a replacement.

In my case, I called their support team, and was offered a similar model for $450. I responded that I didn't think I wanted to give them more money for a unit which may eventually have the same issues. (I've since chosen to purchase a different computer from another company.)

My Surface unit was used approximately every other day and on weekends as my personal computer. It was not an everyday work computer, so never saw continued heavy usage.

Here's a link to the Microsoft Community where the Surface Pro 4 battery discussion has been taking place:
https://answers.microsoft.com/en-us/surface/forum/surfpro4-surfdrivers/microsoft-surface-pro-4-battery-bulgingsafety/cca7387e-ae9a-464f-b0e9-a9f947d3c768?page=1

My Surface Pro 4 was purchased on 05/18/16. The warranty expired 08/16/2017.
