incident_description:
I plugged my Kindle Fire HD in to charge it. Sparks started shooting out of the charging slot. When I unplugged it and removed the cable, the charging cable was on fire and covered in molten plastic.

The engineers in the extended family examined the Kindle and cable and concluded the problem originated with the Kindle, not the cord.

I contacted Amazon about the problem. They seemed unconcerned and did not want to examine the Kindle.

I am concerned because if this is a problem with aging Kindles, other people could get hurt. The only reason this incident resolved w/o injury is because I happened to be the one in the room with Kindle at the time.  If it had been a child, and usually my children are the ones using the Kindle, then injury or property damage could have resulted.

I feel that Amazon is not taking these concerns seriously enough, since electronics should not suddenly burst into flame, even if they're 2 or 3 years old.
justification: The incident resulted in no injury but had the potential for serious harm, as evidenced by the fire and molten plastic, and the involvement of children who typically use the device.

incident_description: I have a first generation Kindle Fire tablet that is about 2 years old. The battery has expanded to almost an inch think and has completely split the case. I'm afraid this might explode or be dangerous. I called Amazon customer support and was told "do not charge the tablet as it might explode" but they offered no help and was not concerned at all that there product was unsafe and could potentially harm someone or burn their house down.
justification: The battery expansion and potential explosion risk warrant a severity level of 2, as no injuries have been reported yet. The likelihood is rated 3 as the customer's concern and Amazon's warning suggest a possibility of occurrence.

incident_description: I have had a FitBit Flex since October of 2014. The wristbands are causing rashes on my left wrist and uncontrollable urges to scratch. I have replaces the bands with new ones and the same thing is happening. My wrist becomes irritated to the point u have to scratch it and when I do, it begins to bleed. I never have had this problem with any watches or other wrist bands I have worn. The rash will start to go away if I do not wear my FitBit even for a day, but comes roaring back if I put it on again.
justification: The incident involves physical injury (scratching and bleeding) and the likelihood is high as the issue persists despite replacing the wristbands.

I called Thermaltake to report the incident but they were defensive and said that my product was out of warranty.

The product was a Thermaltake Purepower 500 power supply.

incident_description:
The consumer purchased the kit from different retailers to go with security cameras (Model # PRO 752). The consumer installed the kit at his new house that is being built. 

The consumer stated that he installed the cameras with the wiring that came in the kit. The consumer had a home inspection conducted. The electrical inspector stated that the wiring does not pass code and that he cannot have that particular wiring for in wall use.

The consumer was informed that he can contact the manf and get a letter from them stating that the wiring is approved for in wall use. The consumer contacted the manf and they informed him that the wiring is not approved for in wall use. He would have to purchase in wall wiring for that.

The consumer stated that the packaging shows outdoor installation and then does not come with appropriate/approved wiring to be able to do the installation while meeting the code.

The consumer stated that the intent of the camera is to be mounted on the exterior. There are directions inside the kit stating that the wiring cannot be used in sunlight or rain. 

The consumer was informed by the company that he would have to put the wiring in a conduit if he would want to use it outdoors. If he wants to use it indoors, he cannot have the wiring hidden in wall.

The consumer stated that the packaging or direction does not instruct the user of all this. The consumer can only find that out by calling the company. The company only offers options to make new purchases.

The caller stated that all of the wirings the manf sells in the kits cannot be used the way they are depicting on the pictures. The manf fails to put proper warning and instructions on the packaging or manual.
justification: The incident involves a product mislabeling issue, which could lead to non-compliance with building codes but no immediate physical harm.

incident_description: I received the Fitbit flex band as a Christmas present.  I started wearing the band almost immediately and did not have issues with it until about 2 months after wearing it.  I developed a rash on my right wrist where the skin was red, inflamed, extremely dry and itchy.  The rash did not go away for about 3 weeks after I was able to get steroid cream and use it on the rash.  The rash then went away about 2 days later. I attempted to wear the band on my left wrist and made sure to wear the band looser, did not wear it in the shower and made sure to clean it with a light detergent once a day to see if this would prevent my wrist from developing a rash.  After about 1 week of wearing the flex band on my left wrist, my wrist also developed the rash.
justification: The individual experienced a rash and itching, which is considered an injury, and the likelihood of reoccurrence is high as it happened on both wrists despite preventive measures.

incident_description:
Within one week of wearing the fitbit surge on my left arm I began to have an uncontrollable itch that felt similar to what one would feel with athletes foot.  I would take the band off for breaks when I was not moving but otherwise would leave the band on almost the entire day and when sleeping.  Afterall, it is an activity tracker and that is what it is supposed to do so you can't really take it off if you want accurate tracking.

After 2 weeks the area started to become red.  After 3 weeks the skin began to become scaly and is now flaking.  I have started applying anti-fungal cream and powder to help heal the rash and prevent it from getting any worse.

While I don't believe it is any materials in the product that are causing the rash, I do believe that the design of the band is to blame.  It is a wide band with no breathable mesh holes to allow the skin access to fresh air or to dry appropriately when sweating.  The tracker is worn when a person is working out or even when they are at rest, but the skin is always exuding oils and other fluids.  The lack of oxygen and drying likely causes a habitat well suited for bacteria to grow on the skin.  

Many times after working out the band and the skin underneath the band will exude a foul odor indicative of bacterial growth.

Fitbit should take some responsibility for their product by acknowledging the design is partly to blame and should rectify by releasing a band that allows the skin to breath properly.
justification: Skin irritation and infection (scaly, flaking skin) caused by lack of breathability in the Fitbit Surge band.

incident_description:

After being charged in a regular 110-volt home outlet, it was not plugged in again nor used to provide power to other devices before the explosion.  (It would typically be used as a way of charging a cell phone or other small electronic device.)

We traveled overseas with the device but didn't end up needing to use it.  Hours after arriving back in the US it spontaneously exploded on a counter top.  It was not plugged in to anything at the time it exploded.  The fire was quickly contained but smoke and other damage occurred.  I am horrified to think what would have happened if the device had exploded in my carry-on during the flight, or while I was carrying it in my backpack.

I immediately alerted the accounting firm of BDO about the incident since they had provided it as a gift.  They put me in touch with Office Depot, the distributor of the device, and another group called [REDACTED] who sourced the devices for Office Depot.  All parties have claimed that they have had no other reported incidents with the device in question but I am pressing BDO to issue an alert to all of the recipients of the device.
justification: The device exploded spontaneously, causing smoke and damage, but no injuries.

incident_description:

The 12 year old was awake walking around March 14th, 2015 around 1:00AM and listening to music when all of a sudden he began screaming then telling his mother that something was in his right ear and was hurting him.  

His mother checked and found that the silicone piece that had been on the plug was no longer attached to the right side but was still on the left side.

The child continued to repeat that the ear hurt while the caller took him to Children's Hospital Emergency room in Aurora, Colorado .

Doctors there used a scope to see that the silicone piece was lodged in his ear.  

They discussed surgery but instead flushed his ear until they could bring the piece into reach. They placed an intravenous catherter.

They were then able to remove the piece with their tweezer tool (alligator forceps).

The 12 yr old was prescribed antibiotics and pain medicine then released.

The caller contacted the manufacturer March 16th, 2015 at 1 (877) 397-8200 and was advised that she would be contacted later that day.  The caller did not obtain the manufacturer's representative's name and she has received no return caller from
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (ear pain and lodged silicone piece) to the 12-year-old autistic child, making it a 'possible' occurrence given the age-appropriateness of the product and the child's autism.

incident_description:
This report concerns the release of potentially harmful or toxic fumes from a particular model of cable TV boxes supplied by Comcast to its cable subscribers. The problem involves a strange odor that comes from my new cable box, a Motorola RNG200N, an odor that has been reported by many other Comcast customers repeatedly over the past few years (see below).  The odor becomes noticeable when the box is connected to power but disappears when disconnected.  The odor seems related to ordinary heating in the cable box (my cable box is fully ventilated according to installation instructions) and, given the nature of the odor and the internal components of cable boxes, it seems entirely possible that the odor indicates that harmful or toxic fumes are being released into the home environment.  I don't have the resources to have the fumes analyzed, but it is very concerning that this odor has persisted ever since I received the cable box a few months ago.  Comcast has denied that there is a problem with these cable boxes, but this problem appears to be widespread and has been reported by a large number of customers to Comcast on its own help and support forum website, dating back to 2012.  See 

http://forums.comcast.com/t5/XfinityTV-and-Equipment/musty-smell/td-p/1514161

and

http://forums.comcast.com/t5/XfinityTV-and-Equipment/bad-smell-coming-from-2-of-my-cable-boxes/td-p/1927857

As the Comcast customer postings explain, Comcast refuses to acknowledge that there is any problem with the cable boxes despite the large number of documented complaints. This lends credence to the idea that the fumes are harmful or toxic - Comcast may be concerned about potential liability relating to this problem and it doesn't want to admit that it has been aware of a problem for a number of years without taking any action. I don't know where else to turn, and apparently neither do the others who have reported this. No one wants their families to be exposed to potentially hazardous fumes.  Please look into this.
justification: Widespread reports of potentially harmful fumes from cable boxes, with Comcast's denial suggesting possible liability concerns.

incident_description:
On Sat, March 7, 2015 at approx. 2:30pm., I discovered  my garage fully engulfed in white smoke,
I immediately called 911 and  Montgomery County MD Fire Dept.(MCFD) responded. Upon arrival, the 
cause of the smoke was determined to have been  a Ryobi 40 volt lithium battery charger located 
on top of a refrigerator in the garage.  It should be noted the charger was NOT plugged  in and  
battery had last been utilized  in Oct. 2014 prior to being cradled in the charger for the winter.
MCFD determined the charger overheating had caused  the resulting small fire/smoke to burn  the
plastic (charger/ battery)  and  paint (top of refrigerator). MCFD utilized  a heat seeking device 
to locate the  source of the fire/smoke after first ruling out the refrigerator plug as the cause. 
The charger/battery were destroyed and refrigerator damaged. Additionally, smoke damage was
evident  behind  the  refrigerator, which leads directly into the family room  of the residence. 
MCFD also  indicated  that  the  timing of my opening  the garage  doors after smelling  the smoke 
in the family room  limited the fire/smoke damage from spreading to other locations inside the  
residence. I purchased the Ryobi charger & battery  in Sept. 2014 from The Home Depot as part of a 
Ryobi Expand It grass trimmer/ tree pruning kit.

On  March 7,  at approx. 3:30pm., I  contacted Ryobi Customer Service and  the CPSC to report  the incident. I was told by Ryobi that the incident was being forwarded to their Safety Division and that a Safety Officer would contact me within 48 hours. On Mon., March 9 the CPSC contacted me; however, I have not been contacted by Ryobi as of this writing (March 10 & 11) to no avail. Ryobi customer service will not allow the consumer to speak with the Ryobi Safety Division. 

The weather conditions were dry, approx. 40 degrees, with snow on the ground.
justification: No injuries occurred, but the incident caused property damage and could have potentially spread to other areas of the residence.

You can find our complete, dermatologist-reviewed instructions at https://www.fitbit.com/productcare. We also recommend that you remove the device if you start to experience skin irritation on your wrist. If symptoms persist longer than 2-3 days after removing the device, contact your physician."

incident_description:
Product: the "iOpener" by ifixit.com

The iOpener is a glycerol-filled container that is heated in the microwave and then used to heat [REDACTED] cases to ease in their opening (by heating the adhesive holding together their cases.)

I used the iOpener very strictly according to the directions. I never heated it for longer than 30s in the microwave and waited significantly more than the 2-minutes between heatings minimum that they recommend.  On the first heating, I wrapped the iOpener in a damp paper towel, as recommended, and on the 2nd and 3rd heatings, it was on top of the damp paper towel.

After the 3rd heating, which was for 30s, the iOpener appeared normal while sitting in the microwave - no obvious leakage or damage.  However, when I picked it up by one end and the iOpener went vertical, it burst about 1 or 2 seconds later as I was walking with it to my work table. When it burst, it sprayed hot glycerol over my torso and then leaked on to my foot resulting in 2nd-degree burns in both locations.  The contents definitely seemed to escape "under pressure" and I have a photo showing how the contents sprayed onto my shirt (the pattern is interesting - not random). 

I would think that even if overheated, the glycerol should not escape under pressure and so my own suspicious revolve around 2 issues;
 1) the manufacture allows too much air into the inside of the iOpener; this air can get superheated, expand, and cause failures,   or,
 2) i was operating the device in Santa Fe, New Mexico at an altitude very close to 7500' above sea level.  perhaps the quantity of air inside the iOpener  and the pressure differential was enough to cause failure at this altitude but the same conditions do not result in failure at sea-level.   

I have photos of my blisters as well.  I notified the company of the failure and they sent me a replacement which I am loathe to use given that it is the most dangerous consumer product I've run across in my 55 years.
justification: The incident resulted in second-degree burns, and the product's failure to contain the heated glycerol under pressure was likely due to manufacturing defects or altitude-related issues, making it a likely occurrence.

incident_description:
Near the very end of 2013, my dad and I bought a Belkin cooling unit for my laptop computer.  For most of the year, while it worked, it did not work well.  I began to notice lighter marks on the grey plastic, about half a year in, and thought nothing of it.  I'd thought them the result of wear and tear on the thing, and probably from continually setting my computer down on it.

Apparently, they were singe marks.  Because on January 29th, at some point between midnight and 5am, my cooling unit caught fire, directly next to my left hip.  I heard sputtering, and wasn't sure what it was, but then noticed the little trail of smoke, emitting from my computer.  Looking down, I saw the open flame, which had burned the USB plug off of its wire, and was spraying flame out for about an inch, next to my flammable pants and blankets.

Immediately, I shut down my computer, to end the power source, and the flame died out.  I wasn't burned and nothing (except the Belkin cooling unit) caught fire.  It caused more white singe marks, around the area where the plug caught fire.  They match the previous singe marks, near the top of the unit.

We took the unit back to Wal-Mart the next day, but they said that it was not their job to report such things, and that we would have to do so.  They encouraged me to take photos of what happened, and contact Belkin directly.  But I did not wish to do so, because I have noticed that most companies do not like admitting to fault, in cases of dangerous incidents.  I doubted that anything would be done.

After some asking around, no one knew where to report this to, so I just typed in "Where do I report dangerous products?" into Bing, and it gave me your site.  Several other sites, listed beneath it, also referenced your site as the place to go.  So.

I've got 3 pictures of the singe marks and melted cable on my Belkin unit.  I'd imagine that several people could be harmed, by the sudden appearance of an unexpected flame.  I hope you guys can use my report, to stop this problem from hurting anybody.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire next to the individual's hip, posing a significant risk of injury.

incident_description:
Product Info: Verizon branded 120 VAC charger for Iphone 5C
Model:  A36-524A

Unit started arcing when plugged in to receptacle.  Examination found that glue securing face of transformer failed causing face to become loose from transformer body.  Face of unit contains "prongs" for insertion in to receptacle.  The "prongs" are connected to transformer strip contacts only via pressure provided by glue connection of face (no mechanical screws or solder).  When glue started failing contact became intermittent resulting in arcing out of the unit. 

Fortunately I noticed and disconnected immediately and there were no combustibles in the vicinity to ignite.  However, had this been plugged in to a receptacle near bedding or other easily ignitable materials and gone unnoticed it easily would have been the source of a fire.  

Currently being a Fire Protection Engineer for the US Navy and retired municipal fire chief, I feel compelled to report such an incident as additional such failures could become the sources of fires and injury if it were near bedding.

Note that after incident I completely detached face of unit to prevent its use.  I can provide photos of item if interested.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident could have led to a fire if combustibles were nearby, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' scenario with a high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
Vantec CB-ISATAU2 SATA/IDE to USB 2.0 Adapter

This product comes with a Flypower power supply, and an AC cable with a standard PC connector (IEC C13), which is labeled '10A 250V'  Mine began MELTING under a load of 2.6A 123V.  10A is the minimum legal rating, which usually requires at least 18AWG conductors, and this cable has those about the size of what you'd find in a USB cable.  I have also received reports that [REDACTED] sells a similar USB hard drive adapter with the same problem.

There are no safety instructions whatsoever in the instructions manual, and Vantec's reply to my email was, "This kit is designed for connecting one Hard drives. It is not intended other purpose.".  This clearly is not an acceptable excuse.  I accidentally mixed this cable in with some other power cables, and when hooked up to a computer, the cable started melting within 5-10 minutes of operation.  If I weren't there watching it, it could have easily started a fire.  [REDACTED], however, has contacted me by phone, saying that they are willing to work to resolve the issue.

Since I've already identified two products with similarly under spec cables, there are likely thousands out there in people's homes.  These types of power cables must be recalled, as well as any products that they are packaged with.  It is impossible to tell the cables apart by look or feel, meaning the only way to avoid a potential disaster is for consumers to throw out all their C13 power cables and buy new ones.

Full details, including pictures with side-by-side comparisons between the faulty cable and a standards compliant one can be found on my blog at http://frysacidtest.com/?p=217

Amazon says they will take the product off the market in 7 days if they agree with my findings, UL says they have no interest since the cable itself is not marked with the (UL) logo, I have yet to hear back from NC's Attorney General's office.  My blog received 30,000 hits in 1 day, and the YouTube video I made got 3,000 hits in 12 hours.  Many people on Reddit have expressed concern that they have similar cables mixed in with good ones.

Please help me get these cables and any product that includes them off the market, before more damage is done.

I'm bipolar, and have been unable to sleep for at least 3 days, while I have been working 24hr/day trying to spread this message.  Please let me know that this issue is being taken care of, because I'm unable to stop, in good conscience, until the matter is resolved.

Thank you.

-[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a power cable melting under normal operating conditions, posing a fire risk but no immediate injuries.

incident_description:
I have an Aurora paper shredder Model: AS1019CS  Serial: ADG1019013635 that was bought in December 2007.  On September 20, 2014, after being gone for about 8 hours, I came home to find my paper shredder running on its own.  I instantly could smell a "burnt wiring" smell when I came into the house.  As I approached the room where the shredder was located I could see the room filled with smoke and smoke pouring out of the top of unit.  I quickly turned off unit with the switch and unplugged it.  Since I was gone, I have no idea how long the shredder was running on its own.  For two days I could smell this smell of "burnt wiring" throughout the house before it finally dissipated.

The power switch was in the "auto" mode which I always had it. In reading the manual it talks about not running the shredder for more then 10 minutes to prevent it from overheating.  However it also talks about a safety thermal overload switch that will shut the power off if it does overheat.  Obviously, this safety thermal switch did not work on my unit and nearly caused a fire.
justification: The shredder running unattended and overheating could have caused a fire, but no injuries or damages were reported.

incident_description: LOREX WL4320: SERIOUS BATTERY FLAW: purchased this baby monitor just under a year ago.  After a few days of use, the battery would not keep a charge (NOT safe to have a baby monitor shutting off shortly after being removed from the AC cable).  Got a replacement battery from Lorex.  A few months later the 2nd battery wouldn't hold a charge and expanded breaking out the battery tray cover (? fire risk).  Got a 3rd battery from Lorex.  Over the past week the 3rd battery is expanding again, and won't hold a charge.  CLEARLY this product should be recalled entirely as a safety risk.   Please CPSC: even if the device does not catch fire, it is a risk to infants if the monitor shuts off very prematurely when on battery power-- you have an unmonitored infant.  As a board certified sleep disorders specialist, let me also add how extremely dangerous this is, to have a completely unmonitored infant, when parents falsely believe their monitor is working.  NOTE: after contacting Lorex today to find out about getting a 4th battery, and finding out they have a technical bulletin on this, isn't that enough for the CSPC to force a mandatory recall and refund program for parents owning this flawed device?
justification: The battery issue, if not addressed, could lead to unmonitored infants, posing a significant risk.

incident_description:
My Philips PowerSquid surge protector nearly burned my 10 year old daughter and her friend.  She plugged in her keyboard, and then left.  Moments later when she returned to attempt to plug in her disco ball, the surge protector arch flashed into flames.  The flames just missed her head and face!   By the grace of God neither one of the children were harmed, but they were in shock!  Unfortunately, the fire severely burned up the surge protector and surrounding area of my carpet.  
I was unable to identify what caused this malfunction.  The only other electronic that was plugged into the surge protector was a TV, but it was not turned on at the time.
I immediately reported this incident to Philips and emailed them several photos of the surge protector and damages carpet.  I was asked to send a copy of my receipt, but I just moved from Montana to Texas.  Therefore, I purged a lot things, so don't believe I'll be able to find my receipt.  
Unfortunately, due to not being able to produce my receipt, I was denied any compensation for the damaged items.  Nor were they interested in investigating their product to determine the cause for the malfunction.  
I also posted a consumer review comment on the Phillips website regarding my experience with this product.  My comment was removed and I received an email stating that my comment didn't follow their review guidelines.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant fire hazard, making it an incident with potential for serious harm.

incident_description: On December 3, 2014 I reached out to Fitbit customer service to let them know that the aqua band had caused a rash on my arm. They advised that I give my wrist a break since and follow the care instructions. I did that. I let it rest until yesterday December 29, 2014. I switched the fitbit back to the original black band since I had no irritation. The rash is back with a full vengeance. It itches and burns.
justification: The incident resulted in a rash that caused itching and burning, indicating an injury.

incident_description: I recently purchased a 4-in-1 outlet strip/surge protector from Harbor Freight Tools. It pretty much blew up in my face when I put a little bit of pressure on the plastic housing because a sloppy solder connection left a long piece of wire close enough to reach the opposite terminal. The extra length instantly vaporized with a flash and a cloud of smoke as soon as they touched. The white interior of the strip was left with a large burn mark and smoky stain. I have a photo.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries but caused significant damage to the device, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is rated 3 as it's possible but not certain that other units of the same product may have similar manufacturing defects.

incident_description:
I bought a Samsung Galaxy 4s late spring or early summer of 2014. The phone started acting up the end of September 2014. I contacted Samsung who at no point indicated what my phone was doing was similar to what happened when the phones burn. I took it to the retail store where I purchased the phone, no one there indicated it could be a serious problem.

Initially the phone got hot when it charged, then it would only charge to 10 -15%. While charging approximately the first of October 2014 the phone literally melted to my counter. The area around the charging port was black and melted. This is not an isolated incident as my daughters did the same thing while laying on a coffee cup. (She knew what mine did and was protecting her property.)

I realize nothing will be done, it seems Samsung has been given free reign to distribute a device that has had more than a few hundred melt and/or burn furniture including beds people were sleeping in.

Samsung did replace my new phone with a refurbished phone but has yet to honor their promise they would also pay for property damage and out of pocket expenses which occurred by replacing the phone. [REDACTED] has stated he wants to work it out with my unit (apt) manager. I am confused as to why he thinks my manager is involved in my personal cell phone matters.
justification: Multiple incidents of Samsung Galaxy 4s phones melting and causing property damage, including beds and furniture, have been reported.

incident_description: I herd a cracking sound and saw little puffs of brownish smoke  from the AC jack on the computer. I pulled the cord from the Laptop and it was very hot to the touch. I pulled the cord from the AC outlet and that part of the cord was very hot and burned my hand. I have been having problems charging the computer ever since. That incident happened over this past summer around the fourth of July.
justification: Injury occurred due to direct contact with a hot power cord, indicating a high likelihood of similar incidents.

incident_description: I purchased a Fitbit Flex in June, 2014, and have been using it daily.  In October, I started getting redness, swelling, & itching on my left wrist under my Flex wristband.  It was mild/annoying at first, but kept increasing in intensity.  I switched to my other wrist and get the same allergic reactions.  I follow the Fitbit instructions for care of the wristband.  I do not use lotions, etc. on my wrists.  I can no longer use my Flex (for which I paid $100) as designed.  Upon investigating, I have discovered that this seems to be not atypical with the Flex, and that Fitbit has previously recalled it's Force wristband for similar reasons.
justification: User experienced allergic reactions and was unable to use the product as intended, causing discomfort and inconvenience.

justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and while it's possible, it's not likely to occur frequently due to the new product and proper usage.

incident_description: I recently replaced one of my surge strips. The strip I replaced was older, and it was recommended to me that I replace any surge strips made prior to 2004.  The strip was a Magnavox, model: m62949(p10015) E14544 The date code on the strip is 03.98c. The strip was working when I replaced it, and this was done solely because of the units age and the recommendation that older strips be replaced. I decided to take the old strip apart, mainly to recycle the plastic shell but also to see the setup and innards.  Upon unscrewing the plastic shell, and separating the two halves I was shocked to see the inside covered in soot around the electronic parts/switch. The strip is beige so the black soot is very noticeable.  Upon closer inspection I found what appears to originally have been blue, round, and what appears to be the MOV to have a hole in the center and covered in soot. It looks as though the mov either exploded or caught fire. Clearly something you do no want to see. I am glad it was not worse, but it easily could have been. There was no indication that there was any damage to the unit. The unit even has a reset switch, but it gave no hint that anything was wrong.
justification: Potential fire hazard indicated by soot and damaged MOV, though no immediate injury or damage occurred.

I was watching TV, there was a pop, a sizzling sound, bright light from behind it and then smoke started pouring out of the back of it. I unplugged it immediately. I contacted Hisense via email and phone on their warranty info page. I'm waiting to hear back. This happened tonight, 12-30-14 at 8pm. 
The serial number for this TV is 55G132777H03963
justification: The TV catching fire is an incident with no reported injuries, and while it's not common, it's not rare either given the age of the TV.

incident_description: Daughter was using her Apple I Mac Pro laptop computer when she smelled something burning. Upon further investigation it was discovered that the ac current battery charger that she was using while using her computer which was plugged into the wall had a wire that had burned through. This wire had been smoldering and could be seen as bare through the wire covering. We took the charger to the Apple store in Syracuse, NY and they stated that the wire had been flexed or bent repeatedly over time and that by not using the built in wire wrapping feet built into the unit the wire had degraded over time causing the problem. They said they had seen this before. The store claims that it is the users fault for not storing the ac wire properly when not in use. They state instructions regarding this issue are in the owners manual. However, it is my contention that even if this is so it is insufficient as the info is buried in the literature. A warning label or better design of where the wire enters the charger might help to prevent a future fire or electrocution. Luckily no injuries were sustained in this incident because we were alert and awake at the time of the incident.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a potential fire hazard due to a faulty charger, warranting a severity level of 2.

incident_description:
It was early on the morning of the New Year 2015, and I was sitting on the couch listening to music from my smart phone with the ear pods inserted into my ears. The maximum volume for the device is (16) sixteen, however, I had my player set on (13) while I listened to the music.  I was listening to the ÃÂOfficial WhipÃÂ song when midway through the song I heard a popping sound in my left ear, immediately removed the ear pods from my ears and noticed that all the background noises in the room sounded muffled through my left ear. In my left ear I could hear a continuous never-ending ringing sound along with a constant pounding that coincided with my heart beat. 			I did not tell anyone right away because I did not think it was anything serious, instead I ask my mom if I could have an ibuprofen for the pain I was experiencing. I went throughout the day and night hoping that the pain would subside and my ear would get better.  However, when I awoke I had blood and a pus like discharge coming from my left ear. Afraid of what may have happened to me, I quickly told my mother what had happened and she drove me to an urgent care facility (Medfast Urgent Care) in Fuquay-Varina, NC without delay. 							
Once at the urgent care facility I was examined by a Doctor who explained to my mother and I that I had a ruptured eardrum -- also known as a perforated eardrum or a tympanic membrane perforation. The doctor explained that my ear would heal on its own, but I now would face the possibility of and ear infection, so he prescribed antibiotic ear drops to help prevent my ear from becoming infected as well as Ibuprofen for pain. The doctor stated that he wanted me to have a follow up treatment in (4) four weeks.
justification: The incident resulted in a ruptured eardrum, causing pain and potential infection, but no life-threatening consequences.

incident_description:
I have owned my iPhone 3GS (16GB) for over 3 years now, and purchased it from its previous owner in pristine condition. It served me very well during that time, and always had great battery life. 3 months ago, I purchased a brand new iPhone 6 (64GB), at which time I stopped using my 3GS regularly. It sat in my desk drawer, until I brought it out last week to use as an iPod. Upon charging it up, it behaved erratically, and would randomly reboot. After leaving it for a number of days, my friend and I came back to find the casing had split open, and the battery had ballooned an alarming amount. The battery expanded so far that it split the main motherboard, and has broken several ribbon cables. As of now, even with a battery replacement, my phone is completely unusable. The SIM card tray was snapped when the screen assembly and main board separated from the back casing, but I have taken pictures to show this, as well as the Serial # and IMEI # for reference. 

I completely understand that my phone is well outside of the warranty period; that is not the issue I am addressing here, as I do not expect Apple to replace the product due to a failure. However, I do believe that this is a legitimate safety concern, and that there needs to be an effort on the part of the OEM (Apple Inc.) to provide consumers with warnings and instructions on what to do in this matter. 

I have researched the issue, and there are countless cases of this exact issue happening. In most cases when the consumer has contacted Apple regarding the issue, the official response has been that "the batteries are only designed to last approximately 2 years, at which point they will do that for safety reasons". If this is truly the case, then not only does that need to be documented with the product, informing the consumer of this when the product is originally purchased, but there also needs to be material giving direction on proper disposal of the product when this occurs, if they are in fact admitting to this issue.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (phone became unusable) and could have caused injury due to battery expansion, given the high prevalence of similar cases.

We purchased the Bayco extension cable a few months back for in our garage.On November 12, 2014 we were out there working on a project (thank god we were out there) and my daughter yelled the cord was sparking. We look up to see it spark and smoke. We grabbed the cord to unplug the items (nothing with a major draw, just a 50 w battery charger for a drill and a light, well under the 1250w 10 amp rating) and the cord had melted and broke into 2 pieces, we even had a flying piece of debris hit my son and burn his shoulder. At this point we had the unit unplugged but it was still smoking so my husband pulled it off the ceiling burning his fingers, but it was burning just inches from the Sheetrock. Once down we went to pull the cord out and just saw a melted bunch of extension cord. Right now I am just glad we happened to be working in there when this occurred or there was a very good chance it could have caused a house fire.

I contacted the manufacturer to report this issue and received the following response:
 "Thank you for bringing this to our attention.  Judging from your email,  it sounds like you have a retractable cord reel as opposed to an extension cord.  One of the Cautions listed in the instructions is that you need to pull out the cord to full length when using the receptacle.  If you use the cord for while it is wrapped inside the reel it can overheat and melt the cord.  It sounds like this is what happened with your cord reel. 
 
Please let me know if this is not correct.  We will be more than happy to take the reel back and inspect it to see what happened.
 
Thank you,
[REDACTED]
Customer Service

Well, no where on the label did it state I had to have the cord fully extended during use and in fact their web site states you can just pull out what you need (I have attached a screenshot of the product description showing this).
justification: Injury occurred when a piece of debris hit the son's shoulder, and the likelihood is high as the incident happened while the cord was in use and the manufacturer's instructions were not followed.

The flashlight did not come on so the consumer tried clicking and tapping it to make it come on. The consumer unscrewed the cap and took the batteries out to check if they were damaged. The batteries did not visibly damaged. The consumer assumed the batteries were run down. 

The consumer put the batteries back in the flashlight and sat it down on his kitchen counter. The consumer sat the flashlight face down. 

The consumer stated that about an hour later he heard something in the kitchen. Soon after (about 15 seconds later), he heard a loud explosion. The consumer stated that one of the battery shot out and is now charred. The consumer stated that something flew out to the ceiling and left a dent. The consumer stated that there was black powder on the ceiling and kitchen. The consumer stated that the second battery was still in the flashlight but it was all burnt and charred. 

The consumer stated that there was acid smell that was burning the nostrils. The consumer ventilated the area. 

The consumer stated that he is trying to clean up the black powder but it is difficult to clean it up. There is some black powder on the wall that he is unable to take off. The consumer stated that the powder got to the walls, counter, ceiling, pots and pans. The consumer stated that when they try to clean it up, the powder just spreads more. 

The consumer stated that he contacted [REDACTED] on 10/1/14. The consumer spoke to [REDACTED] in Product Service department. The consumer also spoke with [REDACTED], who was an engineer. They both informed him that it was the cheap Chinese batteries that caused the explosion. They informed the consumer that it was the batteries and content of the batteries that he was smelling. They asked to have the product sent back and offered a replacement.

incident_description:
In April 2014 I purchased a new LG Enact from Verizon Wireless. It came with the LG MCS-01WR Nexus 4 Micro-USB AC Adapter Charger Kit. 
The problem is with the LG MCS-01WR Nexus 4 Micro-USB AC Adapter Charger Kit. I kept hearing a buzzing or vibrating noise. When I learned it was the charger that was buzzing I checked it for damage which there was none. I then felt to see if the charger was hot to the touch and it was not, it was cool. The USB charger was still making a buzzing noise so I unplugged it from the wall. At that point my domestic partner wanted to see the phone and charger to check for damage when she touched the plug end of the charger and received a electrical shock that left a minor electrical burn with blisters. All this happened after the LG charger was unplugged from the electrical source.
 I tried to address this problem with Verizon Wireless and they were no help. They advised me to buy a new charger and stop using the LG MCS-01WR Nexus 4 Micro-USB AC Adapter. Which I already had done. 
My domestic partner also has a LG Enact that came with the LG MCS-01WR Nexus 4 Micro-USB AC Adapter Charger Kit purchased at the same time that is starting to make the same buzzing noise. Although we have not experienced the same exact problem with my domestic partners charger we have stopped using the chargers. 
I have looked at both the charger and phone for damage and I cant find any.
I still have the LG MCS-01WR Nexus 4 Micro-USB AC Adapter Charger and cell phone. I did not know who to contact regarding this issue so any help would be greatly appreciated.
justification: Minor electrical burn with blisters occurred due to a faulty charger, despite being unplugged from the power source.

The consumer believes it was due to overheating issues despite the fact that the five fans remain turned on so long as the computer is on. The computer monitor was purchased separately.

incident_description:
Bought Goal0 Sherpa 50 Battery approx 4/29/2012 from Amazon.com    

I bought the Sherpa 50 for my bug out bag. I took the Sherpa 50 on a camping trip, and it worked well for that trip. I used it to power some Bose speakers mounted on my backpack for a trial run. A year rolled by since then and I wanted to take it to the beach the following morning to give the Bose speakers some extended play. So, I plugged the Sherpa 50 it in at 11:30 pm. About 2 hours later my sister awoke me that she was nauseous that some noxious burnt electronic smell was coming from my office where she was sleeping near. I rushed into the room where the battery was being charged only to be sickened by the odor coming from the room. The battery had melted from the inside, and produced such a terrible smell, that I had to evacuate the house to a nearby hotel for 2 days to let the house air out. I placed the battery outside. I can still smell traces of the odor in room where I left it about 2 weeks later. When I contacted Goal Zero about the battery problem the next day, they knew all about it...I asked if it was toxic and would I need treatment for the 5 people that were present when the device failed. They stated it wasn't toxic that it was some sort of sodium battery and that it only happened on a few of the batches. They said that what happened was a few cells went dry over the course of a year and that the charger was trying to fully charge the dysfunctional battery bank, that's when the meltdown would occur. They have known about this problem for some time. I was LIVID when I realized that they didn't issue a recall or warning about the battery. It could have saved me a lot of headaches and money at 2:00am. It could have burned down my house if I was not home, killed the family pets, or worse .... if it turns out to be toxic it could have sickened family members. Even after my call to them, they didn't seem to interested in contacting Amazon to issue a recall. Seems morally bankrupt to me. I feel like my family's safety has been priced, a calculated risk because "only a small number fail". Well, that's great, unless your unaware and the owner. I find it criminally negligent not to issue at least a warning to watch it or charge it outside. I own dozens of cordless tools, not one battery charging failure there. I am going to make Amazon aware of this issue. Let me know if your experience was similar. Rest assured this product won't be there for you when you need it the most. It's an expensive hazard in my book. They company took my name and address, and said they would replace the product. So Far, nothing has come through. Empty promises. I'll issue an update on here if they make good on their promises. I'm interested to see if they issue a recall after this or after I flag it for Amazon to examine.

incident_description:
In October of 2012, a customer called to inform one of our HVAC service centers that a fire originating in the outside disconnect box of his air conditioning compressor had burned the side of his home.  The fire department responded and identified the source as the "Supco SCM150, Type 2 SPD,120/140V, 60Hz, Single Phase Surge Protector."  We reported the claim to our parent company, which took over the investigation and management of the insurance claim.  Though we could find no recall on the CPSC site, the center stopped using the Supco surge protectors as a precaution.  A little over a year later, we became an independent company after our parent company sold us and we never learned the outcome of their investigation.  

Unfortunately, in May of this year, a customer of one of our other centers had a very similar incident and our own investigation found that, again, a Supco SCM150 surge protector was involved.  Though we still could find no recall by the CPSC and neither our own parts distributer nor our former parent company reported any other issues, our insurance company did put Supco on notice.  However, Supco claimed that they were just the distributor of these surge protectors and that the manufacturer was a company by the name of Sycom.  Our insurance company's investigation was inconclusive and, because the customer did not seek damages from us, the claim was closed.  Internally, even though we could not be certain that all Supco SCM150 surge protectors were defective, we did notify our Sourcing Department and recommended to all of our general managers that they stop using the Supco surge protectors.

The last straw occurred yesterday, when a third center reported another fire involving the same Supco SCM150, Type 2 SPD,120/140V, 60Hz, Single Phase Surge Protector.  This time, the inspector from the customer's insurance company concluded that the surge protector was the cause of the fire.  Though the first couple of incidents could have been a coincidence, this third incident makes it clear that something is wrong with this product and we need to take the next step.  Our Sourcing Department is contacting our suppliers to ensure the Supco SCM150 is completely removed from our supply chain.  Though this will ensure that we never again install these surge protectors at our customers' homes, because we cannot ensure that any we have already installed are replaced as soon as possible, we are also notifying you in hopes that the CPSC will issue a recall and ensure the safety, not only of our customers, but also of any other consumers who may have had these surge protectors installed at their homes.  Thank you.
justification: Multiple incidents involving the same product model, with the most recent incident confirmed to be caused by the product.

incident_description:
Consumer wants to report a fire safety hazard. 

9/14/2014 In the evening, consumer noticed continuous battery status indicator light on. The consumer proceeded to reference the service manual of the unit but found nothing about the battery status indicator to explain what the problem could be.

The consumer contacted the manufacturer the night of the incident on 9/14/2014 and was transferred to the Executive Resolutions Department. After explaining the situation, the consumer states that the manufacturer responded that they did not know what the problem could be.

The consumer states that she was careful removing the battery to avoid injury by coming into contact with the battery fluid. She noticed the battery in the device had an electrolyte explosion leakage in the battery compartment. The leakage drained into the unit and the battery compartment was intact. A hole was burnt into the battery.
 
Consumer feels that this may pose a fire hazard.

Consumer has no injuries to report.
justification: While no injury occurred, the battery explosion and leakage pose a potential fire hazard, making it an incident.

incident_description:
RCA 7" tablet w/ dual core processor & 8 GB storage model RCT6378W2 Imported by AVC Multimedia UPC 062118463788.
First battery didn't seem to keep a charge.  Then it required unit to stay plugged in to use it.  Case developed a small crack, but had never been dropped or otherwise mistreated.  After leaving tablet plugged in, the battery swelled up and forced the case open.
This is obviously a defective battery or a serious electrical problem.  Unit was unplugged and placed in plastic bag in case the battery ruptured.

incident_description:
08/05/2014 The consumer purchased her smart-phone. For the following two weeks, the consumer stated that her device did not cause her any problems and she had no complaints about it. 

08/15/2014 The consumer was in her home with her device at hand. Suddenly her husband tells her that the phone is smoking. The consumer immediately tosses it on the floor and her husband proceeded to stomp on it. The back cover came off the phone and the battery came out. The consumer states there was smoke everywhere and the battery caught on fire. It was approximately five seconds before the husband was able to get water and pour it on the battery. After ten minutes had passed, the consumer picked up the phone and the battery and bagged them in a [plastic bag]. 

The consumer states no injuries occurred to her or her husband due to this incident. Aside from the consumerÃÂs device, the only property damage reported is a hole with approximate dimensions of two inches by four inches to the coupleÃÂs ceramic tiles flooring. 

8/16/2014 The consumer visited her local T-Mobile store. She explained to a representative the events that had taken place the day before. Without knowledge of what to do, the representative contacted the District Manager and proceeded to explain the incident. The District Manager told the consumer and the representative that there was nothing T-Mobile could do on their hand but to contact Samsung to see what they would do about the matter. 

While at the store, the T-Mobile representative called Samsung. Numerous unsuccessful calls were made trying to reach somebody from Samsung and voice messages were left instead. 

08/30/2014 Approximately two weeks later, the consumer receives a call from a Samsung representative by the first name of [REDACTED]. The consumer explained to [REDACTED] the incident that took place. [REDACTED] asked the consumer to mail her device to Samsung so that they could inspect the phone with the hopes of finding out what the problem may have been. The consumer informed [REDACTED] that her floor had not been repaired. [REDACTED] asked the consumer that alongside her device, to send the quote for the floor repair as well as any pictures she may have taken of the damaged floor. 
 
09/10/2014 Approximately seven to eight business days later and not having heard from him, the consumer contacted [REDACTED]. He explained that he had been trying to reach the consumer and had even left voice messages, those of which the consumer states she never received. [REDACTED] informed her that he had received her package and that the best they could do was replace her phone free of charge. He also informed her that if she was to accept the phone replacement, the issue would end there and she could not take further actions against the company or seek further compensation. The consumer rejected this offer and explicitly told him that she did not feel safe with another one of their cell-phones. [REDACTED] told the consumer that Samsung did not feel liable for her floor damage. The consumer told [REDACTED] that if they were willing to replace her device, they implicitly accepted fault and should repair her floor as well. [REDACTED] told the consumer that unfortunately they would not do such thing but said she was welcomed to file charges against them. She told [REDACTED] she would speak to her attorney. 

9/24/2014 The consumer contacted her attorney and after explaining the situation, she was told that nothing could be done if she no longer had possession of her device. Her lawyer advised her to contact CPSC. 

9/24/2014 The consumer contacted T-Mobile and a representative told her that it was unlikely that Samsung would mail back her device because it was possible that it had already been disassembled for inspection. 

9/24/2014 The consumer tried contacting Samsung to see if they could return her device. She was not able to get a hold of a representative so she proceeded to leave a voice message.

The consumer states that she has not yet repaired her floor. She feels that the device is defective and poses a safety and fire hazard.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident caused property damage and posed a potential fire hazard, warranting a severity level of 2.

incident_description:

incident_description:

The screen was not shattered but  inside were cracked. The television was broken off of the crystal base which is 2 1/2" x  2 1/2 " x 8".

He was given a ticket #[REDACTED].

He was advised that they would have to send one out to assess the damage to the television within 48 hours.  He was given another reference number-[REDACTED]. No one came out

(09/06/2014) The consumer called back and spoke to [REDACTED]. He was advised that he would have to get someone to repair the televison at his expense. He advised her of what was told to him and was told that he received misinformation. 

The consumer stated that this 60 lbs can potentially tip over and kill someone.

Updated from 9/30 submitter consent (wgm): I now have additional information that is related to this report. One week after the incident in which the 50" Samsung TV fell in my living room my grandchildren were experiencing stomach aches. Three of them stayed home from school and were seen by the doctor. The symptoms were headaches, body aches and vomiting. The doctor thought it was a virus. I assumed it was too. Then when I experienced the same symptoms and I lost 7 pounds in one day due to diarrhea, I knew it wasn't a virus. the symptoms my family and I were experiencing was attributed to the plasma gas leaking from the damaged TV. Todays date is September 30, 2014 and we are still experiencing some symptoms especially with the lungs and stomach. I do believe this to be a sickness directly related to the TV.
justification: Potential for serious injury or death due to a heavy object (60 lbs TV) tipping over, as reported by the consumer.

incident_description: internal battery in Samsung NP900xc3-A04 US expanded and deformed bottom of case.  When case removed battery was very enlarged and distorted.  Service technician removed battery and told me that it posed a fire and possibly an explosion risk.  Computer is about 2 years old and battery did not get heavy use.
justification: The battery's expansion and deformation pose a potential fire and explosion risk, making it an incident with no injury (severity level 2) that is possible to occur (likelihood 3).

incident_description:
Vizio 60" TV tipped over and fell. Mounted on stand that came with tv.
TV is broken - unusable. Purchased in July this year (2014) from SAMs Club. Called Vizio who said that there is a recall on other model TVs, but not on Model # E600i-B3, Serial # LFTRPUAQ1701865. Paid $900.00 for TV.

incident_description: I purchased a Curtis tablet Model#LT7033D from HHGREGG on 01/21/2013 . On 08/20/2014 I noticed that the back had came loose on one end, I pushed it back together and continued using it. Later on I had my 2 year old grandson on my lap with the tablet. I was just lucky enough that the battery did not bust open when this happened with my grandson on my lap. incident_description: We purchased a new Vizio Tv and wireless surround system. The tvf and system was turned off and not in use. The subwoofer malfunctioned and caught our home on fire. I do not feel that this product is safe at all.
justification: The incident resulted in a house fire, which is severe, and while it's not likely to happen again (3), it's possible due to the malfunctioning subwoofer.

incident_description: On the evening of October 5, 2014 before I went to bed I kept smelling something that smelled like something burning. You remember the smell from the racetrack we had when we were little. The black one with the metal strips you had to put the car on to make them go? This morning I turned the tv in the living room on and it didn't come on. It just started flashing. I hurried up and unplugged it and took the plug out of the back of the tv and this is what I found. The end of the plug that goes into the back of the tv was burnt and melted. That explains the smell but I was immediately concerned that this may be an issue with more than just this one television. Here ya go, today only we can offer you this smaller 24 inch [REDACTED] vizio television for 195.00 or you can get a 28 inch for 279. Oh yeah, wait, that was your response to no one being injured. I guess if someone had been injured you could have offered me an 18 inch for 500.00. His response to all of this was, "I'm really sorry you experienced this problem. I told him they can keep their defective dangerous tv and I will definitely not be purchasing any Vizio products in the future. Furthermore, I will be letting all of my friends on facebook, and beyond know exactly what kind of company Vizio is and make sure they are aware of how dangerous Vizio products are. He began again with the previous response, "I'm really sorry blah, blah, blah. At this point I hung up before I forgot I'm a Christian and went straight street on him. Please share this information with consumers. It just may save someone's life
justification: While no one was injured, the incident could have escalated to a fire, posing a significant risk to the family and neighbors.

incident_description:
I suffered a serious burn injury from a heart rate monitor I was wearing during the Portland Marathon on Sunday Oct 5, 2014. 

I purchased the RC3 GPS watch and heart rate monitor on Friday Oct 3, 2014 from a company called Polar www.polar.com  

Polar had a booth at the Portland Marathon bib pick-up festival and I purchased the watch and monitor there. 

I followed the instructions carefully.  I set up the watch and heart rate monitor.   I moistened the strap as directed.  I attached the battery component to the strap and connected it around my chest with the battery component facing up and positioned just over the xiphoid process at the lower part of my sternum.  

Everything seemed to be working fine and I was tracking my heart rate, mileage, and time for over 20 miles of the marathon. 

It was a hot day so some of the residents of the homes along the marathon route were standing by the road with hoses to spray down the runners. 

One of them sprayed me with the hose and at that moment I felt an electric arc on my chest immediately under the part of the strap where the battery attaches.  I felt severe pain and there was the smell of burnt skin.  

When I finished the race, I looked at my chest which was then hurting pretty bad and I had sustained a nasty burn in 2 horizontal strips across my chest. I was up all night with pain.  I attached a picture that I took this morning with my cell phone. 

Has this been reported before?  I am fearful that I bought a defective product and that others might suffer a similar fate.  After all runners routinely run in the rain and on hot race days, it is very common for the spectators to hose down runners.
justification: The incident resulted in a serious burn injury, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the common practice of runners being sprayed with water during races.

incident_description: I had been using a Fitbit one for over a month, when one time I allowed it to touch my skin for an extended period on my on my stomach (I was asleep). I woke up with the skin on my stomach ulcerating from the Fitbit contact.  This was over 4 months ago, the injury has healed but the scar remains and will probably be there for years, if not forever.
justification: Skin ulceration indicates injury, though not life-threatening (severity 3). The incident's rarity due to unusual contact duration suggests a 'possible' likelihood (3).

incident_description:
While sleeping in a hotel room ,the tempered glass base of a Philips TV exploded around 1:45 am.
Prior to the incident, the TV was on only for 20 minutes and it was cut off at 8 pm.
It was a very loud explosion that woke me up. The debris field had radius of ~ 12 feet. There were hundreds of pieces of glass. The TV did not appear to be damaged.
This was a spontaneous explosion in the middle of the night with no warning.
The safety hazard is obvious.
I now know that similar episodes have been reported in past.
The public needs to be warned.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries, but the potential for harm was high due to the spontaneous explosion of the TV base, which scattered glass debris across a 12-foot radius.

incident_description: My husband was watching football yeterday 10/5/14 when the screen image went out. The sound went as well after a little while. incident_description:
This is to notify you of an unsafe product sold by Sirius-XM Satellite Radion.  The item in question is the model BB2 Speaker Dock.  The speaker dock runs on 110v ac or battery power.  In addition to energizing the speakers, it also powers one of many different Sirius-XM transportable satellite radio receivers, such as, but not limited to the Sirius-XM Lynx, the radio I use on my BB12 speaker Dock.

The safety issue, which is ongoing is that an electric spark flies from the plug every time the speaker dock is plugged into an electrical outlet.  I have isolated the trouble to the Sirius-XM spekaer dock as this problem does not exist if I plug any other devices into the very same outlet.

It is of greatest urgency that anybody who owns a Sirius-XM BB2 speaker dock be aware of this issue and, if it exists to notify Sirius XM of this safety hazzard ASAP!  Hopefully, Sirius-XM will recall defective units and repair or replace them at no charge to the customer as this is a safety issue which, if not corrected, could result in a fire.

Please note that your form  requests a single static incident date.  This is an ongoing problem.  I own this dock since last March or April. Every time I plug it in, I see an electric spark, which could start a fire.
justification: The incident involves an electric spark from a product's plug, which could potentially start a fire, but no injuries have been reported.

incident_description: Lenovo Yoga Idea pad battery wires are coming out creating fire hazard condition, when I connected the battery charger, spark and smoke came out , I was able to see it and pulled the plug off. I see this as a design issue with this model charger and can case fire in homes or office buildings.

incident_description: Our three year old Vizio tv started shooting sparks out of the top left corner and then flames shot out of the same area.    This lasted about 20 seconds and quit.     No injuries occurred and no damage was done to the room where the tv was located.     In fact, the tv shows very little signs of damage.      Once the fire went out, we unplugged the tv. incident_description: while Sony DVD player was recharging some battery component inflated and split open the case.

incident_description:
Around Black Friday 2013, I purchased a RCA Tablet (RCT6378W2) for my daughter. Sometime two weeks ago, she was watching a video on it. After awhile of watching, she needed to go to the bathroom and set the tablet down. After she returned to it, the tablet was split in two. She told me about it and when I inspected the tablet, what seems to be the battery of the tablet, which was silvery plastic had expanded and had caused the battery to break open. 

I am really concerned as during that time my daughter was using the tablet it was plugged in with its DC adapter. If she had not gone to the bathroom and was actually holding the tablet she would have been seriously electrocuted.  Also, have the tablet been left unattended  and remained plugged on to charge its battery, it could have caused a fire.
justification: The tablet's battery expanding and breaking open while in use and plugged in posed a high risk of injury, as my daughter could have been electrocuted if she had not put it down.

incident_description:
I purchased an iPhone5s in May 2014 on AT&T's NEXT program, and pay a monthly installment on the device.  Since I have owned the device, It has gotten very warm and even hot to the touch when charging at night.  I use an original Apple Charger and Lightning cable with this device.  I took the device out of it's protective case on the morning of September 21, 2014 to clean the inside of the screen protector, and discovered that the device has warped and deformed due to the heat.

This device has an aluminum exterior, and it has overheated to the point the aluminum is warped, and the screen has actually separated from the aluminum housing.  This device shows no other signs of heat damage other than the warped housing; however, the heat had partially fused the protective case to the device on the back.

On Sunday Sept. 21, 2014, I spoke with an Apple Care representative who advised me to contact my cellular carrier AT&T.  I immediately spoke with a representative of AT&T that evening who advised me that this was a warranty situation, and Apple handles all of their warranty claims.

I emailed [REDACTED] at AT&T that evening as well as [REDACTED] at Apple, both of whom are executives in their respective companies.  AT&T reiterated their position of deferring to Apple; however, Apple diagnosed the device.  Apple's diagnosis is that the device is searching for signal overnight while charging and that searching is what is in fact causing this overheat situation.

Apple did not offer a meaningful solution to resolve this problem without me being without a device for several days, or traveling to an Apple Store; however, AT&T is willing to exchange the device free of charge, but they want the original device returned to them within 10 business days.
justification: Device warping and heat damage occurred, but no injuries reported.

incident_description: I purchased the Lorel Care n Share baby monitor with 2 cameras for my children.  Within a month of using it the battery life was cut in half, within 2 months it had to remain on the charger.  From there the sound stopped working.  From there the video stopped showing live and would show a stale image that refreshed every 30 seconds or so.  Now the camera is hot and not working at all and the battery is swollen.  So it went from not working well to being dangerous.  If you visit the Lorex Technology [REDACTED]page you can see that many many others are experiencing the same things.  Lorex won't respond via phone, e-mail or online.  So many people are losing money and being exposed to dangerous products!
justification: The battery swelling poses a fire hazard, making it an injury risk.

incident_description: I have a Lorex baby care monitor, the BB4325X. The battery pack included with this model becomes hot and expands pushing the door off the back of the monitor. I contacted the company and they sent  me a replacement monitor, then the battery pack expanded again within 2 weeks. Now I cannot get ahold of them, they don't return calls or emails and they will not address this unsafe product.
justification: The battery pack expanding and pushing off the door is an incident, and given the repeated occurrence within a short period, it's likely to happen again.

incident_description:
Last night, my laptop all the sudden caught on fire.  I believe the fire started from the battery of the laptop.  I think it overheated, but luckly I did not go to sleep yet.   I used a three cups of water to douse the fire off.  Otherwise, it would have been a different story.

Other serial numbers: NB048UA#ABA.

incident_description: hp pavillion dm3 notebook computer gets very hot, battery has swelled up so bad that it warped the keyboard, I have some time ago(months) sent email to hp via there website with no reply at all.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (warped keyboard) but no injuries, and it's possible that others may experience similar issues with their HP Pavilion DM3 notebook computers.

incident_description: My 10 year old daughter's laptop tipped over lacerating her foot with a four in cut on the top of her foot. Upon inspection of the computer it could be clearly seen that there was an exposed sharp edge from the lid of the computer.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (laceration) to the child's foot, but did not cause death, hence severity level 3.

incident_description:
My husband's five year old cell phone exploded and caught on fire yesterday while it was inside it's case and clipped to his belt. It was not charging at the time. My husband was in his office and they all heard a "pop" sound, and he realized flames were coming out of the phone case. He was able to flip the case off his belt with his left hand, sustaining a burn blister on his left thumb. The phone and case landed on the floor, where fumes came out and it stopped burning.
The entire back of the small flip-phone type cell phone was charred and burned. The burning appears to have melted the back cover off the phone and is fused to the inside of the case. The inside of the case is burned. There are scorch marks on my husband's shirt. This is a Samsung cell phone, model T-109, purchased through [REDACTED}. 

We have contacted Samsung, they want us to return the phone to them but we are not sure we should do that. We are feeling grateful my husband did not have his phone in his pocket, or that he was driving on the highway at the time the phone exploded.
justification: Injury occurred (burn blister) and could have been more severe if the phone was in a pocket or in use while driving.

incident_description:
I was still sleeping but my husband awoke and noticed an unusual odor. He searched our room looking for what could be causing the smell he described as the scent of "something burning." After following the smell my husband located the source--the television. He saw smoke emanating from the A/C adaptor of the television and quickly snatched the power cord from wall outlet. The television was turned off at the time of the incident and the A/C adaptor was plugged directly into the wall outlet. The cable box connected to the television and sharing the same wall outlet was just fine, and there was no damage to the wall outlet. Thankfully there was no damage to anything in our home or the television itself; only the A/C adaptor was melted. The odor just lingered for a couple of days then dissipated. It terrifies me to think what may have happened had my husband not awakened in time--my children and I were still sleeping. 

I contacted Insignia the same day and explained everything that happend to the representative and was provided with a ticket number and the promise that someone would follow up with me. By September 4, 2014 no one contacted me so I called back to customer service. The representative contacted the "Escalations Department" directly and finally someone named [REDACTED] sent me an e-mail requesting a description of the incident--for the second time. I sent the requested information on September 7, 2014. By September 15, 2014 no one responded to my e-mail, so I called customer service again. The representative contacted the "Escalations Department" directly (again) and I was told that someone would contact me within 2 days. On September 16, 2014 I received an e-mail requesting pictures of the melted A/C adapter--which I sent within minutes of receiving the e-mail. It is almost a month later and Insignia has yet to provide any meaningful response/resolution to the incident. It seems that Insignia does not care how dangerous their products are and how their customers are affected.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant risk due to the potential for a fire, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is high as the issue was caused by a product defect and could have recurred.

incident_description:
I plugged a vacuum cleaner plug into the power tap.  The power tap shorted, arced, smoked and the home circuit breaker tripped.

I unplugged the power tap from the home outlet.  I took a picture of the power tap.  I disassembled the power tap.  I noticed that the vacuum plug had contacted both power buses which caused the short.  I inspected the power tap further and notice that the outlet next to the outlet that shorted today had shorted in the past.  I also noticed that the device looks to have been designed so that in the middle of the power tap the distance between the two buses decreases.  This would allow a plug to contact both buses and cause a short circuit.

The breaker on the power tap did NOT trip.

I am a retired Fire Department Battalion Chief with training in fire cause investigation and determination from among other training centers such as the National Fire Academy in Emmitsburg, MD.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident caused property damage and could have led to a fire, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is high due to the power tap's faulty design and previous shorts.

incident_description:
I was using my Mid 2009 Apple MacBook Pro 15" (Serial Number W89231EX642) to do class assignments. Suddenly and without warning I heard a pop, the battery had expanded causing the unibody to expand  and deform slightly, and the trackpad to stop working as designed. An odor was detected and later a white powder residue was found on the desk and within the laptop's interior. During the saving and shutting down of the laptop, the device indicated 179ÃÂ°F on the SMC processor temperature monitor, and I felt the discomfort of the high heat under my left palm when it made contact with the laptop next to the trackpad.
I unplugged the laptop, moved it to the kitchen counter near the fire extinguisher (just as a precaution) and removed the bottom panel to verify my belief that the battery was the root of the problem. Unfortunately I could not remove the expanded battery due to Apple's 3 security Pentalobe screws. After attempting to make contact with Apple Care and the Greensboro Apple Store, I elected to visit the Apple store in person with the laptop.
The store employees removed the battery and placed into their fire safe due to their observation/assessment and would not return it to me indicating the high risk danger of the battery. Instead they offered to order me a new replacement battery at full cost.
The next day, I contacted Apple Care at 1-800-275-2273 and spoke with several individuals, eventually landing with [REDACTED]: [REDACTED], [REDACTED], case number [REDACTED]. He took information and indicated that the battery was over 5 years old and was considered consumed. That the expansion of the battery and the related laptop deformation was normal for a battery that expired/died. He did not address the heat and sudden nature of the failure. He indicated that since I had no ill effects at 24+ hours post incident from the smell, fumes, and white fine powder that the failure of the battery did not present a health risk, and that I would know by now for certain.
Why did they indicate in person and over the phone that the suddenness, heat, volatility, possible toxic exposure, and battery behavior is normal or to be expected? Why would I want a product that is damaged by its internal parts/battery and be expected to accept this outcome or situation? What else could have been damaged? What if I had not been home with the situation occurred; would I have lost my home, my pets, my things of value?
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a sudden and unexpected battery expansion, high heat, and potential toxic exposure, warranting a severity level of 2.
