incident_description:
While driving my vehicle and using my factory iPhone 5s "lightning" USB charging cord (plugged into a 12V cigarette plug adaptor) to charge my iPhone 5s, the portion of the charging cord that plugs into the phone electrocuted me and burned my finger.  I was attempting to plug the lightning end of the plug into my iPhone 5s, and it began sparking and burning.

This is very dangerous, and my wife's iPhone 5s cord is similarly failing and showing exposed internal wires.  This failure of the cord outer coating (at the point connecting the lightning plug to the cord length) is atypical of other cell phone charging cords.  I have never experienced this before, and it is occurring to both of the iPhone 5s charging cords I own.

This sparking and fire could cause a house or car fire, in addition to the electrocution and burn on my finger that I received.  This appears to be a design defect resulting from too thin or inappropriate cord covering, combined with too short and too rigid of a coupling section where the lightning end and the cord length join.

During my inspection to determine where this burning smell was coming from, I powered on the TV.  The TV came on normally, picture was perfect, sound was perfect and with that I turned it off.  Approximately 1-2 minutes after powering off the TV, flames began to shoot out of the back on top of the TV, with smoke and popping sounds  ... the TV was on fire..

incident_description:
I was at home watching television in my living room on a sunny afternoon (no storms at all that day) when the Motorola cable box (provided by Comcast) started screaming loudly, and simultaneously a light on the front of the box lit up and the TV blinked off. I grabbed the remote and shut off the TV, but the cable box kept screaming loudly. I ran behind a wall thinking it might blow up, and tried unsuccessfully to shut off the cable box with the remote control. In that very short time, the smell of electrical equipment overheating was apparent, so I ran into the garage and pulled the circuit breakers. By the time I got back to the living room (a minute), the room was filled with smoke and burning odor, so I unplugged the box and took it outside. Both have remained unplugged since that time. 
Last week Comcast examined for damages/repairs. The Comcast employee/examiner said the cable had been incorrectly installed in my house and was also not properly grounded (done by Comcast, around mid to late 200x). He also said that the cable box that almost caused a fire was very old and had not been used in the county where he works (Montgomery County, MD) for many years. I had just been sent this cable box in 2013, when the previous box quit working following a thunderstorm. At that time, I had asked for new equipment in their Frederick, MD office, and was told they do not have any new equipment available and are giving out only refurbished equipment to customers. I was also told by a Comcast employee on the phone that they would not come out to replace the box, and that I had to either pick one up or receive it by mail and install myself (I was told in a later conversation that this was incorrect and that they should have installed since it was their equipment failure, but this was after the fact.)
The Comcast employee who was at my house last week said the cable is coming into my house in the wrong location (not at the electric box), and that it was incorrectly grounded. That is another story, and if installed correctly the circuit might have shut down when the box shorted out. Even so, if the box had not shorted out there would have been no problem to begin with. 
Hazard: If I had not been in the room where the TV was located and able to take immediate and rapid action to turn off the electricity, the cable box would almost certainly have caused a house fire. 
Shocking: When I visited the CPSC website today, I decided to browse recalls to see whether other cable TV boxes had been recalled. The Motorola DCT2000, recalled in 2002, looks EXCATLY like the DCT2224 that almost caused a fire in my house!  I called Motorola to confirm whether they were the same, and Motorola gave me the run-around and said that the box was now owned by Comcast and they have no information on the DCT2224 model. However, the DCT2000 and DCT2500 have been discontinued. See: http://www.cpsc.gov/en/Recalls/2002/CPSC-Motorola-Inc-Announce-Recall-of-Digital-Cable-Set-Top-Boxes-/
I fear that anyone with any of these old digital cable boxes is in danger of the same unexpected and rapid electrical malfunction, and that these need to be removed from homes as soon as possible. Another likely danger would be other Comcast cable installations performed by the 2 technicians who did it incorrectly in my house in Frederick County, MD.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries but could have caused a house fire, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is high as the cable box was incorrectly installed and not properly grounded, and similar boxes have been recalled in the past.

incident_description:
HP dv7 - quad-core notebook pc has always run warmer than other notebook pc's. And I thought it was normal until I pulled my notebook pc out of my bookbag and the back covering had melted. The notebook was in hibernation mode, which means that it is completely shut off with the immediate memory written onto the hard drive. This allows the system to boot up much quicker than a normal starting procedure. The system was not overly hot when I put the notebook pc in my bookbag before heading to class and the battery was still fully charged when I found the back panel melted. HP claims that the case melted due to a clogged heat sink and sent me pictures of the heat sink. There was dust and dog hair on the heat sink but I do not think that it was by any means "clogged." The dv7 model has received numerous complaints regarding heat issues and I did not think that a laptop could melt before this incident occurred. 

More than anything else: if a laptop can get hot enough to melt then it could easily cause severe 3rd degree burns.
justification: The laptop's heat melted its casing, posing a high risk of severe burns if it had been in use or touched.

incident_description:
For background, the product cited is a case for an action camera. Action cameras are designed to be used in a variety of sports and outdoor applications, including bicycling. Sony, the manufacturer, sells a variety of accessories including a handlebar mount to use the case and camera for bicycling. The point being is that the product is designed and marketed specifically for use as an action camera for bicycling. 
I placed Sony's Action Camera into the AKA-SF1 (skeleton frame for action camera) and attached this assembly to another accessory, the  Sony handlebar mount VCT-HM1. The camera was properly placed into the AKA-SF1. This assembly was properly attached to the VCT-HM1 handlebar mount. 
While riding the bike on a smooth road, the AKA-SF1 case, holding the Sony Action camera flew off the bicycle, nearly striking other riders in the group, and shattering into pieces on the roadway. The camera and case could have easily stuck another rider and/or got caught in a wheel causing serious injury or death. Fortunately, this did not happen during my event. But it is a real risk. 

After inspecting  the camera and case, I discovered that the issue lies with the AKA-SF1 (skeleton frame for action camera). Specifically the problem is that the case relies on two small plastic tabs to hold the case assembly together. These plastic tabs are insubstantial for the designed application and can fail without warning, as they did in my case. I've also discovered that other users have reported similar failings. The AKA-SF1 is designed, advertised and marketed specifically for an application (bicycling). Yet the product is defectively designed for this application. It can fail without warning, potentially causing serious injury and or death.
justification: The case's inadequate design and failure during use could have caused serious injury or death to other riders.

incident_description:
We received a Safety 1st 2-receiver baby monitor as a baby shower gift sometime in April 2014 (date of purchase is not known, registry was created 2/14). We first started using the monitor on 5/10/14 in the afternoon. The receivers have the capability to operate on both AC power as well as batteries (3 standard AAA). Per the instruction manual that was supplied with the unit stated that the receivers can and should be plugged in with the batteries installed to prolong battery life. The unit is not supposed to put power towards the batteries, but offsets it.
I installed 3 brand new [REDACTED] AAA batteries, purchased two weeks ago, yesterday, around 3 pm. I came home from my job this morning, and around 8:30, I went into our bedroom to turn off the receiver that was located on a dresser that is completely open to free air. When I went to turn off the unit, I noticed that there was a burn mark on top of the solid oak, 120+ yr old antique dresser, where the receiver was sitting. Upon closer inspection, I saw battery acid running from the back of the unit, and could smell something "hot". When I touched the receiver, it was very warm to the touch. I turned off the receiver, and unplugged it form the wall. When it cooled down for a few minutes, I removed the battery cover, and saw that the batteries were all leaking. I believe that there is somehow electrical power from the AC controller is flowing towards that batteries, causing them to rupture. The pictures supplied show the burn mark in the dresser, acid leaking out from the battery compartment, battery compartment with cover removed, and the area where the receiver was located.
This situation has my wife and me very shook up, and I am extremely angry that a product that is supposed to keep my daughter safe could have potentially killed her, or destroy our home! I am a firefighter/paramedic, and if there was enough heat to burn a mark in a solid oak (not plywood or particle board) dresser top, there was enough heat to possibly start a fire if not detected early. I am just glad that I discovered it before I went to sleep 10 feet away from it, and even more relieved that it did not start a fire with my wife sleeping in the same room, as well as my 2 week old infant daughter and my mother in the house last night. I am also grateful that it did not start a fire while we gone.
Being that this is a product that is supposed to keep our infants/children safe, and it almost started a fire in my home, I felt it necessary to bring this to the attention of the manufacturer, WI Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, and the US Consumer Product Safety Commission to make sure that this product gets looked into for a possible safety recall. I have contacted the company via email, as this happened on a holiday weekend, and provided them with all of the above information, as well as the photos provided with this form.
In my contact with the Safety 1st/Dorel Juvenile Group, I stated that we are terrified of the unit, which we are immediately replacing with another brand, as we do not feel safe with their product. Again, since this is a holiday weekend, and they do not have a 24hr hotline, I do not expect a response from the company until Tuesday, 5/27, at the earliest.
Pending on their response to my complaint, as well as initial follow-ups from this agency as well as the US WI Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, I believe that this issue should be closely looked into so see if there is a product safety fire issue with their monitors. I hope that Safety 1st/Dorel Juvenile Group takes this issue seriously and reacts quickly to investigate the issue with my unit, as well as other units that are on store shelves and in the homes of countless children and their families. I would also like, but don't fully expect it, that Safety 1st/Dorel Juvenile Group would see my family's fears and concerns with their product, and reimburse us for the cost of a replacement baby monitor. It would be a nice gesture if they did, but is something that I do not expect from a large corporation like this.
I will follow-up with the WI DATCP and USCPSC regarding how Safety 1st/Dorel Juvenile Group reacts to my concerns to this issue.

Thank you for your time.
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the product's design flaw and widespread use.

incident_description:
I ordered the Fitbit Force in January 2014, and received it in the first week of February. My friend had told me about users experiencing rashes, but I didn't think it was very wide spread at that point.  I wore it every day (except while showering) and also overnight.  I really liked it and loved the silent alarm feature!  Unfortunately, almost exactly 1 month later (March 8th), I noticed a red patch of skin on my wrist under the band about the same width as the band itself.  The location was not exactly under the battery charger, but a little to the side of it closer to the LCD screen area.  I stopped wearing it that day. 

That day I googled the Fitbit rashes, and found out about the recall and that many people were affected.  I returned my Force and received the refund about 5 weeks later. 

The rash or burn stayed the same size the entire time, roughly the size of 2 dimes side by side.  It remained bright red for rougly 1 month, was never bumpy, itchy, or painful, so in my opinion, didn't appear to be contact dermatitis.  I finally went to the doctor on April 7th, and she agreed with me that it didn't look like contact dermatitis, but she wasn't sure what it really was.  So, I decided to try prescription steriod cream (Fluocinonide .05% ointment).  I've been using this cream twice a day for about 2 weeks now, and while the area does look slightly lighter, it's still there, and doesn't really look like the cream has helped. (I'm guessing just the fact that it's now been almost 2 months now has something to do with the spot slightly fading).

I'm really concerned that this is a bigger problem than Fitbit is leading on to be.  Is it really just an allergic reaction, or can I wake up a year from now and find out that I have skin cancer?  I've asked the Fitbit support team if they have any new updates, and am only being told that it's contact dermatitis from either the nickel or adhesives from the band.  I'd like to know (from a real doctor) about what exactly this is and if there can be any long term danger from this product.
justification: The user experienced a persistent rash and burn on their wrist, requiring medical attention, but no long-term effects are mentioned.

I was lucky that I was home or we could have suffered major damage to our home, also after a little research i found out that the battery could have exploded in my hands. I contacted HTC via chat ([REDACTED] - [REDACTED]) and was told no big deal, just to recycle the phone. They advised me that there was no risk with that and that there is no liquids, so there is no fire risk.

i pointed out I work as an IT analyst in healthcare and have dealt with the same type of battery issues with laptops and other electronics.   There have been 40+ recalls since 2002 for this type of situation.  My concern is if left on the charger longer, would a catastrophic battery issue happen with a fire.  I've seen reports on the internet about the same battery issue.. and HTC says there is no issue.

Thanks!! I still have the phone in my possession :)
justification: While no injury occurred, the incident involved a potentially hazardous battery issue, with the battery bulging and overheating.

incident_description: I came home to find my Apple iPad charger melting at the site of the charging port of my iPad.  My iPad side volume buttons don't respond and I have no sound even when speaker is adjusted on the touch screen.  There is a black charred and whitish green residue in the charging port as well as on my charger.  The rubber/plastic casing on the wire is slightly visible at the joint of the head piece that plugs into the iPad due to melting.  I called and spoke with the senior advisor of the safety team who asked me a series of questions and had me send detailed photos of the charger and iPad to their safety engineering department.  I was then told that there was contamination in my charging port which caused the over heating, and that it was in no way Apple's problem.  Had I come home 30 minutes later my home could have caught fire.  No where in the manual does it mention how or why it is necessary to clean the charging port (if that really even is the reason this happened).  Overheating is a common issue with the Apple iPad charger and I feel that Apple is trying to avoid any and all responsibility related to the issue.
justification: While no injury occurred, the incident posed a significant risk of property damage or fire, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is high as the issue is common and could recur.

incident_description:
I received a Fitbit Force for Christmas 2013. I started wearing it on my left arm and got a minor irritation right away. I do commonly experience contact dermatitis from nickel, so this didn't suprise me. 

I switched to my other arm and made the fitting looser so it wouldn't constantly be in contact with the same area of skin. After about another month, I started to experience another rash. This one was more severe. I decided then to stop wearing it and it is also about the same time that I saw the reports of other users being affected.

I am accustomed to getting rashes from cheap jewelry, but usually if something is labeled as "surgical-grade stainless steel" it doesn't affect me. Also, this rash was a bit different in appearance than what i usually get, and also took much longer to go away. For these reasons I think that it is not the metal but must be a component of the adhesives or battery port that is causing the rashes.
justification: Although the incident resulted in no serious injury, the widespread reports of similar reactions indicate a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: I purchased the Fitbit Force on Friday, January 24, 2014, and began wearing it later that evening.  I continued to wear the wristband continuously for the next month or so, only taking it off to shower and charge it when needed.  On February 24, a friend notified me of the reports of rashes that were developing with some users of the Force.  At that time, when I examined my wrist, I did not see anything out of the ordinary.  I continued to wear the device as normal.  Beginning on February 28, I noticed that the Fitbit Force was not holding a charge as long as it usually had (usually 7-10 days between charges).  Around this time, the Force would run out of battery life within 3 days, and the time in-between charges was getting shorter and shorter.  I had to charge my Fitbit Force again on March 2, and it was when I took it off on that day that I began to notice small "bumps" under the metal portion of the wristband (specifically, where the charge port was located on the back of the metal).  Fearing that this might be the development of "the rash," I quickly taped the ENTIRE back portion of the wristband, using both packing tape against the entire back surface and then surgical tape to provide some cushion.  I continued to wear the Fitbit for the next three days (March 3-5) with these accommodations.  By March 5 (when I had to charge the Fitbit Force again), I noticed that the "bumps" had spread considerably to an area about 1-inch across on my arm (or just slightly larger than the width of the band itself).  I also noticed a second, smaller area of bumps developing lower on my arm and wrist, closer to where my arm meets my hand (looking back on where the Force was sitting on my arm, I believe that this second area developed because the Fitbit Force would sometimes slide down lower on my arm during the course of the day since it was not snugly fit against my arm).  At this point, fearing the worst, I removed the band from my arm, washed it thoroughly, and let it charge.  Starting on the 6th, I began to wear the band on my other arm to see if something similar would develop.  By this point, I was having to charge my Fitbit Force every other day or so, and when I went to charge it on the 8th, I began to notice a few bumps developing on my other arm as well (still using the tape as a barrier between the band and my arm).  At this point, I removed the Force and have not worn it since.  I requested a return kit from Fitbit to send the Force back.  I can say with 100% certainty that I have no allergies to nicker, rubber, latex, or most other materials that are most likely present in the band.  Due to the fact that the "rash" developed DIRECTLY where the charge port as located on the back of the wristband before spreading, I truly believe that the reaction must have something to do with the port itself.  As of today (March 15), the "rash" has become more swollen and noticeably raised from my skin.  The bumps, which were originally the same color as my skin, have now disappeared and have been replaced by red, swollen, blotchy skin.  The rash is much more noticeable now than it was a week ago.  I believe that the "rash" looks more like a burn (with shiny, rough-textured skin) than a true rash.  I have seen no healing starting to place in the last week...if anything, like I said, the rash has gotten worse.  I saw NO reactions whatsoever for the first month that I worse the wristband, which also leads me to believe that it is not some sort of reaction to materials in the wristband.
justification: User developed a severe skin reaction, likely due to the device's charge port, requiring removal and causing discomfort.

incident_description:
My Fitbit Force, in a small black, was a Christmas gift from my husband,  who ordered it directly from the Fitbit website.  Since it was on back order, we were surprised to receive it on December 23, 2013.  I happily started wearing it right away.

Since I never anticipated any problems, I have no exact dates for the following:

Initially, there were no issues.  I wore it 24/7 removing it only to shower daily and to charge it about every five days or so.  After a few weeks (sometime in late January), I noticed some discomfort and realized that I was continually pushing the device up or down, on my reddened wrist, to massage the area underneath the band for relief. The redness encircled my wrist with a concentrated redness on the top under the charger pins.  I thought perhaps I had gotten an insect bite that was infected. 

Each time I took it off, the wrist area was getting more reddened and looking more irritated.  My husband suggested that perhaps I was wearing it too tight.  I loosened it up and continued wearing it.  Each time I removed the device, the irritation was worse  . . . progressing to what appeared to be tiny blisters and roughened skin.  

I still wasn't too concerned, as I have never had any allergic reactions to bracelets or watches made of both metal and silicone. I tried some OTC skin rash cream, but that did not help. Then I decided it must be my sweat causing a bacterial buildup, so I started cleaning the band daily with alcohol swabs. That didn't help either.  

I finally reluctantly removed from my wrist (wore it pinned to my clothes for awhile - didn't want to lose tracking info) hoping that the rash/burn would clear it up and I could start all over again.  After about a week, my skin was showing improvement. Disappointed that the Force was most likely the problem, I began searching on 03/09/14 for any other persons having similar issues.  I must admit that I was absolutely shocked!

I am very disappointed that I had to find this out on my own.  If the company felt a need for a recall, it's my opinion that all of their customers should have been notified immediately. 

I received my Fiitbit return kit on Friday, 03/14/14.  I was surprised that the return label was to a biohazard recycle center instead of back to Fitbit for testing. I will mail it on Monday, 03/17/14.
justification: The user experienced skin irritation and blisters, progressing to roughened skin, which is classified as an injury.

incident_description:
I received a FitBit Force Activity Tracker for Christmas. It is a wrist band that tracks fitness activities and sleep patterns. Everything was fine for a while, until about last week... Where I noticed 3 little red bumps on my arm. I heard about the 'skin irritation' problem a few days before, so I switched the FitBit to my other wrist. incident_description:
I got a slate colored FitBit Force (size large) for Christmas as a gift and loved it.  In January, my mother mentioned that there were some reported issues with a rash.  I checked it out and saw that FitBit was reporting that this was a very small number of people being effected.  Since (1) I had been wearing it for several weeks at that point, and (2) I have never had sensitive skin or any notable skin reactions or rashes, I noted the issue but kept wearing the Force.
 
On February 24 (two months after I started wearing the Force), I noticed a few small bumps on my wrist where the metal charging port of the Force sits.  By the end of the week, I had a noticeable red rash and immediately discontinued use.  Since then, the rash has gotten significantly worse, so much so that it's now very raised, irritated and oozing.  It's honestly pretty disgusting, and I've left it alone entirely (no itching or self-medicating).

Today, I woke up and took one look at it and decided I needed to see a dermatologist.  It looked awful.  I lucked into an appointment with the dermatologist this morning.  She said it appeared to be a severe case of contact dermatitis, but she was skeptical that it was a nickel allergy and was surprised and puzzled at the fact that it has kept getting worse even after I discontinued use of the Force.  She prescribed some potent topical steroid cream and asked that I check back with her in a week. 

I'm really disappointed by this whole experience.  I've never bought a product from a reputable company, used that product exactly as instructed, and had it cause me a health issue significant enough that I was forced to take time off of work to see a doctor and get medication prescribed to treat it.  Moreover, I'm really unsatisfied with FitBit's reaction to this issue.  In telling its customers that only a small percentage of Force users were encountering this issue, I think the company misled us, either purposefully or unintentionally.  Either way, I don't think simply offering to refund the purchase price of the Force is an acceptable response.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe case of contact dermatitis, requiring medical attention, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the widespread use of the product.

"Tonight, I noticed a burning smell when I set down at my computer, it took a while to determine the source of the odor, but I eventually saw a wisp of smoke coming out of this hard drive."

"It had been connected to my computer and to the power supply for several days. It was setting on a wire-mesh shelf and had plenty of ventilation."

"I am glad I was home and able to disconnect it. I donÃÂt know what failed, but the potential of a fire is certainly a concern. "

Additional Information
After submitting the original report by email, the consumer disassembled the unit to remove the hard drive platters (which contain personal data). The consumer was able to see that there the jack where the power supply plugs into the hard drive had overheated. The consumer still has that part and can send it to CPSC or the manufacturer.
justification: Potential fire hazard due to overheating power jack, but no actual injury or damage reported.

incident_description:
I have a Cambridge Soundworks surround sound system including the P200 powered subwoofer.

Recently the subwoofer made an unusual whining sound then a loud "pop" followed by acrid smoke pouring from the unit and filling the living room. I turned off the unit and removed it to the exterior of the house - the unit was very hot and the hardwood floor below the unit was also very hot.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries but caused property damage, making it a level 2 severity. The likelihood is rated 3 as such incidents, while not common, can occur due to electrical issues in home audio systems.

incident_description: I started wearing my new fitbit force on Feb. 1, 2014. I started to get a slight red spot about 2 1/2 weeks later  but figured it was just a irritation since I have sensitive skin.  It started to become itchy so I tried to adjust my band to wear it higher to avoid the irritated spot.  It then seemed the spot just got larger and more irritated.  I took the band off on feb. 26, 2014 as soon as I heard there was a recall on the product.  The rash is very itchy and rough and isn't getting better. It almost seems to be worse.  The company says it is a reaction to nickel but I've never had a problem wearing earrings with nickel.  Other than that I can't get anymore info from the company as to what I should do. I don't have health insurance so I can't see a dr.
justification: The individual experienced a severe allergic reaction to nickel in the Fitbit Force, resulting in a persistent, worsening rash.

incident_description: On February 23, 2014, after wearing a Fitbit Force for 25 days, a dime-sized red rash appeared on my wrist directly under the device's charging port.. After online research, I immediately discontinued wearing the device. The rash has continued to worsen every day since removal; the main body is quarter-sized and purplish-red, and the lesser "starter" rash (lighter red, slightly bumpy) is spreading around the arm under where the band was worn. The entire mess is both burning and itching
justification: The incident resulted in a severe rash with symptoms of burning and itching, indicating an injury.

incident_description:
I purchased and began wearing the FitBit Force on my right wrist on January 28th, 2014. A few days later, I switched the FitBit over to my left wrist and wore it there until February 20th. That morning I woke up with a terrible rash/burn on my left wrist, and a smaller one on my right wrist. The rash appeared right underneath where the FitBit Force has its charging port.

I stopped using the Force immediately. By Tuesday February 25th my rash/burn had grown across my wrist and become much worse. I went into urgent care, and was given a steroid cream to help clear it up. As of today, March 3, the rash/burn is just beginning to heal, but has a long way to go. It is still very painful and itchy.

I am concerned about what caused this issue, especially because it seems to be systemic. I had not worn the FitBit on my right wrist for over 2 weeks, and the rash/burn still appeared on that wrist, the same day it did on my right wrist. 

I am also concerned about the compromise on the immune system this has created. If my body was fighting hard to respond to the rash/burn, could of it made me vulnerable to other infections. Three days after the rash broke out, I came down with a terrible sinus infection and eye infection. Neither of which am I prone to getting.  I have since heard others reporting similar issues on FitBit's Forum.

The FitBit company has not offered any information yet on what is the definite cause of the reaction. There is only speculation at this point.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe rash/burn requiring medical attention, classifying it as an injury (severity level 3). The widespread and systemic nature of the reaction, along with similar reports, indicates a high likelihood of occurrence (4).

incident_description: Purchased Fitbit Force in December, 2013 and started wearing it January 5, 2014, also the date I registered my purchase on Fitbit.com.  I have developed an itchy, red rash on my left wrist.
justification: The individual developed an itchy, red rash on their wrist after wearing the Fitbit, indicating an injury.

incident_description: fitbit force reaction - chemical burn
justification: Chemical burns can cause injuries, and while not rare, they are unlikely to occur without direct contact with the chemical.

incident_description: Purchased Fitbit Force directly from the company - preordered.  Arrived and I started wearing it around November 10, 2013.  Wore daily and through night for sleep tracking, removed for showering and to charge as needed.  Noticed several (4-5) small red bumps on my left wrist morning of December 26, 2013. Bumps were itchy. Assumed maybe tracker had gotten tight on my arm overnight while sleeping, loosened the band and continued to wear the tracker.  Itching intensified over that day and the next, scratched as little as possible.  Over the next 3-4 days, bumps increased, then began to develop into blisters.  Area of irritation was very small to start - just a few bumps.  By 6 days after the first bumps appeared, irritated area now 3 inches long from wrist bone back towards elbow.  Also now about 1 inch wide.  Bumps have now grown and morphed into large fluid filled blisters.  Incredibly itchy.  Skin surrounding the blistered area is visibly reddened.  Since I am a nurse, I covered my wrists with bandages at work to prevent any cross contamination. Covering the area seemed actually to make it worse, or cause the spreading and itching to increase.  Oral [REDACTED] for the itching.  Area cleansed in the shower, but noticed that getting it wet or warm increased the redness and itching considerably.  Did use [REDACTED] pads and [REDACTED] to cover loosely at work, continued throughout to wear the tracker.  I was assuming at the time that unit had gotten tight on my arm and caused a reaction at the area of the charging port and that once this reaction was fine I would be able to continue to wear the tracker with no problem.  I thought it was my fault/error, not that the tracker was faulty.   1/4/2014 visited with my daughter and she commented she thought it was maybe infected, possibly cellulitis.  I had my concerns about that was well (I am an RN).  Decided to watch it a little longer to see if it would clear up once the blistered area popped and healing could begin.  Continued to cover it at work to avoid comments by co-workers and patients as my wrist now looked angry, red and weepy. Covered the inside of the tracker with moleskin to ease skin irritation from plastic band and to cover the open battery port which I felt was the area causing the skin irritation. The moleskin helped but the reaction continued to progress, now longer than 3 weeks. Went to Urgent Care 1/13/14 and was given antibiotics for infection from having scratched the area.  She also contemplated oral prednisone for the inflammation.  Asked that I move tracker to right arm while left healed, which I did.  2 days later I had areas of redness and bumps on the right wrist, exactly where the battery port area was - even through the moleskin.  This was concerning to me, that even with the battery area covered, the unit was causing a skin reaction.  I began looking online for other reports of irritation from the Fitbit Force and found the online forum at Fitbit.com which was full of reports of hundreds of other people having the same reaction.
justification: The incident resulted in significant skin irritation, blisters, and infection, warranting medical intervention.

incident_description: I got a fitbit force (pedometer/watch Black, size small) in November and started wearing it Nov. 16, 2013.  I wore it daily (but did not get it wet), and recharged it by plugging the dongle into my laptop and attaching it to the force.  On Dec 24th I noticed I had a nasty rash on my right wrist and thought it was from a contact reaction to something.  Not wanting to irritate it further, I moved the force to my left wrist and put [REDACTED] cream on my right wrist and took [REDACTED].  The rash got worse each day on the right wrist and after about two days I realized I had a rash beginning on the left wrist too.  That was when I first realized the force was causing the problem.  I searched online and found some forums on fitbit's website and realized I was not the only one.  It took 38 days for it to start but after that it came on with a vengeance.  It took 9 days for the rash to stop getting worse.  Over the new year holiday an ER doctor friend took a look at it and advised me to cover it and use a topical steroid.  We weren't at home so I used hydrocortisone cream and kept it wrapped (which also helped keep me from scratching).  At it's worst I had small bubbles/blister burns on my right wrist.  It took almost 4 weeks to heal.  Thinking we had a batch issue with the force (no one really had any idea early on), I asked fitbit to send a new one.   When it arrived in late January, I covered the back with electrical tape (over the battery / charger port), and very nervously wore it for a few days on my left wrist.  Most days it was worn over a long sleeve shirt.  It took about 2 days where it actually touched skin for the rash to reappear.  I removed it and sent back the 2nd unit for a refund.  (The same model - FB402BKS ÃÂ small black).  Fitbit has issued a recall for the product but has yet to tell consumers with any certainty what is going on.  I am not allergic to nickel (that was their initial communication with most users).  I can and still do wear stainless steel jewelry with no issues.  The only thing I've ever reacted to this way is the fitbit force.  I've filed this report as I don't think fitbit is sharing enough information with consumers about what may be causing these nasty burn reactions.
justification: The incident resulted in severe skin irritation and blisters, and the likelihood of occurrence is high as multiple users have reported similar reactions.

incident_description:
I developed a rash from wearing the FitBit Force (FB402BK- large black) after wearing for approximately 3 1/2
weeks. I have discontinued wearing the product, but it has been over a week, and the rash is still persistent. It is
red, blistery, and it causes both a burning and an itchy sensation. After reading if other's were experiencing the
same symptoms, I learned of the voluntary recall that the company is offering. I have registered with the site and
am waiting on further instructions on how to return the product and receive my refund. Upon looking at the Help/ Discussion Forum for this topic on their website, many users recommended filing this report.
justification: The incident resulted in a persistent rash with both burning and itching sensations, indicating an injury (severity level 3). The widespread reports of similar symptoms on the company's forum suggest a high likelihood of occurrence (level 4).

incident_description:
2/13/14 Caller stated that while her spouse was cleaning he unplugged the TV to remove it from the wall when he re-plugged the unit, there was sparks emitting from the top rear and from the electrical plug.  She stated that he also smelled an overwhelming odor of something burning.  The unit was immediately unplugged.

incident_description: I was using my Coby 32 inch flat screen tv when i heard a pop noise and went to go turn it on again and got shocked. Apparently looking into it there was a recall of this television or a similar model.

incident_description: laptop has been so hot since purchase it is dangerously hot and last night on 02/25/2014 the ac plug in hole actually melted clear out of it and is now stuck inside.
justification: The laptop overheating and melting its AC plug is an incident with potential for injury, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: I received the Fitbit Force for Christmas.  Love the product.  After about a month of use I started getting this rash, burn on my arm.  At night - I'd switch it to my other arm.  That arm started getting the rash.  The rash is not going away.  My left arm itches and burns and my right wrist (the one I only wore for a few nights) still has a mark and it has been over a week since I wore it there.  They not only need to figure out what is causing this but how to cure it.  I'm afraid my wrists are going to scar!
justification: The user has experienced an allergic reaction to the product, resulting in burns and itching, which is likely to continue if not addressed.

incident_description: I began wearing the Fitbit Force on January 8, 2014. On February 11, I noticed a small, red irritation on my right wrist, and thinking water got under the band, I changed wrists. The rash/burn got larger and became raised and itchy over the next couple of days. The next day I noticed 2 red bumps on my left wrist. I immediately stopped wearing the device. The rash/burn on my left wrist got larger too and raised. I tried leaving both areas open to air, then I tried hydrocortisone cream. The area did not improve, so I sought medical advice and got a prescription for triamcinolone cream BID. The areas are still not improving.
justification: The incident resulted in injuries (rash, burns, itching) and required medical attention, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence given the widespread use of Fitbit devices.

incident_description: After about a month of wearing my Fitbit Force, I developed a rash on my right wrist. It appeared overnight with any warning beforehand.
justification: The incident resulted in a rash but no injury, and while not rare, it's not likely to occur with every Fitbit use.

incident_description: I wear the fitbit force and have developed a painful rash with blistering.

incident_description: Used product (Fitbit Force) as advised, wearing it on my wrist. Did not let it get excessively wet and did not abuse it in any way. After nearly 90 days developed a red rash on my wrist directly under where the product's charging port would rest. Loosened the band of the Force to let it rest further down my wrist. Developed the same rash in the new location of the charging port. Discontinued use, but the rash has persisted for more than a week.
justification: User experienced an allergic reaction to the product, resulting in a persistent rash.

incident_description:
I wore the Fitbit tracker 24/7 from 11/17/13 until 12/19/13.  I noticed a few itchy bumps under the tracker on the 19th of December.  I put electrical tape on the back of the tracker and switched hands.  The next morning, the few bumps was now an area 2"by 1".  It was very red, inflamed, itchy and blistering.  I also noticed that the other wrist had a blister on it.  I went to my dermatologist who prescribed a very strong steroid ointment  and said I had a severe contact dermatitis to a component of the Fitbit Force.  I booked an alergy patch test. The derm prescribed Fluocinonide ointment under occlusion on the first night to get the rash under control.  That worked well and the rash stopped spreading.   It dried out turned flaky and itchy an lasted for about 4-5 weeks.  There is a very slight faint mark where the  wound was that hopefully won't scar.  I know now that I am not allergic to nickel.  

My guess is the adhesives.  Whatever it is, human skin really doe not like ti.

This product should be racalled
justification: The incident resulted in a severe skin reaction, blistering, and lasting discomfort, with a high likelihood of recurrence given the widespread use of similar products.

incident_description:
I received a Fitbit Force for Christmas, and wore it daily from 12/25/13 to 2/7/14.  After wearing the device for approximately 20 days, I developed a rash on my wrist. When I switched the device to the other wrist, I developed a rash there also.  Through a Web search on 1/30/14, I learned that other Fitbit Force users were having the same problem.  On 1/31/14, I sent the company the following email message:
**************************************************
I received a Fitbit Force as a Christmas gift, and I love it.  Unfortunately, I've developed a rash on my wrist from wearing it. (I've attached a picture.)  Could you please advise me how I can continue using your product but avoid the rash.
*************************************************

They sent the following response on the same day:
**************************************************
We are sorry that you are experiencing skin irritation. We want to follow up with some comments and provide some options to assist you.

We are looking into reports from a very limited number of Fitbit Force users, who have been experiencing skin irritation, possibly as a result of an allergy to nickel, an element of surgical-grade stainless steel used in the device.

First, since you are experiencing skin irritation, we suggest that you discontinue using the product.

Second, we want to offer you a full refund or a choice of a different Fitbit product to replace your Force (Fitbit will handle all shipping costs and will provide a refund in any difference in price.)

You can visit http://www.fitbit.com/comparison/trackers for more information about Fitbit trackers.

Please let us know if you purchased your Force on Fitbit.com or at a retailer and whether you would like a refund or replacement for a different type of Fitibt tracker.

We are sorry that even a few consumers have experienced these problems and assure you that we are looking at ways to modify the product so that anyone can wear the Fitbit Force comfortably. We will continue to update our customers with the latest information.

We look forward to your response and finding a resolution for you.
************************************************************************

After reading a few suggestions online, I covered the charging port with electrical tape and continued wearing the device.  Since the rash became increasingly uncomfortable, I discontinued wearing it completely on 2/7/14. 

I am filing this report for two reasons:
1. My rash seems to be getting worse.
2. My stepdaughter (who is not genetically related to me) has developed a similar rash from using her Fitbit Force, which leads me to believe that the problem is more widespread than the email above suggests.
justification: Multiple users have reported skin irritation, likely due to an allergic reaction to nickel in the device.

incident_description: While in use in a residential setting, the surge protector emitted smoke and sparks. The unit appears to have sustained internal heat damage as a result of this incident.
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident caused property damage, making it a level 2 severity. The likelihood is rated 3 as such incidents, while possible, are not common in residential settings.

incident_description:
This is a problem with a Philips LCD "Photo Frame" which I used to display photos of my family. The frame was connected to the included AC power supply, it also has an internal battery.

I reached for the frame to upload new photos and noticed that the back was hot and felt odd. Upon examination I noticed that the internal battery had expand to such a degree it "popped" the metal backing off of the plastic frame housing. The battery was extremely hot to the touch. I unplugged the device and set it face down on a hard surface to cool.

I'm worried that others using this frame - Philips Model 9FFCME/37 (manufactured 2006) might experience this failure, and that they might not be as lucky as I was in a timely discovery. I worried that had I left the frame unattained it might have caught fire....

I have photos showing the extent the battery expanded.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the potential for fire poses a significant risk, making the likelihood of a serious incident high.

incident_description:
Cellphones that have their batteries sealed within the units purchased by caller's company sometime in 2010 with no problems until now.

Caller is reporting that around the beginning of December 2013, his 7 daughter was holding her phone when the screen cracked,  she brought it to her father who noticed that the front and back was bulging.

He contacted the manufacturer who advised him that his warranty had expired and that it could be dangerous for them to attempt repair because the phone had bulging in the back and the front.

December 18th, 2013 his 13yr old daughter brought her phone to him saying it looked weird and when he took it he noticed that the screen is beginning to bulge.

He went online to research, found that this is happening with other phones and he wanted the public aware.

There are no injuries to be repeated.

The caller has not contacted the manufacturer regarding this second phone but does intend to contact them.
justification: Battery bulging in two phones within a short period, indicating a likely recurring issue.

incident_description: The Kawasaki 19.2v cordless drill battery charger (purchased from Tractor Supply some time ago) started melting along with the filtered power strip that I had it plugged into. If by chance I did not check on it one day, this could have burned down my house. Model of battery charger is 690072, sn 0909006865.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and the likelihood of it happening again is high given the charger's defect and the lack of an automatic shut-off feature.

incident_description:
I bought a FitBit Force on 1/21/14.  I began wearing it on 1/24/14.  On 1/29/14, I tried to charge the product and was unable to.  I contacted the company and stopped wearing the device while waiting on a response.  On 2/4/14, I noticed a red, raised, blistered rash/burn.  I had heard about the FitBit Force causing a rash, so I looked it up online to see what it looked like.  Mine looked exactly like this rash.  I went to the doctor today.  The doctor believes this is some sort of burn and prescribed burn cream and steroids.  

I was told by FitBit that the rash is caused by a nickle allergy, but I do not have an allergy to nickle.  They also said that the nickle was on the clasps of the band.  My rash/burn is on the top part of my wrist where the connector is to plug in the device.  

My concern is that there seem to be so many people with this problem and the company is still selling this device and offering replacements.  I am hoping it is just an allergy of some sort and will go away without any long term effects to my health.
justification: The incident resulted in a burn injury, and there are numerous reports of similar incidents, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: My 4 year old and I were playing with his walkie talkies mater and Finn Mc missle disney pixar and I just put fresh batteries in not even five minutes after we began playing Finn Mc missle started smoking in my hands and smelling like fire and Burt wires and I shut them both off.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident of a walkie talkie smoking and emitting a burning smell is concerning and could have led to injury if not promptly addressed.

incident_description: Fitbit is worn like a watch and it tracks the time, calories burned, distance walked, stairs climbed, active minutes and sleep activity.  It is worn on the wrist 24/7, except for showering.  I bought it approximately one month ago and it's been great.  Yesterday, I noticed a rash on my wrist under the Fitbit.  After going online, it looks like this is a reoccurring problem for many people with the Fitbit.  I emailed the company and they apologized and are providing me with a full refund.  Their website says they are investigating the cause, but it is still unknown.  It's scary to not know what caused this skin rash on my wrist.  Many report the rash gets worse before getting better.  I think it would be wise to pull the product off the market until they figure out how to fix the problem.  A great product with a scary result!
justification: Skin rash, potentially worsening, reported by many users, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: I received the Fitbit Force for Christmas and started wearing it on my left wrist on 12/26/13.  I charged it the second time on 1/30/14. On 2/1/14, I noticed some redness on my wrist toward the outside (where the metal portion/ charging port/ altimeter are located on the back of the device) where the Force would rest against my skin. I took it off for that day and the next. I started wearing it again on 2/3/14, with the charging port facing the inside of my wrist. The rash/burn started on the inside of my wrist on 2/6/14. I covered the metal portion with electrical tape to create a physical barrier on 2/6/14. Upon researching causes/ cures, I discovered this was a much more serious, widespread problem and discontinued using the device on 2/9/14.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (skin rash/burn), and given the widespread nature of the issue, it's likely to occur again.

incident_description: I purchased and began wearing a FitBit Force (activity tracker wristband) in Dec 2013. Last week I developed a blister-like burn where the metal on the band touches my skin. The burn has continued to worsen and is now a scaly, itchy patch.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (skin burn) and the likelihood of occurrence is possible, as it took time for the symptoms to develop and affect a significant number of users.

incident_description:
I developed a burn/rash after almost two months of use of my FitBit Force. 

Product: Fitbit Force (A wrist watch/ pedometer) 

I was the only one using my fitbit. 

I started to wear it December 25th 2013 and discovered the issue February 18th. I wore the product 24/7 however removed it to shower. 

The harm was developing a burn/ rash. 

The harm occurred from wearing the watch, however did not present until almost two months after using the device.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (burn/rash) and the likelihood of occurrence is possible given the delay between use and symptom onset.

incident_description: Burn looking rash after wearing the FitBit Force for approximately 6 weeks.  Rash developed where the battery port for the device is located.  46 yof was seen by medical professional.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (burn looking rash) but did not cause death, and while it's possible for such an allergic reaction to occur, it's not common or certain.

incident_description:
While sitting in the charger, the battery for my cordless drill started on fire. I did manage to get it outside. The smoke set of all the detectors in the house. The charger and battery were brought back to the service center. They told me that the battery and charger could be sent to the manufacturer but that the manufacturer was not interested unless I paid the shipping cost to send it both ways. Had I not been home when this started on fire, it could have burnt the home down. This is a safety issue I feel should be followed up on.

Thank you.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident could have caused significant property damage if not attended to promptly.

incident_description:
A week ago I noticed some itchy bumps on my wrist. I put a bandage on them because I have sensitive skin and will itch something until I bleed and these bumps were being irritated by my Fitbit Force. After I took the [bandage] off (I have an allergy to some adhesives and didn't want to leave it on too long) it was worse. So I start putting my Fitbit up higher, above my wrist bone, but the rash was getting worse. That was uncomfortable so I just started wearing the Fitbit loosely. Still got worse. And it was so itchy. Stopped wearing the Fitbit during the day Thursday and just put it on to track my sleep. Told my boyfriend (who bought me the Force) about it over Valentine's dinner and he told me about an article he had read. Came home and read some articles and looked at some pictures and sure enough...It was my Force all along. 

I received my Force on Christmas day and wore it continously until this past Thursday.
justification: The individual experienced an allergic reaction to their Fitbit, resulting in itchy bumps and discomfort, classified as an injury.

incident_description: Got a Force, wore it for two weeks before noticing itching and pain in my arm. Switched it to my other arm; repeat of the problem. Saw a segment on GMA and so stopped wearing it. Fitbit was responsive, as was Best Buy, so I got my FORCE returned and got a One, with no further problems, but while Fitbit is responding quickly to inquiries, and is quick to return or refund, it seems illogical to me that all of these techies, with everything they know about everything, can't figure out what's going on. They are still saying "a small percentage of users," but it looks like a large number of people are affected.
justification: The user experienced injury (itching and pain) due to the product, and multiple users seem to be affected, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: About Feb 4th, 2014, I started getting a rash caused by the FitBit Force. I didn't think anything of it until I saw the notice on the FitBit dashboard. I wore it on my other wrist for one day. I immediately started getting a rash bump on my other wrist so I took it off and went about getting it returned. It didn't matter, the rash kept spreading and getting worse. Some days it would seem better then the other day it was purple like a bruise and now it's really starting to peel like a burn. I had the FitBit Flex previously never with any problems. I'm making a doctor appointment this week just in case it keeps getting worse. It itches like crazy sometimes. There are now over 500 reported consumers with this problem and that's just the vocal minority. I read on an article one user said theirs got so bad it was a hole on their wrist.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe skin reaction, including a rash, purple discoloration, and peeling, affecting over 500 users, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description:
Received a FitBit activity tracker for Christmas. Set it up via [REDACTED] app. Wore it for 3-4 weeks. It synched frequently with my [REDACTED] as I had both devices on me all day long and the tracker 24/7. When I went to work a coworker took one look at it and advised me to google it as she had read an article about the problem. I did and was amazed that many others had same thing - pictures of their burns looked like mine, some even bigger. 

Problem began one day when I shoveled snow and my gloves got damp. As soon as I got back in house I took the gloves off. Later that evening I noticed my wrist was red and itchy and hurt.  Since it was right under where the tracker was I took tracker off immediately. Made sure tracker was dry but put a small [bandage] over the open charging port and put it back on. At bedtime it appeared worse so too tracker off.  Upon rising next day, put new [bandage] on the tracker and put it on my other wrist. That wrist started getting rash/burn so took it off immediately and have not worn since. 

Looked like a very bad sunburn, appeared to go down several layers of skin. Put [REDACTED] and [bandage] on burn but it appeared to get worse so next day took [bandage] off washed both wrists well and started spraying alcohol on it so the burn would cool down. Several small blisters had appeared right below where open charging port is but alcohol appeared to have stopped progression of burn. Continued with washes and alcohol for several day and when they no longer appeared "raw" began to apply a lotion with aloe in it. 

Both wrists are healed up (I guess) but the area that was "burned" is greatly discolored/noticeable. I am hoping with time it will go away completely but this process has taken numerous weeks to heal. I contacted Fitbit who sent refund right away. Have not returned tracker as I read others were advised not to by your agency.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe skin burn, requiring immediate removal of the device and medical attention.

incident_description:
I received a Fitbit Force for Christmas.  I have worn the product on my wrist day and night since then  as recommended by Fitbit.  After about one and a half months of wearing it, I noticed a red, bumpy, itchy rash where the metal part of the wristband has contact with my skin.  I immediately began researching this issue to see if anyone else was experiencing this problem.  I found several news stories and reports from hundreds of Fitbit Force users who are suffering the same problem. I have never been allergic to anything my entire life, especially not nickel.  This product needs to be pulled until someone gets to the bottom of this. incident_description:
I unpacked the unit from the shipping carton.  I removed the unit's front cover and installed a GSM SIM card, all in accordance with the retailer's instructions.  While I was installing the SIM card I observed that there was a loose wire inside the unit.  In investigating where the loose wire should have been connected, I studied the power connections for the switched accessory outlet.  In my study I discovered that the switched accessory outlet was wired with correct polarity -- that is, AC hot, neutral, and ground were routed to the correct pins of the accessory outlet -- but that the device was switching the accessory outlet on and off by interrupting AC neutral instead of by interrupting AC hot.  I validated my observation with a VOM and also with a USA three-prong outlet tester.

I believe this to be a dangerous situation.  The external load will spontaneously begin operating if it finds a ground.  If a person believes the switch is off and therefore also believes the external load is not energized, he might touch the external load in a way that would cause him to receive a 120 VAC shock.  The latter could cause him injury or death.

I informed both the manufacturer and the retailer of my finding.

You can read a lot more about what I discovered by reading the web article I wrote on the subject.  Visit http://home.roadrunner.com/~[REDACTED]/witura-error.html to read my article.
justification: The incorrect wiring could cause a 120VAC shock, leading to injury, if a person touches the external load while believing it's off.

Based on news stories and message board posts I am reading online it sounds like there are numerous people which are having the same issue.  The company's response is that it is a nickel allergy because the material around the charging port is made of surgical grade stainless steel which includes some nickel.  Prior to this I did not have any allergies I was aware of.  It could potentially be an issue with a faulty battery that is causing chemical burns because shortly after this started the battery stopped holding a charge for more than 36 hours.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (skin rash) and there are numerous reports of similar issues, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: After wearing the Fitbit Force for 4 weeks, I have developed a rash/burn on my left wrist, directly under the portion of the product that houses the charging mechanism/battery. It is blistery, oozes and won't go away with over the counter ointments.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (rash/burn) and the likelihood of occurrence is possible, as it took 4 weeks for symptoms to appear.

incident_description: I began wearing my Fitbit Force fitness tracker 12-27-13. I noticed a very red and irritated patch of skin directly under the band a few days ago. Today it seems worse. After some research I discovered I am not alone. I wore it every day and night for over a month. I only removed it to shower. I never got it wet. I never overcharged it. I have never had an allergic reaction to nickel. This product was in contact with my skin for more than 30days and I am horrified to read some of the theories regarding the cause. Please do what you can to find out the cause and hopefully prevent others from potential harm.
justification: The incident resulted in skin irritation but no serious injury, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the widespread use of Fitbit devices and similar products.

incident_description: I had a iPhone 3GS for a couple of years and then upgraded to a new iPhone. I used my old phone (3GS) as an iPod and kept it in a drawer. After a few months of little use and being in the drawer, i pulled it out and discovered the battery had expanded and destroyed the phone. The screen popped off, the boards were broken, and pieces were all over the drawer. When i picked it up, the battery discharged some sort of gas. Given that it is a lithium ion battery, I don't think that gas was healthy. I did not see the battery expand so I do not know how much force was behind it, but given the damage to my phone, I am glad it did not happen in my pocket.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident resulted in significant property damage (destroyed phone) and potential health hazard (battery gas discharge).

incident_description: My Fitbit Force has caused a burn/irritation to my wrist. Many users of this product are reporting the same results.
justification: Multiple users reporting similar burns/irritations indicates a high likelihood of occurrence, but no severe injuries reported.

incident_description:
This product was brand new.  Product was taken out of original package and charging began according to their instructions (enclosed).

The battery charger was plugged into an outlet and the batteries that came with it were being charged.  The batteries had never been used and this was the very first time that the consumer used the charger.  During the charge cycle, the consumer noticed that a light on the unit was blinking red.  This is an indicator that there is a problem.  The consumer felt the batteries and they were extremely hot to the touch.  The consumer was able to remove 3 of the batteries, but one of them was fused to the charger itself.  The consumer left it in as was.

The consumer did not notice any smoke or burning odor in his home, when this occurred.

The following day, the consumer contacted the manufacturer about this incident on 9/4/2013.

He received a letter back from the manufacturer, which is dated 10/10/2013, with the resolution.

The consumer mailed the battery charger back to the manufacturer with original packaging at his expense for packaging not post and he received a check for $20.00 from them.  The correspondence indicated that if the consumer cashed the check, it indemnifies the mfr. of any claims.
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a potentially hazardous situation with batteries overheating and fusing to the charger, warranting a severity level of 2.

incident_description:
After about 1-1.5 months of wearing the FitBit Force I started to get raised bumps and, what I thought was, a rash. It progressed into 1.5-2in long, .5in wide mark that looks like a burn and itches miserably.  Even after discontinuing use of the product the burn remains.  It's been 2 weeks of intermittent and then discontinued use and it doesn't show signs of healing. 
The company is claiming that this is due to a nickel allergy, but I have never been and am currently not allergic to nickel. Given the current state I will be visiting my dr and may have to schedule specialist visits for a dermatologist to preventn permanent scarring.
justification: The incident resulted in a significant injury (burn mark) and ongoing itching, warranting medical attention.

incident_description:
[ your site lost my letter I typed out when I hit submit, so I'm trying this a second time, more abbreviated ]

I purchased a Fitbit Force last October. Received it in November. My wife started to wear it in December. After about 4 weeks she developed a rash on her left wrist where she was wearing the Fitbit Force, where its metal parts meet the skin. She stopped wearing the Fitbit Force, but the rash has continued to worsen and is still ongoing, red, inflamed, itchy. 

Fitbit blames this on a nickel allergy that n% and a very small percentage of their customers have.

Except my wife does not have said allergy.

I question the safety of the product and specifically the metal composition; as the "highest grade stainless steel" which Fitbit claims is used; is several shades darker and more textured than any stainless steel that I am familiar with through for instance my [REDACTED] wrist watches and tools. 

I think action should be taken to protect other consumers who are unaware they are likely to get a severe rash with prolonged use of the defective product.
justification: Wife's persistent rash and itching, despite ceasing use, indicates a severe allergic reaction.

incident_description: I developed a rash that turned into an open wound on my wrist after wearing a Fitbit Force activity tracker.
justification: The incident resulted in an open wound, classifying it as an injury (severity level 3), and while not common, it's possible for such reactions to occur with wearable devices (occurrence likelihood 3).

incident_description:
I was given the Fitbit Force as a Christmas gift. I began wearing it immediately. Within three weeks, I had a rash from where the display portion of the bracelet touched my skin. The rash has gotten worse, although I've stopped wearing it. To date, it is red, lumpy and is weeping. It also itches.

I switched wrists, thinking that moisture and/or wearing it too tightly was the problem. I now have a rash on my left wrist as well that itches. It is developing bumps, although I stopped wearing the bracelet the moment the area became red.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe skin reaction, including itching, lumps, and weeping, which is classified as an injury.

incident_description: TV Lamp door and dual connectors burned and melted.  I discovered the damage after smoke and fire alarm going off.  I tried to replace the lamp with a new one but could not get the wiring to connect since the connection box in the TV melted and won't hold wires in place for connection to the lamp.  There isn't any slack in the wires to try to individually connect each wire.  I talked to Sony and they sent a guy to look at it.  Nothing has been addressed.  I'm thinking about trying to solder any extension wire between the hookups.  Totally frustrated that I spent all the money on this TV and also replaced bulbs 5-6 times.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident resulted in significant damage to the TV, making it unusable.

incident_description: blistered rash from product on wrists about 30- 37 days or so after started wearing. area blistered and burned like appearing occurred where skin made contact with battery port. No reaction from band or clasp. first right wrist, then occurred on left wrist when tried there. area healing, scabbed, right wrist still slightly tender and red 2 weeks after no longer wearing device.
justification: Skin injury (blisters, burns) occurred, not a rare event but not inevitable given the product's design.

incident_description:
Let me start by saying I am a physician, an OB-GYN, so I am writing you from the perspective of a doctor.  I received a Fitbit Force for Christmas and started wearing it on Dec 26.  The product was wonderful, and though I had heard of some issues with skin irritation, I had never had a prior problem with metal allergies and really was not concerned.  However, on Jan 29 I placed the Force on my arm soon after charging (prob the third time ever it was charged).  Later in the day I noted a dark red mark on my wrist, more on the lateral aspect near the ulnar side of the arm. I removed the Force and I have had it off for 5 days now.  There is no itching, it is bumpy and raised, it is very red and has the appearance of a burn, but there is no pain.  I tried using a topical rx steroid bid for several days without relief. If anything, the lesion has spread and gotten larger.  I went on the Fitbit website only to find literally hundreds of other people who are having the exact issue.  Most occur right after charging, most are after the Force was charged 2-3 times, all appear to have burn lesions and many have needed to seek medical attention.  

Fibit claims this is a nickel allergy.  There is NO WAY this is a nickel allergy.  Those who claim to have responded to steroids have taken weeks to improve - they likely would have improved anyway.  Someone suggested Aloe Vera - which I used yesterday and I actually thought it had improved a bit.  Today, it actually looks like it is going to peel. There can be no coincidence that so many are affected.  Please look at the community blog about "burn" on their website.
justification: Multiple users reporting similar symptoms after charging, suggesting a widespread issue causing injury.

incident_description:

I gave up and had to drill a few extra wholes and the tv still isn't stable 100% with also 4 kids in my house it is scary. The size alone and weight is very dangerous and with kids in the home 100% NOT safe. Also see the comment son amazon all having the same issue.

incident_description:
We purchased a Philips Flat Screen television, model 37PFL5332D/37.  Some months later, the television began to emit smoke and flames from just behind the upper right side of the viewing screen.  We phoned Philips and they said it was two months out of warranty and there was nothing they could do about it.  We had no idea the set was out of warranty!  They were very rude and quite adamant that the product was out of warranty and wanted nothing more to do about it.  I told them we didn't have the money for a disposable $1,200 television and they, again, said it was out of warranty and there was nothing they could or WOULD do about it.

We had the television repaired at a Philips-approved repair facility for nearly $300 and it worked great.

However, last night, the same exact problem occurred in the exact same place on the television.  We are several years out of warranty, but my concern is that this piece of electronics that we invested in is now a smoking and burning pile of junk.  Again, Philips wants do to NOTHING to help us, and we feel this is not only poor customer service, but a complete and total lack of ethics as this issue is a KNOWN problem with one of their products and they are blithely doing nothing about it.

When the television caught on fire last night, the entire house VERY QUICKLY filled with a very noxious odor and my entire family began coughing horribly. 

This is not not right and could end up costing a family their lives if the television were to catch on fire after they've left the house or gone to bed.  This is a complete and total disregard for not only consumers, but individuals for greed and profit.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (coughing) due to noxious fumes, and the likelihood of reoccurrence is high given the previous repair and Philips' refusal to address the issue.

incident_description:
Apple iPhone 3Gs battery expanded during charging.  This caused the screen to separate from the case.  This also caused the circuit board to crack and pulled the screws out of the case.  I have two issues with this:
1. This is a potential hazard as the battery could catch fire or explode causing injury.
2. The nature of the failure has rendered an expensive piece of equipment useless.

The manufacturer had to be aware of this as reports across the internet date back to 2011.  At no time did they tell their customers that this was a potential problem. Had I known about this I would have replaced the battery.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (expensive equipment rendered useless) but no physical harm, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the widespread reports dating back to 2011.

incident_description: I wore the Fitbit force on my arm for about a week when I noticed a red area under the band.  I thought maybe I got soap or something under the device, so I switched it to my other wrist. After two days, there was a red mark on my left wrist, and my right wrist looked worse, the red spot had blistered.  At that time, I went to the Fitbit website and checked the discussion boards for allergic reactions.  I found many people had the same issue, but they believed it was a chemical burn from the battery port.  A week after removing the Fitbit, my arm still has not healed.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (blister) and the likelihood is high given the numerous similar reports on the Fitbit discussion boards.

incident_description: I received a Fitbit Force at the end of December from my husband for a Christmas present. I have been wearing it every day. Today when I took it off to take a shower, I have a weird burn or rash on my arm.  It is a reddish area with two raised "bumps" in it. I believe this is caused by something having to do with the device. It has appeared since Monday, which is the last day I had it off of my arm. I did not notice any problem then. I have photos if anyone wants to see them.
justification: The user developed a rash and raised bumps on their arm after wearing the Fitbit, indicating a possible allergic reaction (severity level 2), which is a possible occurrence (likelihood 3).

incident_description: I purchased a fitbit Force on 11/11/13 and wore it without incident unitl I began to notice a red, itchy, blistery patch on my right wrist.  I switched the Force to my left wrist and then began to experience the same red, itchy blisters on that wrist within hours.  After two weeks of treatment and not wearing the Force during the day my rash/burn is barely healing.

I take it off when I am showering.  This morning I noticed a rash appearing on the top side of my wrist right below where the charging port is on the Fitbit Force band.  I did a search on the Internet and noticed that LA Times (http://www.latimes.com/business/technology/la-fi-tn-fitbit-force-skin-rash-refund-20140114,0,1950912.story) had an article about other people having rash issues.

I have since been on the company's community site (https://community.fitbit.com/t5/Force/Fitbit-burned-arm/td-p/3661) and there are many posts of people experiencing the same issue -- some more severe than mine.

incident_description:
I began wearing the FitBit Force watch on my non-dominant left wrist.  After 2+ weeks of wearing the FitBit, I began to notice a rash forming under the charging port of the band.  Assuming it was bacteria related, I began cleaning my FitBit Force watch with alcohol.  The rash persisted.  I attempted switching the watch to my right wrist, and again, the same reaction.  

After visiting with my dermotologist, I have been informed that it is due to contact dermatitis, a condition in which the skin becomes red, sore, or inflamed after direct contact with a substance.
