justification: Hearing loss and constant ear roar due to a loud, shrill noise from the cell phone, affecting job performance.

incident_description: Ryobi 18 volt battery pack blew up while in charger in garage causing multiple fires
justification: The incident resulted in multiple fires but no reported injuries, hence severity level 2.

incident_description: I have a HP Photosmart Premium Printer C309a. The product started smoking and caught the paper in the tray on fire while trying to print.
justification: The printer catching fire poses a significant risk, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: Ryobi lithium battery pack got very hot while charging then would not work.  I have two of them and same thing happened to both.  They were both too hot to touch when i took them off the charger.  Its model 130429008. Both were less than 6 months old when problem occured.
justification: Both batteries overheated and became unusable, posing a potential fire hazard but no injuries reported.

incident_description: I bought an iPhone 3GS from Apple 3 years ago and one day I made a call, during the call it exploded to 4x the size caused by the battery
justification: The incident involved a product malfunction but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: My iphone 3gs was dead so I plugged it in to the charger and set it on the couch.  An hour or so later, husband hears a loud pop and smells a foul odor.  Unplugged iphone from charger, but didn't realize what had happened until my daughter brings me the phone.  The battery exploded and the pressure of the explosion popped the iphone open.  Had we not been in the living room when it happened, it could have caught the couch on fire.  This is a serious safety issue and needs to be addressed asap!  I still have my original iphone that's 6 years old and it is still fine.  My kids use these two phones as their ipods and I definitely don't feel they are safe anymore.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (destroyed iPhone) and could have led to a fire, posing a significant risk to the occupants.

incident_description: iPhone 3gs was stored on a shelf with no liquid anywhere near it. When I looked at it today, it had basically expanded all by itself, so that the glass screen had separated from the body by about 2cm in some spots, though it was still adhered to it. I learned that there is a not-so-uncommon phenomenon of the batteries failing and essentially bursting. I consider this not only a product defect, but more imporantly, a serious safety hazard. I have no use for the iPhone at this point and it's not even salvagable by replacing the battery. I was informed by a friend who used to work for Apple that I should immediately place it in a [REDACTED] bag because the innards of the battery are TOXIC and that I should then take it to the Apple store ASAP as they actually have safes designated for this to store the items while awaiting disposal. They also stated that on at least one occasion in this person's store that they had to make a rush trip to the ER in response to just ONE of these devices behaving in this manner while in the store. THIS IS ABSOLUTELY UNACCEPTABLE from a company as reputable as Apple. Aside from their knowledge of this defect, this is just irresponsible and should result in some sort of repercussions for putting public health at risk. I have a small child and had she been using it at the time it decided to self destruct, I would be far more livid.
justification: The incident involved a battery failure that caused the iPhone to expand and potentially release toxic substances, posing a serious risk of injury.

incident_description:
Hewlett Packard cs rep admits to me the laptop that burned me is Hewlett Packards fault. Admits The blank  screen saying Operating System Not Found is also HP fault. Then says to me sorry but the Pavilion is obsolete and Hewlett Packard will do nothing to fix this  serious fire hazard. Had I not unplugged it or left the house with it plugged in ... My dog.  

I spent 3000.00 on two Pavilions the end of 2008 and this is how they treat customers? I don't care if I only spent 20.00. A fire hazard is a fire hazard PERIOD. The other Pavillion is warm and won't use it. When I burned my hand on the first Hewlett Packard I unplugged the other one. I experienced first hand how dangerous these laptops are. 

People if you own a HP laptop, unplug it. Especially if you have children or pets.

I told the cs rep I'm going to the BBB and states atty with this fire hazard! All he could say was sorry Hewlett Packard can't help you that I'm on my own!
justification: Injury occurred due to a laptop overheating and burning the user's hand, and the likelihood of this happening again is high given the company's refusal to address the issue.

incident_description: Battery pack split open while in use revealing the two batteries inside. One of the batteries had expanded and forced the cover to split open. I have removed the battery from the building due to concerns of fire or contamination, but it is available for examination if desired.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a battery pack splitting open, posing potential fire or contamination risks, making it an incident with possible reoccurrence.

incident_description: Bought a Kurio 7 Tablet for my daughter and it overheated today. Tried to pick it up and I couldn't even touch it, it was too hot, I had to use a jacket I had laying around to pick it up. [REDACTED] Still waiting to hear back from tech support, but seems this is a common problem among many others which is a shame, I was happy till today!
justification: The tablet overheating to the point of being unsafe to touch indicates an incident, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: My power supply caught fire.
justification: Power supply fire is possible but not common, and no injuries were reported.

incident_description: Laptop operates very hot and has on numerous occasions ejected hot air that burns.  Unit is constantly operating at high temperatures.  I am afraid to use for fear of fire or battery explosion.
justification: The laptop's overheating and ejecting hot air that burns poses a high likelihood of causing a fire or battery explosion, which could lead to property damage but not necessarily physical injury.

incident_description: Apple iPhone 5 Lightning to USB Cable gets hot, melts and burns.
justification: While the incident resulted in property damage, no injuries were reported.

incident_description: I was working on my laptop and heard a noise on the floor.  I looked done and there was fire and arcing.  I promptly unplugged the computer and adapter.  The floor is a hardwood floor.
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a fire and arcing, posing a potential risk to the individual and the property.

incident_description: On April 6, 2013 the light in my home office flickered several times followed by a sound reminiscent of arcing of electricity.  In a period of one to two minutes it reoccurred several times. Concerned, I looked out the window of the room and observed smoke exiting the attached garage from   the side of the garage door.  I immediately went into the garage thru a kitchen door and observed fire in the corner of the garage on a work bench where I had a Ryobi Battery and charger along with a few other tools.  I grabbed a cheap red mop and began hitting the flames in an attempt to extinguish the fire.  The mop broke and a grabbed a second mop.  Eventually I was able to get the fire out but not before thick black smoke from the ceiling to about chest level was through the garage. I then exited the garage and called the 911.  While waiting for the fire department, I opened the garage door to ventilate the smoke.  By the time the fire department responded, the smoke had cleared and the firefighters checked to ensure the absence of further fire.  They determined the cause of the fire to be the Ryobi charger and battery.
justification: Although there was a fire, no injuries were reported, hence severity level 2. The likelihood is rated 3 as the cause was a faulty charger and battery, which is possible but not certain.

incident_description: 9V battery was installed properly in integrated smoke detector as backup power for at least 6 months (likely 1 year) when one cell inside of it spontaneously exploded. This happened during the middle of the night in a house with no known environmental changes of significance.
justification: While no injuries were reported, the spontaneous explosion of a battery in a smoke detector poses a potential risk to occupants, making it an incident with possible occurrence.

incident_description:
Mild electical shock from Magnavox digital converter box. Model# TB100MW9 s/n's U21828984,U14828268,U27831703.

These three converter boxes show 32-42 Vac between the threaded part of the rf connector and earth ground.  
When the coax is disconnected and held in the hand it provides a good grounding of the hand and when touching the rf connector with the grounded hand a shock was felt.
I have been working around electronics for about 30 years.
This was a mild shock for me but I thought it worthwhile to mention to Magnavox and you.
I called Magnavox just to report the information and did not pressure for replacement boxes. The person I was talking to seemed indifferent.
justification: Mild electrical shock occurred, but no injury reported.

incident_description:
Acer Notebook Computers Aspire  is overheating on the bottom left side directly below the keyboard and when she uses it leaning it on  her legs they become burned but if she places it on a table it begins overheating within ten minutes.

She is asking that this laptop be inspected by compliance, recalled with repair at manufacturer expense.

Caller contacted the manufacturer around May or June 2012 and was advised only that the product warranty is no longer active.

No injuries have been reported
justification: While no injuries have been reported, the potential for burns due to overheating makes this a possible incident.

incident_description: Batteries have overheated and leaked into the Wii remotes. I lost 2 of the 4 Wii remotes because of the defective charger system
justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident resulted in damage to property (Wii remotes) due to a defective charger system.

incident_description: FIRE/PERSONAL INJURY HAZARD - Product is the Apple iPod Touch Lightning charge cable used for the Apple iPod Touch 5th Gen. On December 24th I purchased the fore mentioned products that came as a single unit for sale at Bust Buy stores. The devise functioned properly for the first 2 weeks or so and had a lighting cable failure. The failure was witnessed by my 16 y/o daughter. the devise was charging with the supplied lightning cable and wall charging adapter. She stated that there was a small flame and then the iPod charger stopped functioning. The cable had a 2mm hole burned through the outer jacket at the male iPod input coupling with obvious charring around the hole. I contacted the retailer and had received a replacement Apple brand - lighting charging cable. Thinking this was an isolated case of product failure we changed to monitoring the iPod device while it is charging. I have had 3 other cables fail at the same location without visible flames buy the cable was seen bulging at failure site and was very hot to tough when it failed. the retailer replaced the cable 3 times without questions. The most recent time, two days ago, I contacted Apple Warranty line to inquire as to the cause and request another new cable. They refused to indicate whether there where high incidence of failure in the cables and refused comment about the initial cable failure stating I could sent the iPod to the for testing / replacement. I have looked on the internet and found the failures are very common at the same location in the cable as all four of mine.
justification: Multiple instances of cable failure with potential fire hazard, no injuries reported.

incident_description: I left a 3 year old iPhone 3GS on charge and the battery expanded to such an extent that the lcd screen was pushed out of it's casing.  This is the second iPhone 3GS to have this problem in my household.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident of the iPhone 3GS battery expanding and pushing out the LCD screen is possible to happen again given the history in the household.

incident_description: I woke at 3:30 am to feed my infant and smelled burning plastic. I picked up my phone and burned my finger on the cord where it connects to the mophie case. As I pulled the cord from the case it sparked and was melted. It came apart: half of the USB connection still melted into the case and half on the cord.  This was the mophie juice pack plus. It was a replacement from the company from December 2012 because my first case broke after 11 months of use.
justification: Injury occurred due to melted plastic from the mophie case, indicating a possible design flaw or manufacturing defect.

incident_description: I purchased an iPhone 3GS 3 years ago. In the last couple of months the iPhone battery started expanding and couple of weeks ago the case broke.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning device, causing property damage but no physical harm.

incident_description:
Bought a NEW Dell Inspiron 15R Special Edition had for a few days - arrived 3/14 sent back 3/19 - incident 3.18

Monday 3/18 after recharging all night on a TV Table - wife awoke to smoke in house and fire alarms.  Fire department Determined/Concluded Laptop was cause of smoke and blown circuit breaker saved fire or further damage.  Wife saw smoke coming from Laptop

Just an FYI in case we are not the 1 in a Million customer.

In theory we are getting money back - but it will take 30-45 days.  This seems slow....

I wanted to share since wife who saw the smoke and called 911 is traumatized and now nothing we own can be plugged in.  So I'm hopeful this will help others.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident caused significant property damage and emotional trauma.

incident_description:
My Acer Aspire 8951G laptop computer has a removable battery-powered trackpad that can be used wirelessly away from the rest of the computer.

On the night of 2/27, the laptop was ON in sleep mode with the LCD screen off.  I heard a loud POP, and came downstairs to investigate.  When I looked at my laptop computer, I saw the laptop's trackpad no longer sat flush and level with the body of the laptop.

The battery cell inside the laptop trackpad had exploded and bulged outward due to heat.  The entire plastic body of the removable trackpad no longer can stay closed due to the bulge in the center.  The trackpad is no longer useable due to the fact it cannot sit flush and interface with the pins on the laptop side -- not to mention the hazard of future trying to charge a damaged battery.

On 2/28, Acer assigned me a RMA number of [REDACTED] and issued me a FedEx ground tracking label to return the laptop.  I elected to return only the wireless trackpad with the exploded battery due to sensitive personal data still on the laptop.  Days later, Acer claims they still are not able to find the defective module returned to them and refuses to help further, other to demand that I send the rest of the laptop to them without guarantee of return, repair, or compensation!

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in damage to the laptop's trackpad but no injuries, and while it could happen again, it's not likely to occur frequently.

incident_description:
I was never notified of the recall, that I have just been made aware of through an internet search. According to my two daughter's testimony, the RCA Audio Receiver smoldered and melted the front of the unit, made a loud pop through the [REDACTED] speakers (which I cannot test if they have been damaged yet). I witnessed scorching of the cabinet shelving bottom it was sitting on and smoke throughout the entire first floor.  

My daughters were watching a movie last night, after I retired for the night, and rushed into my bedroom to wake me, screaming that the receiver was on fire. When I came running downstairs, the entire first floor was covered in a light film of smoke and the smell was that of electrical/plastic burning. The smoke irritated our throats for a while, but we are okay. I am so fortunate that they didn't fall asleep or our entire house could have been engulfed in a fire and possibly deaths occuring.

Manufacture date: June 2002
Model: RT2600
SN: 223400782
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire hazard with potential for serious damage or injury, making it a significant incident.

incident_description:
(12/30/2012) The consumer stated that she was charging the product. It had been charging for about a minute when the consumer detected a burning smell coming from the tablet. The consumer felt heat at the bottom of the tablet. The consumer unplugged the product. 
(12/30/2012/ The consumer contacted the manufacturer.  She advised them of what happened. She was sent a replacement.
(01/07/2013) The consumer received the replacement. She stated that she charged the product and it worked fine for about 10 days. After the ten days, it wouldn't work properly. The product wouldn't turn on. The consumer charged it again and got the same burnt smell.
(01/08/2013) The consumer emailed the manufacturer. The company have not responded. 

The consumer got on the Toys R Us web site to check reviews. There were over 200 reviews. She did not read them all, but she did see one that indicated the same issue that she had. 

The consumer considers the product to be a fire hazard.

Representative [REDACTED] from Techno Source, the US distributor for CIDE Interactive from France (also known as KD Interactive)  (Techno Source - 20 West 22nd St. Suite 1101 New York, NY 10010)
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a product emitting heat and a burning smell, indicating a potential fire hazard, which is likely to occur again based on the consumer's experience with the replacement product.

incident_description: On 3/7/2013 After a day of numerous static shocks when touching metal, I was talking on my HTC Evo 4G and at the moment I felt a static shock on my chin my phone screen sent out a higher than normal static discharge to my face and ear and the phone screen pulsed as though something inside pushed it out and it shattered and continued for a minute or so afterward to pop and snap and continue to show more breakages. Slivers of glass kept popping like popcorn popping off the screen. I now see how that same static charge can ignite and cause fire while pumping gas as I've heard so I always avoided using my phone while refueling, but never have I heard of it shattering a screen nor sending a shockwave of mild pain in someones ear from the glass explosion. Having a screen protector would have prevented the glass from cutting me and kept glass somewhat intact so others should be notified as well as exactly where I felt the static shock at the beginning is where the charging port is located at the bottom of the phone where my chin was located. Requiring cell phone companies to place a rubber cover that fits over those outlets whether located on the side (where fingers would touch when holding phone) or at the bottom would prevent this front happening. Just move rubber seal to charge and replace when not in use. Im surprised it did not fry the internal circuits but it had been acting strange a day or two prior where it would act up like someone was touching screen and I would have to restart phone in order to stop it or remove the battery if phone didnt respond. If lets say someone had it on speaker during a call and away from face or using it otherwise and had it in close proximety to their face the shattering and spraying of slivers of glass could easily damage a person's eyes. I urge and beg you to look into this. Oddly, the glass seems to still keep showing more cracks than it did yesterday when it happened and once I was looking at it while I seen yet another cracked appear with a popping noise when it happened.
justification: The incident resulted in injury from shattered glass, and the likelihood is high given the common use of mobile phones and the potential for similar static discharges.

incident_description: I was charging a Dewalt DC9096 18 volt battery in a Dewalt DW9116 charger.  When I entered my workroom about 2 hours after the battery was placed in the charger, I could smell an acrid smoke in the room.  I went over to my workbench, and the smell was very strong.  I attempted to remove the battery from the charger, but it was so hot that I couldn't hold on to it.  I unplugged it, grabbed a pair of gloves, and put the battery/charger outside to cool.  I brought it back in to the house after an hour, and was able to remove the battery from the charger.  Both the battery and chargers plastic cases has started to melt, neither is usable.  The date code on the battery is 200725.  I suspect that if the battery had been charging much longer that it would have started a fire.  I had used the battery in a DeWalt 18 volt cordless drill earlier in the day without incident.  I contacted DeWalt customer service through their web site, and their e-mail reply indicated no concern about this serious safety issue.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a significant safety hazard (melted battery and charger, potential fire) and could have resulted in property damage or injury if left unattended.

incident_description: North Andover Fire Dept Incident #[REDACTED]  Fire Department called to [REDACTED] on 2/6/13 for an electrical problem with a cell phone charger. Upon arrival FD found a cell phone charger melted at the cell phone end. The end that plugs into the Edison wall outlet was undamaged. The cell phone charger had been plugged into the cell phone overnight on a bed under a pillow. The cell phone end of the charger had some of its plastic melted and the top left portion of the metal prong showed signs of possible arching. The cell phone had no damage and was working normally. A portion of the pillow and bed's comforter were damaged due to the heat produced from this incident. This phone had been charged under a pillow at least once prior according to the owner, but wasn't a regular practice. This charger was the one that came with the phone ([REDACTED]) and the owner had this phone for about a year.
justification: No injuries occurred, but property damage (pillow, comforter) resulted from the melted charger.

incident_description: Have an iPhone 3GS that was sitting on a table - noticed that it had "busted open" and that the insides of the case were buldged out and had a slight electrical smell to it.  Apple has assured me that it is 'safe' and did not say that I needed to dispose of it unless the contents of the battery starts to leak.
justification: The iPhone 3GS had a physical deformation and electrical smell, indicating a potential hazard, but no injury was reported.

incident_description: i woke up on the couch because my television was crashing down., the neck stand broke and now the screen is broken
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no physical harm, and it's possible for such an event to occur due to equipment failure.

incident_description:
I bought a Golf buddy Tour GPS on 6/16/2011 with a DECA system  LP-C04-01 LI-Polymer battery pack made in China. Yesterday on 3/5/2013 I charged the GPS, and went to play golf.  at 7:15am I attempted to turn on the GPS when the battery exploded in the TPS in my hand.  I took off the back of the GPS and the battery back had become separated from the rest of the battery.  The battery paper backing was inflated.  
 
I don't know if this is the same type of battery problem that the Boeing 787 is having.  This is for you information only.  aloha, [REDACTED]
justification: Battery explosion caused injury to the user's hand, but not severe enough to cause death.

incident_description: My grand daughter received a Nabi tablet for Christmas. My daughter purchase her a carrying  case  to put the tablet in. She notice a few day later that the tablets wasn't charging properly and that the screen looked different. I call the company in feb to make the aware of the problem. the of the problem. They asked me to send them a picture of the tablet which I did. I received a call back from a [REDACTED] badge number. He stated that if this tablet have any type of pressure form the sides back or front. That the screen could break. I am afraid that I a child apply any pressure on this screen the could get seriously injured especially since the product is used by very small children. I also explain to him that my daughter place this in the bag with the  charger he stated that they carry bags for this product. I feel that this product should have warning sticker on it telling you not to use another brand of carrying  cases do to possible breakage. Also making sure that no one child is injured.  I aslo asked for there phone number and address [REDACTED] refuse to give it to me.
justification: The tablet's screen is prone to break under pressure, posing a high risk of injury to small children who may apply pressure while using it.

incident_description: Cellphone over heating, battery swelling, battery jumps down in charge after heat. Phone shuts off. Restarts with no battery reserve.  Fear of battery fire.
justification: While no injury was reported, the incident involved a potential fire hazard due to battery overheating.

incident_description: I just had a samsung HP -s4253/HP-s5053 catch on fire .
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident of a Samsung printer catching fire is a possible occurrence.

incident_description:
3 year old iphone3gs "exploded" open. Came home to see battery had expanded so big that it popped open the iphone case, breaking the internals, found screws strewn about floor and bloated li-ion battery remains.  

This is unsafe. This was never mentioned in any documentation.  The battery is not user replaceble and Apple knows this will inevitably happen breaking the product. This is unacceptable.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the non-user-replaceable battery and lack of warning.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that she purchased a laptop and approximately a year and a half ago it was subject to a recall. She stated that she followed the instructions and the manufacturer replaced the laptop with this new one. 

The consumer stated that she was using her laptop for approximately 4 hours and decided to turn it off. The consumer stated that she turned off the computer and left the room where she was located at the time. She stated that approximately 10-15 minutes she started to hear a crackling noise. She decided to walk back into the room where the laptop was located and found that it was emitting sparks and smoke. 

The consumer stated that she immediately unplugged the adapter, but the smoke and sparks did not stop. She stated that she proceeded to remove the battery and the sparks stopped immediately. The consumer stated that the smoke and sparks were being emitted from the right corner were the battery was located. 

The consumer stated that she did not notice any visible damages to the laptop. 

The consumer stated that there were no damages to her home structure and she was not injured. 

The consumer stated that she hasnÃÂt used the laptop since the incident.

The consumer stated that she contacted the manufacturer and they advised for her to not use the computer and to remove the battery. Also they offered to repair the laptop, but she would have to pay for parts and repairs.

The consumer stated that she believes this product should be investigated due to the safety hazard that it poses to the consumer.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the laptop emitting sparks and smoke poses a significant risk, making it likely to happen again.

incident_description:
My iPhone 4 exploded when it was in a cabinet unused for two months. It is normal and an advanced feature that protects me as a user, says Apple Store in Stockholm/Sweden!
I claim that itÃÂ´s a manufacturing fault that should be solved by my rights in EU Consumer Law (http://www.apple.com/uk/legal/statutory-warranty/).

The iPhone is almost 2 years old and the EU Consumer Law in Sweden give me 3 years warranty IF itÃÂ´s proved to be a manufacturing fault as I claim. Apple Store in Stockholm/Sweden says itÃÂ´s totally normal and not a problem with a battery explosion in my iPhone 4! I had to pay about ÃÂ79 to get a replacement iPhone since the casing is destroyed.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident resulted in property damage, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' case. The likelihood is 'possible' as it's not common but not rare either.

incident_description: I left my iPhone 3GS turned off in a closet for some days, and when I pick it again I saw it was about to explode, the screen had popped out and cracked and the motherboard was cracked too, due to battery expansion.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage (iPhone) but no injuries, and while possible, it's not a common occurrence due to modern battery safety measures.

incident_description: I have an iPhone 3Gs, which I still use as my cellular phone. Today, it began to noticeably swell. The back has now completely severed from the front of the phone, and the battery keeps swelling. I can no longer use my phone, and it appears dangerous.
justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident caused significant damage to the phone, rendering it unusable and potentially dangerous due to battery swelling.

incident_description:
Our 9 year old son was sleeping in his bedroom with the door shut when the smoke alarm sounded.  My husband ran to check (he was in the next room) and when he opened the door smoke was coming from the television.  
As he approached he saw a small flame inside the tv.  Within seconds the flames quickly spread.  In less then 30 seconds from when the alarm sounded the tv was engulfed in flames.  My son was sleeping less then 12 inches away from the tv.  

My husband grabbed the tv and ran outside with it.  The tv, even in a mound of snow continued to burn for several minutes.  Burning pieces fell from the  tv and I had to stomp  out fire on 3 sections of carpet as I tried to get my son out of the room.  I then noticed a piece on fire by the front door and had to stomp out that fire.  

THe upper left side of the tv is burned right through the back.
justification: Injury was likely due to the proximity of the sleeping child to the rapidly spreading flames.

incident_description:
I had given my daughter my old Apple iPhone 3GS last year after upgrading my phone.  She uses it as an iPod.  This morning she noticed the screen pushed out of half of the case, and the back of the case was very bulged and rounded.  Additionally, I can see a crack in the motherboard through the now open side.

It appears the battery swelled.  We did not notice any plastic or other odor emanating from the device.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a malfunctioning device with a swollen battery, posing a potential risk.

incident_description:
The connection between the stand and standguide which comes with the Samsung PN42C450B1D television broke. There are plastic screw bosses in which screws are inserted to connect the two parts of the stand which is integrated with the flat screen tv. The plastic screw bosses broke in several places which the TV was moved and set back down. 

This created a safety hazard as the flat screen TV could have fallen over and hurt someone especially a child. In my opinion, the design of the stand using plastic screw bosses to connect the two parts of the stand is too weak to allow for a reasonable amount of stress on the connection. Simply moving the TV and setting down again resulted in the break.
I have contacted Samsung regarding the issue and they informed me that there has been no recall or other measures taken due to the poor stand design. Since the TV was purchased in 2010 and is out of warranty, they can be of no assistance. Initially, the representative with whom I spoke did not even offer to report the issue.
justification: The incident could have resulted in injury, as the TV could have fallen and hurt someone, especially a child.

incident_description:
Laflen-Cunningham Agency, Ltd., my employer, purchased a Quill Corporation brand paper shredder on 10/19/11.  The model number is QL-TXC15A, and the serial number is 111601723. On Thursday, February 14, 2013, my co-worker and I were emptying the collection basket of the paper shredder and cleaning out the paper that was stuck in the shredding teeth.  We unplugged the machine, emptied the basket, and then vacuumed the teeth to remove the remaining paper.  After putting it back together, we plugged it in and shredded a sheet of paper to make sure it was not clogged.  The paper shredded just fine, but the motor did not shut off automatically as was set to do.  We unplugged it and vacuumed the teeth again.  We plugged it back in and started to run another sheet of paper through the shredder when it popped and a fireball blew open the collection basket.  My co-worker was feeding the paper through when it happened, and she sustained minor burns on her hand and her hair was singed.  

I kicked the collection basket closed and the fire went out on its own.  No other damage was done other than the shredder itself, but it could have potentially been much worse.

[REDACTED]
justification: Injury occurred due to the shredder's motor not shutting off as designed, leading to a fireball and minor burns.

incident_description: I purchased a pair of Skullcandy Supreme Sound Inked yesterday at Target and used them on a half marathon today.  Shortly after the race began, the rubber bud got deeply lodged in my ear canal.  They were stuck so deep that they were invisible to the naked eye and  I was in a great deal of pain.  I was able to finish the race and went to the medical tent where they were able to tweeze out the earbud.  The experience was extremely scary and disconcerting to say the least.  I have used both skull candy and earphones in the past and this was not a case of user error.  I did nothing unusual to dislodge the rubber bud.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury, and while it's not common, it's possible given the design of the earbuds and the physical activity involved.

incident_description:
I had a Apple iPhone 3GS, out of warranty, where the battery was swelling.  It caused the back of the phone to expand.  I googled this and saw where other 3GS phone cases cracked, glass fronts came off, and some even exploded (battery exploded).  I took it to an Apple store and they would only replace the battery for $150.  An authorized Apple repair center told me to go to another Apple store ASAP because the expansion of the battery causing the hard plastic case to expand around the battery (very visible) indicated that the battery was seriously swelling and could explode.  (the case seemed expand over a period of only a few days after noticing a dark spot on the screen, the first sign of the battery swelling)  I took the phone to another Apple store and they acknowledged a battery problem and offered to sell me a replacement phone for $80.  
The fact that batteries can explode after 2 - 3 years of use of a very expensive phone AND the fact that the manufacturer does not disclose this to consumers is egregious.  They should issue a recall for all phones with this battery and replace the phones.  This is a dangerous situation and Apple should not just sit by with a sketchy program to replace the phones only to those who scream loud enough or have the insight to take the phone to less busy stores that are more service oriented.  What if the phone exploded in my pocket or my hand?  People are using older phones either as phones or ipods so they're not being quickly retired.
I tried to find some information on Apple's website and the only thing I found was in the user support community where a few people - in the US and abroad - had registered incidents.  I am fortunate to have learned of the problem before it became a hazard.
justification: While no immediate harm occurred, the potential for battery explosion makes this a high likelihood incident with potential for severe injury.

incident_description: My Logitech Harmony 900 has been problematic since day 1. It wouldn't hold a good charge without being left on the charger every day. At times the remote will lock up like a computer. To overcome this the battery has to be taken out to restart the device. Initially the battery slid out with some effort but recently when attempting to unlock the remote the battery was almost impossible to budge. Upon getting it out of the remote it looked extremely swelled to the point of bursting. I went online to do some research and the 3.7 volt lithium battery in this remote is a known issue which Logitech takes no responsibility for unless the item is under warranty. This would be like saying we should continue flying the 787 with known battery problems and the company shouldn't have any responsibility. Lithium batteries are known to explode when overheated and whether it is a faulty charger or the battery I don't know but it seems when this many people are complaining about the same issue the company should correct the problem.
justification: Potential for severe injury due to battery swelling and explosion, given numerous user reports and known lithium battery issues.

incident_description:
Dear Sir or Madam,

My Macbook Pro laptop computer's battery "exploded" in last month. 

It's the same problem as other users complained this issue on internet. You can search the key words, "macbook battery exploded", then you can see the pictures similar to my Macbook's battery exploded.

Apple, Inc. must recall the batteries exploded, no matter expired of warrantee or what excuses. 

Very dangerous and terrified bombing computer Macbook Pro made by Apple.

I still keep this exploded battery in our closet, as an evidence, however the Macbook's battery looks as a bomb which can burn/exploded anytime.

Best Regards
[REDACTED]
justification: While no injuries were reported, the incident of the battery exploding poses a significant risk of property damage and potential injury, as evidenced by similar incidents reported online.

incident_description: I plugged in my HP pavilion dv6500 laptop and turned it on. Aproximately 5 minutes later I heard what sounded like a shot gun blast. The laptop had exploded. I was sitting about 7 feet away in my kitchen. The laptop was on the island. I jumped up, took the laptop off of the island (it was burning the countertop) put it on the stove and put the flames out. I started to assess the damage to the countertop and take pictures with my cell phone, then it burst into flames a second time. I put it on the floor and extinguished it again....I then took it outside for fear of another explosion and called HP. There was damage to the countertop, the stove and the kitchen was covered in black soot.
justification: Laptop explosion caused fire, resulting in property damage and potential injury, but no reported injuries.

incident_description:
I purchased a Sansa Clip Zip 4gb MP3 player from a local Radio Shack store.

 I was injured when I tried to remove the product from it's packaging. 
There was an outer box (stiff paper product) that wasn't a problem.
However, inside the box there were two layers of an extremely stiff plastic that
was VERY difficult to open. Even though I was being very careful when I tried to
get through the plastic, I cut myself badly. I wasn't cut by the instrument I was
using, I was cut by the stiff plastic packaging material itself. The plastic material was rigid
enough to act as a "knife" when it had an exposed edge.

I accept that packaging needs to protect the product from damage, however, this could/should be
done in a way that doesn't risk the safety of the consumer.

When I called Sandisk about the incident, the customer service rep told me that I could find a video on You Tube that shows you how to open the package safely!!
justification: The incident resulted in an injury, and while the likelihood of occurrence is possible, it could have been prevented with safer packaging design.

incident_description:
The Lithium Ion Rechargeable Battery Pack ( NP-FX110 ) for our Sony DVD player has had one of it's cells expand to the point that it has cracked the plastic case that houses the cell.  It is pressurized to the point that it seems like it will explode if anything punctures the cell's membrane.  The unit is now inoperable.
It's safe to say that this is happening with MANY other units and this is not a fluke occurence but a manufacturing defect that could potentially hurt someone.  Sony has to realize that these DVD players are primarily used by children and a curious child whose DVD player stopped working could potentially puncture the pressurized cell, exposing the child to its chemicals.
I'd like to know what Sony will do about this and if they are interested in keeping a long time customer.
justification: The expanded battery cell poses a high risk of injury to curious children who might puncture it, exposing them to harmful chemicals.

incident_description:
The consumer says that she noticed a plastic burning smell.  It was coming from the back of her TV.  No smoke was present.  She unplugged the unit to the surge connector.  She says the cord was very hot at the time of the incident.  

The consumer says that the plug to the connector was melted.  

UPDATE: No injury occured because we were home in the middle of the night. Had we not been home we would have had a fire because it would have caught on fire and travelled through the walls.
justification: Although no injury occurred due to timely intervention, the incident involved a potential fire hazard, hence severity level 2.

incident_description:
The plastic cuff connecting my Haier 42" TV to its base failed. I was watching TV from the couch when the plastic cuff forcefully broke into pieces in front of my eyes, ripping out the screws connecting the TV to the base. The TV toppled over and fell onto the ground, damaging one corner but otherwise still functional. The stand itself did not move an inch. The cuff was in pieces about the floor. Nothing was touching the TV at the time.

The weak plastic of the cuff is not strong enough to support the weight of the TV. A falling TV could cause injury.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injury, and the likelihood of a similar event happening again is high due to the faulty design of the plastic cuff.

incident_description: I am writing to report a defect in the Samsung Galaxy S3 cell phone.  I was leaving work and the phone screen shattered in my hand.  I was in a warm building and as soon as I got outside in the cold weather, the screen shattered and I got glass lodged in my hand. I am under the impression that cell phone screens can withstand hot/cold weather. I did not drop my phone.
justification: The phone's screen shattered unexpectedly due to temperature change, causing injury from glass lodgment.

incident_description:

incident_description:
The 'Pro' version of the TV-B-Gone has a non-replaceable, rechargeable battery. My unit was charged and used a total of 6 times. For the initial use, I charged it per the instructions. It worked as advertised. Two days later, I went to use it again but the battery was dead. I charged it and again, and it worked. The unit was dead again after the 2nd day. It was very frustrating to use as I always had to 'anticipate' its use by re-charging beforehand. I could never pick it up and have it ready. After the sixth charge, I discovered that the battery had expanded to three times its width. The battery had also melted the front and rear covers. It created so much pressure that it popped off the back cover and landed more than 2 feet away. I've sent repeated emails to the company, as well as [REDACTED], the president. After several weeks, still no response.

I am very lucky that the battery did not start a fire. I charged the unit according to the instructions, and had around 10 minutes of total use. The idea is great but the implementation is not. I have included pics of the damaged unit with the swelled battery and separated cover.
justification: The battery swelling and melting the covers, along with the forceful expulsion of the back cover, poses a high likelihood of injury.

incident_description:
We had a secretary at our Fire Department HQ who unplugged a Belkin Surge protector from a wall outlet in order to move it to another location.  This particular model, #F9H620-CW, comes packaged with a longer screw meant to replace the short screw that keeps the protective cover plate over the outlet box.

When she removed the long screw and proceeded to pull the surge protector out of the outlet, the metal cover plate slid down onto the two metal spades of the surge protector as it was still making contact with the outlet.

There was an immediate flash, with minor, scorching damage to the device and the metal cover plate.  Although she wasn't hurt and no fire ensued, she was understandably shaken and recognized the potential for a more serious or tragic outcome.
 
I work in the Code Enforcement side of our County's Fire Marshal's Office, and was asked to look into the matter.  My first intentions were to see what - if any - info I could obtain about the product and how it was supposed to be used.  Unfortunately, the original packaging had been discarded after the initial purchase, so I was unable to find out if the instructions indicated power to be shut off to the outlet prior to removing the protective cover plate from the intended outlet.

Although the product is UL listed and is manufactured by a large, established, well known consumer products company, I was unable to find any operating info on the manufacturer's web page.  Subsequent emails and phone calls to the customer service departments were less than fruitless.  Their initial claim was that no instructions, literature or user information included with the product; in fact I was told there was no packaging at all.  

I pointed out that I was looking the product on their web-site, and it was clearly packed in a clear, protective plastic sales/display arrangement you would typically see in any hardware or Home Depot/Lowes store.  Also visible in the picture was the descriptive information about the product, though it is unreadable on line.  After an extended 'hold', I was informed that the product's packaging had no information regarding its installation or removal from an electrical outlet.
 
Staff from the Investigation side of our office advised that this scenario has played out in fire calls in the past, and suggested that we forward information to your organization for possible further action. Having found no recalls showing on the manufacturer's web page or the CPSC site, I request assistance from you in order to try to prevent further instances.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident resulted in minor damage and could have been more severe, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' with a 'Possible' likelihood of occurrence.

She says that smoke filled her house and smelled burning plastic.  There was no fire, just smoke and fumes filling the entire home.  She says the smoke was coming from the DVR box. I noticed it bulged, but I thought it was an optical illusion due to the case it was in. Well, when I was powering it down yesterday, I saw light emitting from the sides of the glass, underneath. incident_description:
This is one of several incidents I have experienced involving leaking Duracell batteries in the past year.

The device is a [REDACTED] LED headlight for bicycles, which is powered by 4 AA batteries. The batteries in the device were dated to expire on March 2012. The device has been used as a general purpose flashlight for inside the house rather than as a bicycle headlight.

The flashlight has been in regular use and today my wife informed me that it had stopped working yesterday. Because I have seen many devices damaged by Duracell batteries recently, I immediately opened the flashlight to assess the damage. 

The inside of the battery compartment is contaminated by a white material that has leaked from the batteries and has begun to corrode the battery contacts in the flashlight. This material irritates the skin and I am concerned it may contain toxic chemicals.

The leaked material has pooled on the surfaces of batteries, contacts, and the inside of the flashlight. This flashlight was working less than a day ago, so the leakage was not caused by the flashlight sitting unused for weeks or months. The batteries possibly started leaking before the light stopped working, because the leaked material has a dry crystalline quality to it, although the flow of the residue suggests that the material was fluid at the time it first leaked.

I was born in 1950's and leaky batteries were common in the 50's and 60's. Since improvements to batteries in the 70's and common use of Alkaline cells, battery leakage has become very rare. But now many Duracell batteries are leaking and are leaking much sooner in their lifespan. 

I have opened four devices in my home this month with similar damage. One of these devices was a valuable guitar with active electronic circuitry inside.

I think Duracell batteries may be unsafe and may put consumers at risk for burns and toxic effects. Please follow up with me to discuss what can be done about this problem. If you go on the Duracell website you will see that many consumers have the same problems.
justification: Leaking batteries caused damage to multiple devices, including a valuable guitar, posing potential injury risks from burns and toxic effects.

incident_description:
As an amateur radio operator, [REDACTED], I run my station on batteries so that it can be available in an emergency when no utility power is available.  

To charge the batteries and maintain their charge, I bought a 5 amp BatteryTender Part No. 022-0157-1, S/N 3412-100698C, from Amazon.com on 7 Dec 2012 and connected it to a [REDACTED] battery.  To test the charging, I deliberately ran the battery down to a 12 V level.   The wiring was standard for the setup in my upstairs radio room.

I woke up in the middle of the night and smelled an acrid odor in the house and found the BatteryTender warm, but not hot, and the battery warm.   The red light on the BatteryTender was on continuously, as it had been all day.  The red light indicates the charging mode. The battery had boiled over, warping the top.

Apparently, the BatteryTender had failed to go from the charging mode to the maintenance mode, over charging the battery.The battery's internal water was converted to hydrogen and oxygen.  The result is well known to be an explosion or fire hazard.  The BatteryTender should have stopped charging and gone to a maintenance mode automatically.  That's why it's called a "Tender" not a "Charger".

This is a product which is dangerous when it fails to work as intended.

I sent an e-mail to service@batterytender.com on 12/18/12 and have not had any response.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident involved a battery boiling over and potentially causing a fire or explosion, hence severity level 2.

We were charging it for 2 hours, and when she went to get it, we noticed that the screen had popped out, and the case was broken and bent. The battery had expanded considerably, and destroyed the case. I went online to check for other incidents, and I found many descriptions of this problem at apple.com forums. Our phone is out of warranty, so I doubt that Apple will do anything to help us, but there was no warning of this happening. It doesn't seem fair that a product would essentially self-destruct, even if it is to avoid the possibility of injury. I have called APPLE India and someone from their team has promised to look into the matter. Incase I do not hear from them within 72 hours, I have been advised by our lawyer to file a case on them in the Consumer Courts of India. This really is a dangerous thing to happen. My daughter could have seriously been injured.

I can send in pictures of the device if they are needed.

incident_description:
On December 26, 2012 at 7:00pm--I started to smell smoke/a definite electrical burning smell--I check all appliances, christmas tree. garage, attic, walls--smell started to get stronger. Finally I gave up and decided to wait for my husband to arrive home--I sat down to watch TV with the thought that if it gets any worse I am going to call the fire department. I turned on the TV and watched [REDACTED] for about five minutes--then I heard a couple of pops and then the screen went black--smoke and flames started to come out of the right hand side of the top of the TV, (the only thing I did not check). I immediately unplugged the set and disconnected the cable box. Scared the life out of me--husband arrived home. With the set unplugged the smoke and smell stared to lessen. Called Vizio to report--they took the info but I am out of warranty with Vizio--called BJ's as I have an extended warranty. They informed me that some one from Roth's Electronics would come to the house on Friday, December 28th between noon and 5pm. On December 27th someone called from Roths  to cancel. Spoke with the service manager--he stated that he knows exactly what is wrong and if I give him the serial and model numbers he will order the parts, I did that. I told him I was not comfortable with a set in my house that had fire damage. He said that it is impossible for a TV to catch fire. It appear that I am just a stupid old lady and I should be thankful that he knows so much without seeing the TV.  There is a melted spot on the back of the TV. I am also lucky that the service manage will call when parts arrive. It appears that I have no choice but to keep a TV that has caught fire or just toss it and call it a life lesson.
Serial Number LAQKHFA1401376
Model Number E47OVL
Purchased 5/6/11 from BJ's Wholesale

1/2/13--received a call from Roth's electronics--they will come on the 7th or 8th to install a new power something--not sure what. I checked out Roth's and cannot find where they have registered with the State of Florida, of course, they can always be using another name. I guess there is nothing I can do except accept the fact that we threw away over $600 on a TV. Vizio isn't interested--BJ's is definitely not interested. It seems that fire and smoke in a TV means nothing to anyone but me.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant fire risk, with smoke and flames coming from the TV.

incident_description:
My laptop Acer Aspire 6740-6491,  Shut down on its own while a child was using it on a hard table with adult supervision doing his homework.  When they picked it up,  they received a burn on their thumb bad enough to blister from the battery.  I do not see any recall notices on this make and model.  It is a few years old and out of warranty, I get that, but that does not make it alright to physically burn a consumer.  The battery is the original battery,  works fine and  holds a charge that lasts a couple of hours.  The system does not overheat and the battery does not get hot when you are using battery power only.  The problem seems to be when the unit is plugged in.  It was not a one time event.  It happens all of the time now.  The power cord sometimes gets hot, but not always.   The power cord gets hot enough that it is uncomfortable to hold but it does not cause burns.  It takes about 20 mins of electrical power for the battery to get to the burning point.  It does not seem to get hot if the unit is powered down  and but left to charge the battery.   So it is either the battery or the powercord, but I am thinking it is the battery.

I tried calling the toll free number for Acer multiple times but could not get past their automated phone system to report it.  [REDACTED] I am very disappointed in this company, who is not responsible enough to take consumer hazard calls regardless of warranty dates.  That makes Acer all the more at fault.     Had someone talked to me I would have been happy to accept a replacement battery and to send the current battery back so the issue could be researched and verified with appropiate recall notices issued.     I tried and email address that I found on a 3rd party recall site, and they replied back telling me to use there automated system.  Real bad.
justification: The incident resulted in a burn severe enough to blister, and the issue has occurred multiple times, indicating a high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
The caller stated that after the machine was installed there was a continuos odor emitting from the unit.  He stated that it smelled like (toner plastic melted to the paper).  He had contacted the dealer and they have replaced filters but this did not solve the problem.  He feels that the machine might be a health hazard in emitting chemicals that is being inhaled.

(10/24/12) The dealer was contacted and he advised them that he would file a report with the agency.

Statement of Facts
When this machine prints or copies to paper, fumes are emitted.  This is evidenced by the strong odor produced.  The process taking place is the heating of tiny bits of plastic to the point they melt on to the paper.

These fumes build up immediately with use, and expand over the course of the day.  We have installed an [REDACTED] air purifier that stands next to the machine.  We have also just installed an exhaust fan directly over the machine.  The air purifier provides no relief.  The exhaust fan provides a little assistance, but does not solve the problem.  One worker, a male and owner of the CPA firm, works in the room next to the machine.  He gets headaches, sinusitis, and ill feelings of malaise and discomfort from the fumes.  In fact, after a couple ofhours, there is even a distinct taste in his mouth from the fumes in the air.

Since the machine has been installed, there have been 3 female employees working in the same room as the Kyocera 5500i.  All 3 have complained about their eyes burning when the machine runs.  Their eyes all tum red, and one woman's  eyes have swelled up.

We have complained to the dealer, Advanced Business Systems, which sold and services the machine.  Several times the dealer sent in technicians to check the specifications.  The technicians couldn't  solve the problem so they brought in the manufacturer's own technician.  This technician could not remedy the problem so the manufacturer designed and installed two additional filters for the machine.  Neither filter offers any relief for the discomfort of the employees and the destruction of air quality in the office.

At this point the manufacturer says there is nothing more it can do.  We have asked for specifications of what chemicals are released when the toner is heated and melted to the paper, but the manufacturer has not provided this.  They contend that the product had to pass a test before it could even be imported to the United States.  Our fear is that the model has changed the chemistry of the toner and this particular toner has not been subjected to the rigorous tests required.

Further, our concern is that this dealer, Advanced Business Systems, has over 60 installations of these machines now in our area.  The fumes produced are noxious and hazardous to one's  health.  Particularly, since plastic is made from petroleum, we request the proper tests be done that show what chemicals and/or dioxins are being released and whether or not they are carcinogenic, let alone harmful to asthmatics and other people's lungs and bodily systems over a period oftime.
justification: Multiple employees experiencing symptoms such as headaches, eye irritation, and a distinct taste in their mouth from the fumes, indicating a high likelihood of injury.

incident_description:
I purchased a [REDACTED] seahorse about 3 weeks ago from Amazon.com.  A couple months before that I purchased Sanyo Eneloop Rechargeable Batteries from Amazon.com as well.  The seahorse worked fine for 2 weeks, but then started to lose its power so I replaced the batteries with the Sanyo ones.  I took my son to the bath and when we returned about 10 minutes later I went to put it in his crib and it burned my hand.  I turned it over and the battery area had melted some of the plastic, released battery fumes, and caused extreme heat.  The toy began smoking as well.  This is a baby toy that is supposed to assist in falling asleep! I am assuming it is the battery's fault, but the glow seahrose did lose power very soon after it was purchased.  If I had not held the toy before putting it in his crib, my infant son would have been burnt and exposed to toxic fumes and could have potentially gotten battery acid on his face.  The batteries that were put in were brand new and had never been used before.

I would really like someone to take a look at this toy and figure out the cause because it would be devastating if this happens to a child or anyone else for that matter. I have not contacted either company because I know they would want me to ship the items back and would probably offer a replacement, which is really not what I want.  

I appreciate your help.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (burn) and could have exposed the infant to toxic fumes, making it severe despite no lasting harm.

incident_description: I purchased a Stanley "relocatable power tap" (3' power strip with 9 outlets) a week ago at Fry's in Portland, OR.   I plugged it in this afternoon and when I switched it on, it failed with a loud "pop" (almost an explosion) and visible flash.   The GFI protecting that circuit tripped and prevented further damage.  When I removed the back plate from the unit, the circuit board under the switch was visibly blacked and melted.

incident_description: We had upgraded our iPhones last year, and gave our old iPhone 3gs to our children.  It has been working fine, until we found it this morning.  We were charging it overnight, and when we went to get it, we noticed that the screen had popped out, and the case was broken.  The battery had expanded considerably, and destroyed the case.  I went online to check for other incidents, and I found many descriptions of this problem at apple.com forums and http://www.howardforums.com/showthread.php/1742082-iPhone-3GS-Battery-Expanded-and-Pushed-Out-Front-Glass among others.  Our phone is out of warranty, so I doubt that Apple will do anything to help us, but there was no warning of this happening.  It doesn't seem fair that a product would essentially self-destruct, even if it is to avoid the possibility of injury.

incident_description:
I had placed my 32GB IPhone 3gs in a drawer for about two months without use. I decided to use it again and decided to charge the phone. I noticed the charge on the phone was not holding very well. After about a week of charging everyday, while the phone was disconnected, I noticed the screen had separated from the case and was pushed up. In addition, the body of the phone was bulging and warped.  The phone no longer powers on. 


A simple [REDACTED] search confirmed what I suspected, the battery had exploded inside pushing causing tremendous pressure against the case and screen of the phone. This is very dangerous as the item could have ignited and burned my house down. There was no signs or warning of defect. 

There is a thread about this on the apple site:

https://discussions.apple.com/thread/3718734?start=0&tstart=0

Here is another thread:
http://www.philmug.ph/forum/f126/bloated-3gs-battery-exploded-iphone-3gs-83799/

A general [REDACTED] search for 3gs battery explosion will return several results. This product has serious defects that can cause injury. It needs to be recalled by apple.
justification: The battery explosion caused physical damage to the phone, and could have potentially led to a house fire, posing a significant risk of injury.

incident_description:
For four and a half years I have had a small Staples Mailmate M3 paper shredder next to my desk. The chad falls into a pull-out plastic drawer which holds maybe a gallon or two of volume. The main power switch is on the back, but then a round button on top must be pushed to activate the motor. For the last several months that button switch has been temperamental, sometimes working on the first try, sometimes requiring several hard pushes before it wakes up.

Late on the morning of October 1 I shredded a dozen or so pages, and the switch was acting up. I put in another few pages, pushed the button, and--BOOM! A blast, a flash of fire, I and my desk chair rolled back, and I sat stunned, trying to collect myself. An acrid smell filled the air and my lungs, but there was no more flame. My eyes were apparently unaffected--maybe I blinked fast enough. After a few moments I managed to get up and unplug the unit, noting to my surprise that neither the power strip nor the circuit breaker had been tripped, though a whisper of smoke continued to rise from the machine.

[REDACTED].

ADDED FACT:  The Staples representative just asked whether the unit had been cleaned with canned air.  The answer is, yes, sort-of: sometime shortly before the explosion, in an effort to remove dust which might have collected in and interfered with the button switch, an apparently futile attempt was made to force canned air into the very narrow crack around the perimeter of the button on the top of the unit (but it was not blown into the cutting blades or otherwise inside the machine).  I now see a warning on the can not to use it on shredders.  It is conceivable that the switch ignited the canned air vapors rather than or before the airborne dust.
justification: The incident resulted in an injury (shock and potential lung irritation) and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the repeated issues with the switch and the use of canned air, which is now known to be a risk factor.

incident_description: This incident occurred near the end of August or beginning of September 2010.  My laptop was plugged in and charging on an end table - nothing else on it was on the table and the laptop was off.  I was at a friend's house and fell asleep on her couch after working on some items on my agenda.  At some point, the unit malfunctioned and caught on fire.  I was the only one in the room, there were no pets, no liquids, etc. around the laptop or the table and there was no sign of external catalysts as being the sign of the cause.  Thankfully, my friend and her roommate heading out to grab a bite when they noticed the flames coming from my laptop.  They yelled waking me up - and me walking up to flames less than two feet from my body.  Thankfully there was no injury, but the likelihood of injury was great had I not been awoken.  Again, there were no external causes for the fire; the unit was plugged into a surge protector, free of any likely causes of danger, and it was still under the 3 year warranty afforded to business class notebooks.  Prior to the incident, the unit had malfunctioned (stopped turning on if I recall correctly) and an on site repair was scheduled for the next day (the day following this incident).  Obviously the repair was unable to occur and ever since this, there has yet to be a resolution to this issue.  Subsequent to this, HP failed to take timely measures to rectify the problem and failed to even assess the situation.  No attempt was made to retrieve the unit and no direction was given when requested regarding the unit by HP.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the laptop catching fire while in use and near the sleeper posed a high risk of injury.

incident_description:
8/2/2012) The consumer stated that she plugged in her clock/radio for the first time. After having it in for approximately 2 weeks, she noticed that she would become very nauseous, migraine headaches, eye throbbing, etc. The consumer also started to smell an odor in her room as if something was burning. She immediately unplugged the unit. Her symptoms seemed to have dissipated after she had done this. 

The consumer stated that she had done research on the Internet for clock/radio and radiation symptoms.  The information given was the same symptoms that she was experiencing.

 The consumer had not contacted the manufacturer.

Note: The consumer did not receive medical attention.
justification: Symptoms were non-life-threatening and ceased after unplugging the device, indicating a possible but not certain occurrence.

incident_description:

The consumer stated that the power cord area and the power cord have melted.

Eventually the set went off and stayed off. The consumer stated that he called Samsung and a technician was dispatched. The technician replaced a part (the consumer is not sure what part). 

The consumer stated that Samsung was called in reference to the incident that happened on 08/03. Their response was that someone would call back in a few days. He was given a work order #[REDACTED]. We unplugged the charger, put out as much of the blaze as possible.  I took the laptop outside, still on fire. I was never notified of this recall and on day of purchase I was told it was a very good laptop. I feel this could of ended in a very bad situation if I left it unattended.

incident_description:
We bought from Target in Virginia Beach, VA a 46 in Westinghouse TV Model # VR-4625 at last years (2011) Black Friday Sale.

I turned on the TV and noticed the picture was gone, showing only colored lines.  I called Apex and was told that it is no longer under warranty. incident_description: Sony DVD Rechargeable Battery Model Number NP-FX110 over-heated.  Inside the battery case, one of the two [REDACTED] 3.7V Lithium Ion Battery Cells Model Number 5548135 swelled without bursting the protective metal jacket that protects the lithium ion batteries from the air.  However, the swelling was great enough to burst the exterior, plastic, protective-case of the NP-FX110.  Fortunately, the lithium-ion battery did not burst when my children tried to squish the battery case back together.  Had the lithium-ion battery burst when squished, it may have caused a fire.

The consumer stated that the manufacturer would not acknowledge that the notebook gets too hot. incident_description: I have a sony vaio laptop computer model VPCF115FM. Sony issued a recall on this computer due to a potential burn hazard. Sony states that by downloading a BIOS update, it will fix the problem. My computer will not accept the BIOS update as it says that my BIOS is up to date. My computer has over heated and shut down over 10 times. the computer gets so hot that you cannot touch the left hand side of the keyboard and you cannot put it on your lap as it will burn you. I have called sony and was told that i needed to send my computer to them, however, since my warranty is expired it will cost me 200-300 dollars to fix the computer. I want to fix the computer as this would be cheaper than buying a brand new one, however, I dont understand why I have to pay to have a recalled item fixed. If they know there is a problem with this series of computers and their fix did not fix my item, I would think they should be responsible for the computer. Anytime in the past that i have dealt with a recall, you take the product to the manufactured and they fix the problem free of charge, warranty or not. I will be happy to pay shipping to ship the computer back to sony but i just dont understand why i have to pay several hundreds of dollars to have it fixed when it was recalled by them in the first place and their supposed BIOS fix did not fix this model.
justification: The laptop's overheating, causing potential burns, poses a significant risk of injury.

Apple folks gave me a new battery and took away the old battery. I got a call from you folks and the lady told me I should not have given the bursted battery to Apple.

This morning I came to use the mouse and found it was very hot to the touch and took extra effort to get it out of the cradle. I looked at the underside of the mouse and it was melted. I searched the web some and found quite a few other reports of this same issue. I haven't opened it up. The battery compartment seems to have melted around the batteries. The plastic is deformed from melting.

I'll let you decide how big of an issue this is, just thought I should report it as it's likely a fire hazard.

Faulty touchpad.

Contacting Sony about this issue hasnt sovled the problem and they dont seem eager to admit there is a problem. I paid over $1500.00 for a product that is a lemon and defective.

I found the DVD player and it had heated, melted, burned the couch cover, begun to burn a significant hole in the seat cushion itself.  I dont know the source or cause but the place where the battery is stored is completely burned.

incident_description: I purchased a Sony 50" TV model #KF50WE610 from "The Good Guys" in Santa Clarita, CA in July of 2004. I had the TV serviced through the extended service plan in July 2009 by SoCal Tech, Inc (818) 505-8500. They determined that the motherboard was damaged as well as the LAMP and both were replaced under extended service plan warranty. Fast forward to September 2012, the TV stop functioning and needs service again. Upon removing the front trim cover, I noticed that the lamp cover was burnt, melted and deformed. After removing the lamp, I also saw that the internal housing was also cracked, melted and separating from the intense heat. I registered my TV when I purchased it and I should have been notified of these safety recalls. Had I've been notified, I would have taken the necessary step to fix the TV in order to avoid extra damages.  I enjoy using my TV and just want it fix under the extended warranty recalls that that were issued but not notified of. Thank you in advance for taking the time to read this.
justification: The TV's internal components were damaged due to heat, posing a potential fire hazard, but no injuries were reported.

She says there is no reason for it to happen.  No spillage or mishandling of the product.  A technician friend of hers took it apart and said it is the screen causing the problem.  He turned it back on and the unit started getting hot again.
